findings.title: The swap loop pays for every bitmap word and every initialized tick on its way, and a HyperEVM small block holds 3,000,000 gas
findings.difference: HyperEVM produces small blocks with a 3,000,000 gas limit every second and big blocks with a 30,000,000 gas limit about once a minute. A sender reaches big blocks only after setting the usingBigBlocks flag on its HyperCore account. I sampled blocks 51958402 to 51958471 through the public RPC: 69 had gasLimit 3,000,000 and one (51958443) had 30,000,000. For comparison, state/networks.json records an Ethereum block gas limit of 59,999,943, and EIP-7825 specifies a cap of 16,777,216 gas per transaction. I did not confirm in this session that the cap is active on Ethereum.
findings.mechanism: Pool.swap runs one loop iteration per step (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437). Each iteration reads one tick bitmap word from storage (Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:85-121), computes the price of the next tick and runs one swap step. When the step ends on an initialized tick, crossTick reads the tick slot and reads and rewrites both fee growth slots of that tick (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). The repository gas snapshots give 2,242 to 2,287 gas for the bitmap search, which includes the cold storage read, and 919 to 1,565 gas for a swap step with liquidity. I use 2,242 gas as the floor for one iteration and leave out the swap step, TickMath and loop bookkeeping. A crossing adds one cold read (2,100) and two read and write pairs. Each pair costs 5,000 gas when the slot changes from one nonzero value to another and 22,100 gas when it is written for the first time. That gives about 14,342 gas per crossing when both fee growth slots change, and about 48,542 when both are written for the first time. With the repository figure of 123,144 gas for a simple swap as fixed cost, a 3,000,000 gas transaction fits at most about 200 crossings, about 59 when the fee growth slots are written for the first time, and about 1,283 empty bitmap words. The real numbers are lower, because the floor leaves out the computation. I did not measure gas on HyperEVM. Three things an ordinary account controls raise the iteration count of other people's swaps. First, modifyLiquidity lets anyone add a position of one liquidity unit on any aligned tick pair of a pool without a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, Pool.sol:159-181). In my transcription of the source, 200 such positions on [t, t+1) below the price of a pool with tick spacing 1 made every tick initialized, each cost 1 base unit of one currency, and a swap that moved the price by 100, 200 and 400 ticks ran 101, 201 and 401 iterations, each with a crossing. Second, a step with zero liquidity in range consumes nothing and moves the price to the next word boundary (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75), so a swap that runs past the last position toward its price limit visits every word on the way. From tick 0 to the lower limit that is 3,468 iterations at tick spacing 1, 349 at spacing 10, 60 at spacing 60 and 20 at spacing 200, which is at least 7,775,256 gas at spacing 1 from the bitmap reads alone. Third, initialize has no access control and accepts any price from MIN_SQRT_PRICE up to one unit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (PoolManager.sol:117-142, Pool.sol:100-107), so a third party can create a pool id at an extreme price before anyone else uses it. The gap to the market price then has to be walked with swaps that take no tokens and still pay for every word.
findings.impact: No funds leave the PoolManager and no position is frozen. Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (Pool.sol:146-238), so removals fit in a small block in every case I looked at. The cost falls on swappers and arbitrageurs in pools with tick spacing 1 or other small spacings. In a pool where every tick carries a dust position, one small block transaction can move the price by at most about 59 to 200 ticks, which is 0.6 to 2.0 percent at spacing 1. A larger move needs several transactions with nearer price limits, or a big block. A swap that names the extreme price limit and exceeds the liquidity on its side runs out of gas in a small block where it would otherwise end with a partial fill. A contract that must complete one large swap in one transaction, for example a liquidation, can stall until it is sent to a big block. The dust positions cost the attacker about 161,276 gas each by the repository snapshot for a simple add, plus one base unit, and stay until the attacker removes them.
findings.preconditions: The pool has a small tick spacing, since at spacing 60 a move of 59 crossings is already more than 40 percent. The attacker pays gas for each dust position. The victim sends the swap to a small block, or the swap sits inside a contract that cannot split it. Any account can undo the third case by walking the price in several transactions.
findings.mitigations: Routers and keepers on HyperEVM can pass a price limit close to the expected end price and split large swaps. Contracts that depend on one atomic swap can use pools with a wider tick spacing or send the transaction to a big block. Pool creators can initialize the pool ids they intend to use at the market price before announcing them. Liquidity providers do not need to act, because removal does not loop.

sources.supports: Fast blocks last 1 second with a 3M gas limit and slow blocks last 1 minute with a 30M gas limit. A sender is directed to big blocks by the HyperCore action evmUserModify with usingBigBlocks true.
69 of the 70 sampled blocks report gasLimit 3,000,000 and block 51958443 reports 30,000,000.
The HyperEVM uses the Cancun hardfork without blobs. That the gas schedule equals Ethereum's Cancun schedule is my inference from this sentence.
COLD_SLOAD_COST is 2100 and SSTORE_RESET_GAS becomes 5000 minus COLD_SLOAD_COST, which is 2900.
SSTORE_SET_GAS is 20000.
The cap of 16,777,216 gas per transaction that I quote for Ethereum as comparison.
nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord costs 2,242 to 2,287 gas in the repository snapshots.
computeSwapStep costs 919 to 1,565 gas in the repository snapshots.
A simple add of liquidity costs 161,276 gas and a simple swap 123,144 gas through the test routers.
One loop iteration per bitmap word or initialized tick, with the tick crossing at lines 413 to 428.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the Hyperliquid page on the dual block architecture. It states a fast block duration of 1 second with a 3M gas limit and a slow block duration of 1 minute with a 30M gas limit, and that a sender is moved to big blocks by the HyperCore action evmUserModify with usingBigBlocks true. I queried eth_getBlockByNumber on https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm for blocks 51958402 to 51958471 myself: 69 blocks report gasLimit 3,000,000 and block 51958443 reports 30,000,000, as the finding says. The largest gasUsed in the sample was 1,860,095. The HyperEVM page states that the chain uses the Cancun hardfork without blobs. I tested the gas schedule for storage reads instead of inferring it: eth_estimateGas for PoolManager.extsload(startSlot, nSlots) with 1, 2, 51 and 101 empty slots returned 24,293, 26,473, 133,821 and 244,561 on HyperEVM and the same four numbers on Ethereum, which is about 2,200 gas per extra cold slot on both. The cold read cost of 2,100 that the estimate rests on therefore holds on HyperEVM. I fetched EIP-2929 (COLD_SLOAD_COST, SSTORE_RESET_GAS equal to 5000 minus COLD_SLOAD_COST), EIP-2200 (SSTORE_SET_GAS 20000, SSTORE_RESET_GAS 5000) and EIP-3529 (refund cap of one fifth of gas used). I did not measure SSTORE cost on HyperEVM, so the write costs rest on the Cancun statement in the docs. I fetched EIP-7825 and EIP-7607: the 16,777,216 gas cap per transaction is part of Fusaka, which activated on Ethereum mainnet on 2025-12-03, so the comparison value is in force. The repository snapshots hold the numbers the finding quotes (snapshots/TickBitmapTest.json:5-10, snapshots/SwapMathTest.json:2-9, snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json:12 and 16). I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. Not confirmed: the gas of one loop iteration of the deployed bytecode on HyperEVM was not measured by the researcher or by me. The public endpoint limits eth_getLogs to 1,000 blocks and rate limits, so I could not list pools to quote against.
verification.codeCheck: I read the swap path and wrote my own transcription of BitMath, FullMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap and Pool from the source text. Pool.swap runs one loop pass per call to nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-348), and that call reads one bitmap word from storage (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:98 and 111). A pass that ends on an initialized tick calls crossTick, which reads and rewrites feeGrowthOutside0X128 and feeGrowthOutside1X128 and reads the slot that holds liquidityNet (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). No guard bounds the number of passes other than the amount and the price limit (Pool.sol:344). With liquidity 0 a step consumes nothing and ends on its target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75), so a swap toward a far limit visits every word. modifyLiquidity has no access check for a pool without a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184) and Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (Pool.sol:146-238), so removals are not affected. initialize accepts any price that getTickAtSqrtPrice accepts (PoolManager.sol:117-142, Pool.sol:100-107, src/libraries/TickMath.sol:121-129). In my transcription 200 positions of liquidity 1 on [t, t+1) for t from -200 to -1 in a spacing 1 pool cost 200 base units of currency1 in total, and a swap that moved the price by 100 and 200 ticks ran 101 and 201 passes. An empty pool walked from tick 0 to the lower limit ran 3,467 passes at spacing 1, 348 at spacing 10, 59 at spacing 60 and 19 at spacing 200, and returned the delta (0, 0). The arithmetic of the bounds is right: (3,000,000 - 123,144) / 14,342 is 200, / 48,542 is 59 and / 2,242 is 1,283. At 2,100 gas per cold read alone the spacing 1 walk needs more than 7,280,000 gas, which is above a small block. Actor check: every step is open to an ordinary account, the affected pools need no hook and no attacker token, and the victims only swap. The actor value unprivileged is right. Severity check: no funds leave and no position is locked, a swap can be split or sent to a big block, so low is right and the effect degrade is right.
verification.corrections: The finding says it did not confirm that the EIP-7825 cap is active on Ethereum. It is active since Fusaka on 2025-12-03. The run with 200 dust positions cannot give 401 passes for a 400 tick move: my transcription gives 203 passes (201 crossings of the ticks from 0 down to -200 and two further passes to the word end and to the limit), and 401 passes need about 400 dusted ticks. My pass counts for the empty walk are one lower than the finding's (3,467, 348, 59 and 19), which changes the bitmap floor to 7,773,014 gas and changes no conclusion. The 48,542 gas case needs both fee growth outside slots of a tick to go from zero to nonzero. That happens for a tick above the current price when it is crossed upward for the first time while both global fee growth values are nonzero (Pool.sol:533-539, 608-609). Dust placed below the price starts with both slots equal to the global values, so those crossings fall in the 14,342 gas case or lower. The attacker can bring a tick back to the first time state by removing and adding the dust position again. Refunds for slots set to zero are paid after execution and do not lower the gas limit a swap needs. The evidence grade can move from inferred to primary for the block limits and the cold read cost. The per pass total on HyperEVM stays an upper bound on the number of crossings until someone measures it.

findings.title: One transaction can use the whole per-block budget for new state on MegaETH, and the node skips every later candidate of that block
findings.difference: MegaETH counts new accounts and new storage slots per transaction and per block, and both limits are 1,000 entries. Ethereum has no such counter. The block limiter admits the transaction that brings the block counter to the limit and then rejects every further candidate before execution, whatever that candidate would do. The base fee has stayed at its floor of 1,000,000 wei in every block sampled.
findings.mechanism: A sender submits one transaction that creates 1,000 new state entries, for example a contract creation that writes 999 fresh storage slots. eth_estimateGas accepts that creation at 22,559,525 gas, which at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei is about 0.0000226 ETH, and rejects a creation with 1,000 slots. Storage gas is zero for slots in buckets of minimum size, so the cost is the compute gas of the writes. After this transaction the block counter for state growth equals the block limit. BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check then returns StateGrowthLimit for every later candidate of that block, including a liquidity removal or a take that creates no new state. Those candidates are skipped and can enter a later block. A sender who repeats this in every one second block spends about 1.95 ETH per day. Calls to modifyLiquidity and take on the PoolManager have no path that avoids the block limiter. What the sender achieves depends on where its transaction lands inside each block. Candidates placed before it are included. The ordering rule of the sequencer was not confirmed, so the share of each block that the sender can close was not established.
findings.impact: Removals, swaps and claims on the PoolManager can be delayed block by block while the sender keeps paying. No balance moves and no position changes. The delay ends when the sender stops or when users' transactions are ordered ahead of the sender's.
findings.preconditions: The base fee stays near its floor, and the sender's transaction is ordered early in each block. No role is needed. A full stop of withdrawals would need the sender to be first in every block, which the public record does not show to be possible.
findings.mitigations: Core has no setting for this. Users can resubmit, pay a higher priority fee if the sequencer orders by fee, or use the L1 deposit path, whose transactions are placed at the start of a block in the OP Stack design. That placement was not confirmed in the MegaETH node source. The chain operator can raise the block limit above the transaction limit or price new state entries in minimum-size buckets.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the four cited sources and reran the chain queries on 2026-11-22. constants.rs sets rex::TX_STATE_GROWTH_LIMIT and rex::BLOCK_STATE_GROWTH_LIMIT to 1000 (lines 206 and 211). limit.rs builds the block limits for Rex through Rex6 with block_state_growth_limit taken from that constant (lines 381 to 399). BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check returns MegaBlockLimitExceededError::StateGrowthLimit for a candidate when block_state_growth_used is at or above the limit (lines 880 to 890), and the is_deposit flag gates only the two data availability tests (lines 821 to 845). post_execution_update_raw adds the usage of an executed transaction without a test, and its comment says the last transaction is allowed to exceed the limit (lines 895 to 943). The specification page states that the first transaction that brings the block to the limit must be included and that later candidates must be skipped before execution. The Rex upgrade page lists state growth of 1,000 per transaction and per block as a new limit. gas.rs computes the storage gas of a new slot as 20,000 times (multiplier minus 1), which is zero at multiplier 1 (lines 49 to 51). On chain, eth_estimateGas for a contract creation that writes n new slots returned 120,922 gas for n = 1, 22,559,391 gas for n = 999 and 'execution reverted' for n = 1,000 and n = 1,001, so the transaction limit of 1,000 entries with the new account counted as one is live on mainnet. The latest block and blocks 10,000,000, 20,000,000, 25,000,000, 30,000,000 and 32,000,000 report a base fee of 1,000,000 wei, and eth_feeHistory over the last 100 blocks shows the same base fee and a median priority fee of zero. At that price 22.56 million gas is 0.0000226 ETH, and 86,400 such transactions cost about 1.95 ETH. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. Two links stay unconfirmed. I did not observe a mainnet block that was closed in this way, so the behaviour of the live sequencer rests on the reference implementation and the specification. The ordering rule of the sequencer is not documented in the pages I read. A podcast transcript with the MegaETH founders says the team rejects tip auctions per block, which is a secondary source.
verification.codeCheck: The finding needs nothing from the PoolManager code beyond the fact that its calls are ordinary transactions. modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184) and take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) require the unlocked flag, which exists only inside a call to unlock made in the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, src/libraries/Lock.sol:11-27). No function in src/ reads a block field or offers a path that a third party could execute for a user after a delay, so a withdrawal that is skipped for one block has to be included in a later block as a whole transaction. No state of a pool changes while the transaction waits, apart from what other included transactions do to the pool price. I found no guard in src/ that bears on this, and none is possible at contract level.
verification.corrections: The gas figure differs slightly with my own init code (22,559,391 against 22,559,525), which does not change the cost. The specification says later candidates are skipped when they depend on the exhausted resource, while the reference limiter skips every candidate. The finding follows the limiter, and that is the stricter reading. The precondition is stated too narrowly. The finding says a full stop needs the sender to be first in every block. If the sequencer serves pending transactions in arrival order, a run of N such transactions submitted together from several accounts would close N consecutive blocks for every transaction that arrives after the run, at 0.0000226 ETH per block. If the sequencer orders by priority fee, the same run with a priority fee of 1 wei outranks the current traffic, whose median priority fee is zero, until users pay more. This extension follows from the limiter logic and was not observed on chain. The severity stays low for the confirmed part, which is a delay inside one block. It would be medium under the scale if the multi-block case is confirmed, because liquidity operations would be blocked without loss for as long as the sender pays. The operator of the single sequencer can exclude such transactions, so the stall would last until the operator reacts.

findings.title: A HyperCore transfer makes the node call a linked contract with 200,000 gas ahead of every signed transaction in the block
findings.difference: HyperCore credits a spot transfer to the EVM through a system transaction that calls transfer(recipient, amount) on the contract linked to the token, with the token's system address as sender, gas price 0 and 200,000 gas. The docs state that the linked contract may have arbitrary bytecode and give no guarantee about what its transfer function does. Deploying and linking a spot token is open to anyone; the deploy auction stood at 500 on 2026-11-22. System transactions are placed before all signed transactions of the block and their gas does not count toward the block gas limit. On Ethereum only the block builder decides which code runs first.
findings.mechanism: An account deploys a spot token on HyperCore, links it to a contract it wrote and sends the token to the token's system address. The node then calls that contract's transfer function at the top of an EVM block, before any signed transaction. Inside the call the contract is an ordinary caller of the PoolManager. It can call unlock, which calls unlockCallback on it (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), swap, and settle with tokens or ERC-6909 claims it holds (src/PoolManager.sol:187-227 and 322-336). The PoolManager gives the system address and the linked contract no role, and transient state is cleared after the system transaction like after any other, so nothing carries into the signed transactions. What the account gains is position: it reaches every pool before transactions that paid a priority fee, for the price of one HyperCore action. That is the first leg of a sandwich, or first place for arbitrage after a price move. A swapper loses at most what the price limit and slippage setting of the swap allow. Reserves, positions and claims of other users are not reachable this way.
findings.impact: Swappers in any pool can be traded against from the first position of a block by an account without validator rights. The loss per swap is bounded by the swapper's own limits. LP principal and claims are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: The attacker deploys and links one spot token. The pool action must fit in 200,000 gas; I did not measure a complete swap against that limit. I did not confirm how HyperCore orders several system transactions inside one block, which EVM block follows a given HyperCore action, or whether pending EVM transactions are visible to the attacker in time.
findings.mitigations: Swappers and routers should set tight price limits. Routers should not treat a quote from one block as valid at the top of the next. Pools that need protection from first position trading have to add it in a hook.

On chain I read eth_getSystemTxsByBlockNumber for 40 blocks ending at 51,966,640. Four system transactions came from 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000157 and called transfer on the linked contract 0x33af3c2540ba72054e044efe504867b39ae421f5 with 200,000 gas and gas price 0. In block 51,966,623, which holds two system transactions, the first signed transaction has cumulativeGasUsed equal to its own gasUsed (325,780), so the system transactions are not counted. The public RPC returns no receipt for a system transaction hash, so the statement that they execute before the signed transactions rests on the block layout in the archive client and its README. spotDeployState returns a gas auction with startGas 500.0, endGas 500.0 and currentGas null; the finding quotes currentGas 500.0. The dual block page states that the HyperEVM mempool is onchain state of the L1, which is relevant to whether pending transactions can be seen. I found no source that contradicts the finding.
verification.codeCheck: unlock is open to any caller and calls unlockCallback on msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). swap, modifyLiquidity, take, settle, mint and burn check only the unlock flag (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99, 187-227, 291-336). No line in src outside src/test reads tx.origin or compares msg.sender with a fixed address other than the hook self call test (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175) and the owner and controller tests (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29 and 36 and 48). A linked contract that runs inside a system transaction is therefore an ordinary caller. It must leave every delta at zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so it pays for what it takes. The pinned revm fork clears transient storage in commit_tx, so the unlock flag, deltas and synced currency do not carry into the first signed transaction. The effect is position in the block and nothing else: reserves, positions and claims of other users are not reachable through this path.
verification.corrections: The finding's own open points stay open: I did not measure whether an unlock with a swap and settlement in claims fits in 200,000 gas, and I did not confirm the order of several system transactions or how early a HyperCore action must be sent to land ahead of a given signed transaction. One addition: the exchange API documents a sendToEvmWithData action that calls coreReceiveWithData on the linked contract with a gasLimit and a data field chosen by the sender, so the 200,000 gas figure may not bound what a linked contract can do at the top of a block. The auction field that reads 500.0 is startGas and endGas. This is an ordering hazard for swappers within their own price limits and is no path to funds held for other users.

findings.title: A native payout sent to a withdrawal predeploy, a fee vault, an EntryPoint or a Celo core contract is lost to the caller on Celo and X Layer
findings.difference: Both chains have contracts that accept a plain native transfer and book it to msg.sender or keep it. On Celo these are L2ToL1MessagePasser (0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016), the fee vaults at 0x11, 0x19, 0x1a and 0x1b, the L1BlockNumber predeploy at 0x13, the wrapped native predeploy at 0x06, the three ERC-4337 EntryPoints, and the Celo core contracts FeeHandler, MentoFeeHandlerSeller, UniswapFeeHandlerSeller, Reserve and Governance. On X Layer the fee vaults, 0x13, both Wrapped OKB contracts and the EntryPoints accept value. The X Layer L2ToL1MessagePasser refuses value because the chain runs in custom gas token mode.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(address(0), to, amount) debits the caller by amount and makes the PoolManager send amount of the native asset to the recipient with empty calldata (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). The recipient sees the PoolManager as msg.sender. 2. On Celo, L2ToL1MessagePasser.receive() calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data). The CELO leaves the L2 and the withdrawal names the PoolManager address as L1 target. That address has no code and no balance on Ethereum. 3. An EntryPoint books the amount as a deposit of the PoolManager. The PoolManager cannot call withdrawTo, and the EntryPoint spends a deposit only after the account answers a validation call that src/ does not implement. 4. A fee vault, the Reserve, the FeeHandler contracts and Governance keep the amount as their own balance. 5. The wrapped native contracts mint wrapped tokens to the PoolManager address. A caller who syncs the wrapper first and settles afterwards is credited that amount under the wrapper's currency id, which is an ordinary wrap at one to one. 6. In every case the caller still owes amount in currency address(0) and must pay it before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are unchanged in total. 7. A caller who syncs an EntryPoint, takes native value to it and settles is credited amount under the EntryPoint's currency id, because the EntryPoint's balanceOf is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). The EntryPoint has no transfer function, so that credit can never be taken (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86).
findings.impact: The loss is the amount of one payout and falls on the account that chose the recipient. No pool reserve, no claim of another user and no protocol fee is reduced, and an attacker gains nothing by doing this on purpose.
findings.preconditions: A user, a router or a front end passes one of these addresses as the recipient of a native take. Core gives no third party a way to choose the recipient of another account's payout. Whether the deployed routers and the PositionManager filter recipients was not read.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends can refuse the predeploy range, the EntryPoint addresses and the Celo core contract addresses as recipients of native payouts. Users who want CELO on Ethereum should take to their own account and withdraw from there.

Step 7 should add that the credit under the EntryPoint id has to be cleared or minted before unlock returns. The op-stack-eth unit recorded the same hazard for the ETH chains, and the two entries can be merged.

findings.title: A native payout sent to L2ToL1MessagePasser, an ERC-4337 EntryPoint or the L1BlockNumber predeploy is booked to the PoolManager's own address and is lost to the caller
findings.difference: OP Stack chains have a withdrawal contract, L2ToL1MessagePasser at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016, whose receive() starts a withdrawal to L1 for msg.sender and uses msg.sender as the L1 target. Ethereum has no contract with that behaviour. The legacy L1BlockNumber predeploy at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000013 accepts ETH with any calldata and has no function that pays it out. The ERC-4337 EntryPoint, which also exists on Ethereum, credits a plain ETH transfer as a deposit of msg.sender.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(address(0), to, amount) debits the caller by amount and then makes the PoolManager send amount of ETH to the recipient with empty calldata and all gas (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-52). The recipient sees the PoolManager as msg.sender. 2. If the recipient is L2ToL1MessagePasser, its receive() calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data). The ETH is taken off the L2 and a withdrawal is recorded with the PoolManager as sender and the PoolManager's address as the L1 target. The PoolManager addresses of all seven chains have no code on Ethereum. If the withdrawal is proven and finalised on L1, the ETH is delivered to that address, where nothing can move it. The value call returned success in eth_call on OP Mainnet, Base and Unichain. 3. If the recipient is an EntryPoint, receive() calls depositTo(msg.sender) and the amount becomes a deposit of the PoolManager. withdrawTo pays out only the deposit of its own caller, and the PoolManager cannot call it. The EntryPoint spends a deposit only after the account answers validateUserOp or validatePaymasterUserOp, and src/ has neither function, so the deposit cannot be spent. 4. If the recipient is L1BlockNumber, the fallback keeps the ETH and returns the L1 block number. 5. In each case the caller still owes amount in currency address(0) and must pay it with msg.value before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are unchanged in total: amount left and amount came back in. The caller has paid for a payout that reached nobody. 6. A caller who first calls sync(EntryPoint), then takes native ETH to the EntryPoint and then calls settle is credited amount under the currency id of the EntryPoint, because balanceOf(PoolManager) on the EntryPoint is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). That credit can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim and can never be paid out, because the EntryPoint has no transfer function and take reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). The native debt from step 1 remains and must still be paid in full.
findings.impact: The loss is the amount of one payout and falls on the account that chose the recipient. No pool reserve, no other user's claim and no protocol fee is reduced, and an attacker gains nothing by doing this on purpose. One sign that the L1 twin addresses do receive stray value: the Base PoolManager address holds 0.0588 ETH and no code on Ethereum. How that ETH arrived was not traced.
findings.preconditions: A user, a router or a front end passes one of these addresses as the recipient of a native take, for example in the belief that sending ETH to the message passer bridges it to the user's own L1 address. No third party can choose the recipient of someone else's payout through core. Whether the deployed Universal Router or PositionManager filter recipients was not read.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends can refuse the predeploy range 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000007ff and the EntryPoint addresses as recipients of native payouts. Users who want ETH on L1 should take to their own account and withdraw from there. Nothing in core can be configured to prevent it.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the four cited contract sources and reran the chain queries on 22 November 2026. L2ToL1MessagePasser.sol on the develop branch has RECEIVE_DEFAULT_GAS_LIMIT = 100000 at line 21 and a receive function at lines 60-62 that calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, RECEIVE_DEFAULT_GAS_LIMIT, bytes('')). initiateWithdrawal records msg.sender as sender and the first argument as target, so a payout from the PoolManager names the PoolManager address as the L1 target. StakeManager.sol at tag v0.7.0 has receive() calling depositTo(msg.sender) at lines 42-44, balanceOf returning deposits[account].deposit at lines 38-40 and withdrawTo debiting deposits[msg.sender] at lines 134-146. EntryPoint.sol at v0.7.0 lowers a sender deposit at line 504 after the validateUserOp call at line 490 and a paymaster deposit at line 535 before the validatePaymasterUserOp call at line 538, and a revert of either call ends in FailedOpWithRevert (lines 496 and 547), which undoes the debit. L1BlockNumber.sol has payable receive and fallback functions that return the L1 block number as one word and no other state changing function. On chain I used eth_call with the PoolManager code overridden by a forwarding stub, so the target saw the PoolManager as msg.sender and a separate tx.origin. On all seven chains a 0.001 ETH call with empty calldata succeeds at L2ToL1MessagePasser, at EntryPoint v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8, at L1BlockNumber and at the fee vaults, and reverts at L2StandardBridge with 'StandardBridge: function can only be called from an EOA'. On OP Mainnet and Base a Multicall3 call showed the effect: balanceOf(PoolManager) at each of the three EntryPoints went from 0 to 1000000000000000 after the value call, and messageNonce() of the message passer rose by one (0x8b67 to 0x8b68 on OP Mainnet, 0x209c2 to 0x209c3 on Base). transfer(address,uint256) from the PoolManager reverts at all three EntryPoints on all seven chains, and L1BlockNumber answers transfer and balanceOf with the L1 block number (0x193eea2 at the time), which is never 1. On Ethereum, eth_getCode is empty and the nonce is 0 at all seven PoolManager addresses, and eth_getBalance at 0x498581ff718922c3f8e6a244956af099b2652b2b is 58773641109313318 wei. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. I did not read the EntryPoint v0.6 and v0.8 sources and rely on the eth_call results for those two versions.
verification.codeCheck: take requires only the unlocked flag, debits msg.sender by amount and then transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For currency address(0) the transfer is call(gas(), to, amount, 0, 0, 0, 0) and reverts only if that call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:45-53). Nothing in that path looks at the recipient, so a recipient that accepts the value and books it to msg.sender leaves the PoolManager as the owner of the deposit or withdrawal. The debit is a negative delta of the caller under address(0). unlock reverts while any delta is open (src/PoolManager.sol:112), and a native debt can be closed only by settle with msg.value while the synced currency is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354, 364), by burning address(0) claims (332-336) or by a pool credit, so the caller pays the full amount. Step 6 also holds. sync has no lock check and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) of any address that returns 32 bytes (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). After the native payout to the EntryPoint, settle with zero value computes reservesNow - reservesBefore = amount, resets the synced currency and credits that amount under the EntryPoint id (src/PoolManager.sol:356-364). The credit can be minted as a claim (322-329). It can never be paid out, because take would call transfer on the EntryPoint, which reverts, and the transfer check then reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). I looked for a guard that the finding missed and found none that applies: the msg.value check at line 356 only blocks a native settle while an ERC-20 is synced, the int128 cast at line 294 only bounds amount below 2^127, and the delta count check is what forces the caller to pay. I also looked for a way to turn this against other users and found none in core: the recipient of a take is an argument of the caller, the hook split and fee collection never send native value to an address chosen by a third party (src/PoolManager.sol:177-183, 220-226, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and the PoolManager balance of ETH ends where it started.
verification.corrections: No change to actor or severity. The actor value unprivileged is right in the sense that no role is needed, and the reader should note that the only party who loses is the account that named the recipient, so this finding gives no path to funds of other users. Three additions. First, the value call succeeds on all seven chains, where the finding reports results for OP Mainnet, Base and Unichain only. Second, take(address(0), L2ToL1MessagePasser, 0) also succeeds, creates no debt because a zero delta is skipped (src/PoolManager.sol:369), and still makes the PoolManager start a zero value withdrawal and raise the message nonce. It carries empty data and the PoolManager address as target, which has no code on Ethereum, so it gives no authority on L1. Third, L1BlockNumber is a proxied predeploy, so the statement that no function pays the ETH out holds for the current implementation, and the chain's proxy admin could change that.

findings.title: A payout sent to an EntryPoint, a precompile address or a protocol custody address is lost to the caller on Arc and Tempo
findings.difference: Arc and Tempo carry addresses that accept a payment from the PoolManager and book it to nobody the caller controls. On Arc the three ERC-4337 EntryPoint contracts accept native USDC with empty calldata and record it as a deposit of the sender. Precompile addresses 0x01 to 0x08 and 0x100, the codeless addresses 0x12 and 0x13 and the system log emitter 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe accept value, and the USDC face accepts a transfer to the Native Coin Authority address and to its own implementation. On Tempo the FeeManager, StablecoinDEX and TIP20ChannelReserve precompile addresses hold TIP-20 balances for their own bookkeeping and accept a plain transfer without crediting an internal account.
findings.mechanism: 1. A caller inside unlock calls take(currency, to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The PoolManager debits the caller's delta by amount and then pays: for address(0) with a value call and empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52), for a token with transfer(to, amount) (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). 2. On Arc, if to is an EntryPoint, the EntryPoint credits a deposit to the PoolManager address. The PoolManager can never call withdrawTo and answers no validation call, so the deposit stays there. If to is 0x01, 0x12, the log emitter or the Native Coin Authority address, the USDC sits at an address without a spending path. 3. On Tempo, if to is 0xfeec..., 0xdec0... or 0x4d5050..., the TIP-20 balance of that precompile address rises by amount and no internal balance of any user is credited. I simulated each of the three with 1 unit of OUSD. I did not find a function that returns such a surplus and did not read the three precompiles in full. 4. In every case the caller still owes amount and must settle it before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 349-364). Pool reserves are whole: amount left and amount came back. 5. A caller who first calls sync(EntryPoint) on Arc, then takes native USDC to the EntryPoint and then calls settle is credited amount under the EntryPoint's address as currency id, because EntryPoint.balanceOf(PoolManager) is the deposit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360). An eth_call of sync(EntryPoint v0.7) on the deployed PoolManager succeeds. The EntryPoint has no transfer(address,uint256), so that credit can become an ERC-6909 claim and can never be taken.
findings.impact: The amount of each such payout is lost to the party that named the recipient. Other users, pool reserves and claims are not affected. The hazard is real for routers or scripts that let a user name any recipient, and for anyone who accepts ERC-6909 claims under the EntryPoint id.
findings.preconditions: The caller, or a router acting for the caller, must name one of these addresses as recipient. No third party can redirect someone else's payout. On Tempo the native variant does not exist because value transfers fail.
findings.mitigations: Routers and front ends on these two chains can refuse recipients in the precompile ranges, the EntryPoint addresses and the Tempo custody precompiles. Users should not accept ERC-6909 claims whose id is one of these addresses.

A self transfer of 1,000,000 units returns true and leaves the balance unchanged. verification.codeCheck: take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) debits msg.sender through _accountDelta (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378) and then calls Currency.transfer with the recipient the caller supplied. The native branch is a CALL with empty calldata and all gas (src/types/Currency.sol:45-53). The token branch accepts empty return data or a 32 byte value of 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). Neither branch looks at the recipient. The debit stays in transient storage and unlock reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:112 unless the caller settles it, so reserves are whole. sync has no lock modifier and accepts any address (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the rise of balanceOf under the synced id and rejects msg.value while an id is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). The sequence in step 5 therefore leaves the caller with a credit under the EntryPoint id and an equal debt under address(0) that must be paid. The recipient of a take is always a parameter chosen by msg.sender, and the recipient of collectProtocolFees is chosen by the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), so no third party can direct another user's payout to these addresses through core. I found no guard that the finding missed.
verification.corrections: The TIP20Factory address 0x20fc000000000000000000000000000000000000 also accepts a plain OUSD transfer from the PoolManager and its balance rises by the amount, so it belongs in the Tempo list. I tested value calls on 0x01, 0x04, 0x12, 0x100 and the log emitter and did not repeat 0x02, 0x03, 0x05 to 0x08 and 0x13. The actor value needs no change because no role is required. The only party that loses is the caller who names the recipient, or a person who accepts a claim under an EntryPoint id, so this item is no path to funds of other users.

findings.title: The USDC implementation address on Arc mirrors the PoolManager's USDC balance, so a third currency id can be credited and never paid out
findings.difference: On Arc the USDC proxy at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 delegates to NativeFiatTokenV2_2 at 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6. The implementation computes balanceOf from the account's native balance divided by 10^12, with no use of its own storage, so a direct call to the implementation returns the same figure as the proxy. Its transfer function calls the Native Coin Authority precompile, which accepts only the proxy address as caller, so a direct transfer on the implementation reverts. An ordinary ERC-20 implementation called directly reports a zero balance.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(X) accepts any address and stores X.balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). With X set to the implementation address the stored figure is the PoolManager's real USDC balance in 6 decimals, 2,445,327.82 USDC at block 32,584,426. 2. Any USDC that reaches the PoolManager while X is synced, through USDC.transfer on the proxy or through a forced native send, raises X.balanceOf. settle then credits the difference to the caller under currency id X (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). settle with msg.value reverts in that state (src/PoolManager.sol:356). 3. take(X, to, amount) calls transfer on the implementation (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The precompile rejects the call because its caller is the implementation and the take reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. 4. A positive delta in X can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim, cleared, or used as liquidity in a pool that names X as a currency (src/PoolManager.sol:310-336). None of these turns it back into USDC. 5. The same payment cannot also be credited under 0x3600 or address(0): one sync slot exists, a native credit needs that slot to be zero, and each inflow is counted in one settle. The USDC that was paid in stays in the PoolManager and backs no claim under address(0) or 0x3600.
findings.impact: USDC paid in under the implementation's id is stranded for the payer, and claims or pool positions denominated in that id can never be redeemed. Reserves of address(0) and 0x3600 pools are not reduced. The loss falls on whoever pays into that id or accepts claims in it. A proxy upgrade changes the implementation address and the behaviour of the old one.
findings.preconditions: Someone must sync the implementation address and pay USDC before settling, or accept claims or a pool in that id. An attacker cannot make another user's router sync a different currency than the one it pays.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces on Arc should list address(0) and 0x3600 as the only USDC currency ids and warn on pools or claims whose currency is 0xc6ad664ac6679f4ce74e10e91449c93ec1ae3ca6 or any later implementation address.

findings.title: A zero amount transfer of qiAVAX from the Avalanche PoolManager runs Benqi reward accounting for it, and anyone can ask Benqi to pay the accrued QI to the PoolManager
findings.difference: This is the reward bearing token case of the Ethereum finding, found on Avalanche with numbers. The PoolManager holds 2,305.6 qiAVAX, the Benqi market token for AVAX. Benqi pays suppliers in QI and in AVAX through its Comptroller, and claimReward(uint8,address) is public and pays the named holder.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every qiAVAX transfer calls Comptroller.transferAllowed, which updates and distributes supplier rewards for the sender and the recipient (Comptroller.sol lines 595 to 608). take(qiAVAX, to, 0) records no delta (src/PoolManager.sol:294, 368-369) and still makes the PoolManager call transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:73), so any account can run this accounting for the PoolManager at no cost. The call used 140,444 gas against about 5,000 for a plain token and changed no balance. 2. rewardAccrued(0, PoolManager) is 14.844 QI and rewardAccrued(1, PoolManager) is 0.1286 AVAX. 3. claimReward(0, PoolManager) can be called by anyone and transfers the accrued QI to the PoolManager when the Comptroller holds enough QI (lines 1234 and 1287 to 1291). 4. A caller who runs sync(QI), then the claim, then settle inside one unlock is credited the QI that arrived and can take it (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-364). 5. Today the Comptroller holds 0.1096 QI, less than the accrued amount, so the claim pays nothing: in simulation it succeeded and the QI balance of the PoolManager did not change. The AVAX reward cannot be paid at all, because the PoolManager has no receive function, and claimReward(1, PoolManager) reverts.
findings.impact: 14.84 QI today, once the Comptroller is funded again, plus whatever accrues later on the qiAVAX that pools hold. The qiAVAX balance is worth about 54 AVAX at the measured mint rate, so the sums are small. Without a caller the QI would sit in the PoolManager as a surplus that no pool can withdraw, so liquidity providers do not receive it in either case.
findings.preconditions: Pools or claims in qiAVAX or another market token of a lending protocol whose reward claim can be made for a third party. The Benqi Comptroller must hold at least the accrued amount of QI. I did not check other lending forks on other chains.
findings.mitigations: None in core. Liquidity providers in reward bearing market tokens should expect to lose the rewards. A hook could claim and donate them to the pool.

The Comptroller source in the Benqi repository matches this behaviour: transferAllowed runs the supplier reward update for source and destination (lines 595 to 611), claimReward(uint8,address payable) is public (line 1234), and grantRewardInternal pays QI only when the amount is at most the balance of the Comptroller and otherwise leaves the accrual in place (lines 1287 to 1306). verification.codeCheck: take with amount 0 passes toInt128, and _accountDelta returns at once for a zero delta (src/PoolManager.sol:294, 368-369). The library still makes the CALL to the token with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/types/Currency.sol:60-74), so any account inside an unlock can run the token's sender side logic at no cost. sync has no lock check and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the caller with the whole rise since the sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and take pays it out (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The caller ends with all deltas at zero, so the count check in unlock passes (src/PoolManager.sol:112). No function in src/ pays out a balance surplus to pools: collectProtocolFees is limited to protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). A QI payment that reaches the PoolManager between sync(QI) and settle is therefore credited to whoever opened the window. The guard at src/PoolManager.sol:356 does not apply because no value is sent. The path is the one already recorded for Ethereum under this reference.
verification.corrections: The zero amount transfer is not needed. claimReward updates the supply index and distributes to the holder by itself before it pays. findings.title: MegaETH blocks are not ordered by priority fee, so a queue of transactions that each fill the block budget for new state delays every later transaction by the length of the queue
findings.difference: MegaETH skips every candidate transaction of a block once the block has reached 1,000 new state entries, and its sequencer does not sort a block by priority fee. Ethereum has no per block cap on new state and orders by fee.
findings.mechanism: 1. BlockLimiter::pre_execution_check rejects every candidate once block_state_growth_used has reached the block limit of 1,000 (block/limit.rs lines 765 to 893), and the transaction that reaches the limit is itself included. Cycle 2 measured the cost of one such transaction at 22,559,525 gas, about 0.0000226 ETH at the base fee of 1,000,000 wei. 2. New in this cycle: in 232 of 300 sampled blocks a transaction with a lower priority fee sits ahead of one with a higher fee from another sender, so a user cannot move ahead of the filling transaction by paying more. 3. If the pool hands out pending transactions in arrival order and skipped ones keep their place, a sender who queues N filling transactions from several accounts closes N consecutive one second blocks, and a withdrawal that arrives later waits N blocks. The documentation allows 500 pending transactions per account and names no other rate limit. The sequencer's pool is not public, so this ordering is an inference from the block contents. 4. The delay is bounded by the queue that stood when the user's transaction arrived, and each second of delay costs the sender about 0.0000226 ETH. An hour costs about 0.08 ETH and a day about 1.95 ETH. 5. A liquidity removal or take through the PoolManager has no path around the limiter (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, 291-297). 6. The L1 deposit route stays open. Deposits sit at index 1 in all 25 sampled deposit blocks, ahead of sequencer transactions, and the L1 portal sells at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits per L1 block, which pays for fewer than 900 new slots at about 22,500 gas each. The deposits of one L1 block can therefore not reach the limit of 1,000 before the last of them runs. 7. No use of this was found on chain: among 400,000 recent blocks the largest state growth of a traced heavy transaction is 27 entries.
findings.impact: No funds are lost. All users of the chain, including liquidity providers who want to withdraw, wait as long as the sender keeps a queue and pays for it. A user can leave through an L1 deposit, which costs L1 gas and lands within minutes.
findings.preconditions: The sender funds several accounts and pays about 0.0000226 ETH per second of delay. The sequencer keeps its present ordering and does not filter the sender.
findings.mitigations: Integrators who must exit under load can send the exit as an L1 deposit through the OptimismPortal. The operator can order or filter the pool so that transactions with large state growth do not come first in each block.

verification.factCheck: Confirmed parts. block/limit.rs of mega-evm at tag v1.7.3 is byte identical to the main branch. pre_execution_check returns StateGrowthLimit for every candidate once block_state_growth_used has reached block_state_growth_limit (lines 880 to 890), and post_execution_update_raw adds the usage of an executed transaction without a test, with the comment that the last transaction may exceed the limit (lines 940 to 943). block/executor.rs calls pre_execution_check for every transaction of a block, deposits included (lines 498 to 507), so a validating node rejects a block that carries a transaction after the limit was reached. constants.rs sets TX_STATE_GROWTH_LIMIT and BLOCK_STATE_GROWTH_LIMIT to 1,000, so one transaction can fill the block budget. The resource limits page states the same rule and says a skipped transaction has no receipt and may be reconsidered in a later block. Ordering: I sampled 80 blocks between 32,610,921 and 32,614,160. After removing deposits and the zero price transactions of 0xa887dcb9d5f39ef79272801d05abdf707cfbbd1d, 954 transactions remain. In 133 of 874 neighbouring pairs from different senders the later transaction pays the higher priority fee, and 59 of the 80 blocks contain such a pair. Blocks are therefore not sorted by priority fee, which agrees with the research sample. The base fee was 1,000,000 wei in every sampled block, so 22,559,525 gas costs 0.0000226 ETH. Deposits: the OptimismPortal 0x7f82f57F0Dd546519324392e408b01fcC7D709e8 on Ethereum names SystemConfig 0x1ed92e1bc9a2735216540eddd0191144681cb77e, whose resourceConfig has maxResourceLimit 20,000,000. For 12 deposits from the explorer list I read the block: each deposit is at index 1 and the first transaction that is no deposit is at index 2. The FAQ states the limit of 500 pending transactions per account and no rate limit per account. Unconfirmed link. Step 3 and the title need the sequencer to take pending transactions in arrival order and to keep skipped ones ahead of later arrivals. The mini-block page and the FAQ say nothing about the order of pending transactions, the pool of mega-reth is closed source, and no block with a full state budget exists to observe. My sample cannot tell arrival order from fee order inside one mini-block of about 10 milliseconds. The delay of N blocks for a queue of N filling transactions is therefore an inference. Not repeated: the gas figure of 22,559,525 for 1,000 entries (measured in cycle 2), and the scan of 400,000 block headers with 30 traces.
verification.codeCheck: Every exit from the PoolManager is a transaction that reaches unlock and then modifyLiquidity, take or burn (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 145-184, 291-297, 332-336). The contract has no path that pays out without a transaction on the chain, so a block that admits no further transactions delays every exit until the next block that does. Nothing in src/ reads block fields or depends on timing, so the delay changes no accounting. The actor value unprivileged is right for the part that is confirmed: any account can send a transaction with 1,000 new state entries. The victims did nothing unusual.
verification.corrections: The title states the queue delay as a fact. Only this much is confirmed: one filling transaction closes the rest of its one second block for every later candidate, deposits excepted because they run first, and a higher priority fee does not place a transaction ahead of it at block level. That is the cycle 2 statement of F-042 and it remains confirmed at low severity. The delay by the length of a queue is plausible and depends on lead L-170. If the sequencer keeps arrival order across blocks, the hazard is a standing delay for everyone at about 1.95 ETH per day, and medium would fit the scale because liquidity operations would be held back without loss. Step 6 gives the wrong bound for deposits, and the conclusion still holds. The cheapest state growth by deposits is a deposit from a sender address that does not exist on MegaETH: the Rex5 rule records one new account for the caller of such a deposit, and the portal accepts a gas limit of 21,000 (minimumGasLimit(0) on the portal). 20,000,000 gas buys at most 952 such deposits per L1 block, against fewer than 900 slots by storage writes at the 22,559 gas per slot that cycle 2 measured. Both are below 1,000, with a margin of 48 entries. I did not confirm that a deposit that fails for lack of intrinsic gas (60,000 on MegaETH) is counted as state growth. If it is not counted, the bound is lower.

findings.title: Measured on the deployed contract, one empty bitmap word costs about 5,900 gas in the swap loop, so a small block fits about 500 words and a big block cannot hold a walk across the whole range at tick spacing 1
findings.difference: HyperEVM small blocks hold 3,000,000 gas and big blocks 30,000,000 gas, and a sender reaches big blocks only after a HyperCore action sets a flag on its account. In 4,725 sampled blocks 78 were big blocks. F-039 derived the cost of the swap loop from repository snapshots and gave about 1,283 empty words per small block. This entry replaces those estimates with measurements on the deployed PoolManager.
findings.mechanism: Pool.swap runs one loop iteration per bitmap word or initialized tick on its way (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:85-121). I called the deployed Quoter for 63 swaps of 2^100 input units in hookless pools at block 51,997,409 on an archive node, took the gas of the PoolManager.swap frame from callTracer and counted the bitmap slots and tick slots the frame read with prestateTracer. The 49 swaps without a tick crossing read 11 to 63 words and fit a line of 5,871 gas per word plus 39,059 gas. Two pools with tick spacing 10 read 179 words and used 1,080,157 and 1,080,189 gas, which is 5,816 gas per word. One tick crossing added 10,917 to 31,243 gas and two crossings added 61,692 gas (Pool.sol:413-428 and 602-612). The floor of 2,242 gas per iteration in F-039 counted the bitmap read only. The measured figure includes the price computation and the swap step of each iteration. With these figures a 3,000,000 gas transaction holds at most about 504 empty words or about 95 to 270 crossings. At tick spacing 1 the walk from tick 0 to the price limit is 3,466 words and costs about 20.4 million gas, which fits a big block only. A walk across the whole range at spacing 1 is about 6,932 words and about 40.7 million gas, more than a big block holds, so it must be split into at least two transactions with intermediate price limits. At spacing 10 the walk from tick 0 is 347 words and about 2.08 million gas, which fits a small block when the transaction does little else. The deployed routers make the long walk the default: Universal Router 2.1.2 passed MIN_SQRT_PRICE + 1 or MAX_SQRT_PRICE - 1 in 5 of 5 traced swaps and seven other swap callers did the same in 29 traced swaps. A swap sent through them that uses up the liquidity on its side walks every remaining word (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75) and runs out of gas in a small block at spacing 1. The three levers of F-039 stay as described there: dust positions on every tick (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), a swap past the last position, and a pool id initialized at an extreme price by a third party (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). The measurements were taken on the contract deployed at 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F. The cycle 3 critic notes that this is other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so the figures describe the chain's price for the storage reads and writes that the loop in src performs and may differ by small amounts for a new build.
findings.impact: No funds leave the PoolManager and no position is frozen. Two mined liquidity removals used 60,628 and 60,415 gas in the modifyLiquidity frame, and Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238). The cost falls on swappers, arbitrageurs and contracts that need one atomic swap in the 9 pools with tick spacing 1 and the 31 pools with spacing 10. A swap that crosses more than about 95 freshly written ticks, or more than about 504 empty words, has to go to a big block or be split.
findings.preconditions: A pool with tick spacing 1 or 10. For the dust position lever the attacker pays the gas of one liquidity addition per tick. The victim sends the swap to a small block through a router that passes the extreme price limit, or the swap sits in a contract that cannot split it.
findings.mitigations: Routers and keepers on HyperEVM should pass a price limit near the expected end price and split long walks. Contracts that depend on one atomic swap should use pools with tick spacing 60 or more, where the walk from tick 0 is 58 words and about 380,000 gas. Pool creators can initialize the pool ids they intend to use at the market price.

verification.factCheck: I repeated the measurements on the archive endpoint at block 52,006,549. The Initialize logs since block 45,998,366 give 344 pools with tick spacing 200 in 165, 60 in 139, 10 in 31 and 1 in 9, and 103 pools without a hook. I called the deployed Quoter with 2^100 input units for the 10 hookless pools with spacing 1 or 10, in both directions, and read the gas of the PoolManager.swap frame with callTracer and the PoolManager storage slots with prestateTracer. The two spacing 10 pools used 1,080,157 and 1,080,189 gas with 186 slots read in one direction, the same two numbers the finding reports, and 1,711,372 gas with 295 slots in the other. The eight spacing 1 pools used 10.5 to 24.7 million gas for one direction. Two of them give the whole range: 21,919,151 gas for 4,104 slots downward plus 16,118,924 gas for 2,835 slots upward, 38.0 million in total, and 14,726,539 plus 23,572,512, 38.3 million in total. The cost per slot read is 5,340 to 5,700 gas on these long walks. A walk across the whole range at spacing 1 therefore costs about 38 million gas, which is more than the 30,000,000 of a big block, and one direction alone fits a big block only. In 1,000 recent blocks 984 had gas limit 3,000,000 and 16 had 30,000,000. The dual block page states a 3M limit for fast blocks, a 30M limit for slow blocks and the evmUserModify action. I counted 2,283 Swap and 842 ModifyLiquidity events since deployment. Traces of the three latest swaps of each frequent sender show that Universal Router 2.1.2 (0xeD270A1Bcdc63cf1356D695e7f40961d4819d6bF) and 25 other senders passed 4295128740 or 1461446703485210103287273052203988822378723970341 as price limit. Transaction 0xa17080717f in block 51,684,430 holds two removals that used 60,628 and 60,415 gas in the modifyLiquidity frame, and nine other recent removals used 31,574 to 75,899 gas. I did not measure the cost of a tick crossing again. That figure rests on the finding's traces and on the two storage writes in the code.
verification.codeCheck: The loop at src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437 runs until the amount is used up or the price equals the limit. Each iteration reads one bitmap word (src/libraries/Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:85-121), computes the price of the next tick (line 359) and runs one swap step (lines 362-368). With zero liquidity in range, computeSwapStep finds amountIn 0, takes the branch at src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:69-74 and returns the target price with nothing consumed, so the loop moves one word per iteration until the limit. Nothing bounds the number of iterations. The limit must lie strictly inside MIN_SQRT_PRICE and MAX_SQRT_PRICE (src/libraries/Pool.sol:322-338), which is what the two router constants are. crossTick rewrites both fee growth slots of a crossed tick (src/libraries/Pool.sol:606-609). modifyLiquidity in PoolManager has no access control beyond the unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), so any account can place a position of one liquidity unit on any aligned tick pair of a hookless pool. initialize has no access control and accepts any price that TickMath accepts (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Pool.sol:100-107). Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and take, burn and settle have none (src/PoolManager.sol:291-336), so exits stay within a small block. No funds move to the attacker on any of these paths.
verification.corrections: The actor unprivileged and the severity low are right. Three figures need adjusting and none changes the conclusion. First, 5,871 gas per word is the slope of the short walks. On the long walks at spacing 1 the cost is 5,340 to 5,700 gas per word, so the whole range costs about 38 million gas, where the finding says 40.7 million, one direction from tick 0 about 19 million, and a small block holds about 500 to 550 empty words. Second, more than one caller passes its own price limit: 0xbaf9961ba462abee6d4f86d9509c0bdd15f9a044 and the hook 0x6227f0128935079abc6993f1166dc5d716032aec did so in each of three traced swaps and 0xfe6bace2e548fd06735a4242bbd46a3c842e02b1 in one of three. Third, the profile counts 53 hook addresses, and the logs hold 52 distinct hook addresses plus the zero address. The victims of the dust position and far price levers are swappers in hookless pools with spacing 1 or 10, of which 10 exist today.

findings.title: Dust positions on fresh ticks make each first crossing cost about 505,000 gas on Tempo, so a price raising swap through more than about 58 such ticks cannot fit in one transaction
findings.difference: Tempo charges 250,000 gas for a write to an empty storage slot, where Ethereum charges 20,000, and caps a transaction at 30,000,000 gas. Calls to the PoolManager also share a general limit of 30,000,000 gas per block.
findings.mechanism: 1. Pool.updateTick copies the global fee growth into a newly initialized tick only when the tick is at or below the current tick. A tick above the current tick starts with both fee growth outside values at zero (src/libraries/Pool.sol:532-538). 2. Any account can initialize ticks above the price by adding positions with a dust amount of liquidity in a pool it does not own. In simulation each such add costs about 540,000 gas when neighbouring positions share ticks. 3. When a swap that raises the price (currency1 in, currency0 out) first crosses such a tick, Pool.crossTick writes global minus outside into both slots (src/libraries/Pool.sol:602-611). With fees accrued in both currencies both writes go from zero to nonzero. 4. I measured this on the pathUSD and USDC.e pool with fee 375 and spacing 4 through eth_simulateV1 with state overrides: 5,819,042 gas for a swap over 11 fresh ticks and 10,865,864 gas for 21, against 267,513 gas for the same swap without crossings. That is 504,684 gas per crossing. With only one nonzero global fee growth the figure is about 254,500. 5. A transaction of 30,000,000 gas therefore holds about 58 first crossings with both slots fresh. A swap that has to move the price further runs out of gas and reverts as a whole. 6. Once a tick has been crossed its slots are nonzero and later crossings are cheap. The account can remove and add its dust positions again to reset ticks above the price to zero. 7. Liquidity removal does not cross ticks. It writes at most the two fee growth inside values of the position from zero to nonzero (src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102), about 500,000 gas, so withdrawals stay possible.
findings.impact: No funds are lost and no withdrawal is blocked. Swappers who buy currency0 in the affected pool pay up to 30,000,000 gas per 58 ticks, which is 0.018 USD at the base fee floor and 0.36 USD at the cap, and a trade that needs a larger price move has to be split with a price limit over several transactions. One such swap fills the general gas limit of its block. On a spacing 1 stable pool 58 ticks are a price move of 0.58 percent. The account that plants the ticks pays about 0.0003 USD per tick at the floor.
findings.preconditions: A pool with fees accrued in both currencies. The planted ticks must lie above the current price and below the price that a later price raising swap reaches. Swaps that lower the price cross ticks whose slots were filled at initialization and are not affected. No role is needed.
findings.mitigations: Routers and integrators should pass a price limit and accept partial fills on Tempo, and should size the gas limit from a simulation of the actual route. Pool creators can use a wider tick spacing, which lowers the number of ticks per price move. Nothing in core needs to change.

The endpoint reports tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97. Block 50,378,538 has gasLimit 500,000,000, mainBlockGeneralGasLimit 30,000,000 and baseFeePerGas 600,000,000. I ran a gas probe with eth_estimateGas and override code at an unused address: a call that stops at once costs 274,318 gas, one SSTORE from 0 to 1 costs 530,642, two such writes cost 784,951, and a write over a nonzero slot costs 279,364. A fresh slot therefore costs 256,324 gas for the first and 254,309 for the second, and a rewrite costs 5,046. Two fresh slots per crossing give about 510,000 gas, which agrees with the 504,684 of the finding. crates/precompiles/src/storage_credits/accounting.rs charges 245,000 gas up front for each creation in the default Refund mode on top of the 5,000 residual, so the gas limit must cover the full amount. crates/payload/builder/src/lib.rs lines 561 to 604 defer a transaction that is no payment when the general gas already used plus min(gas limit, cap) exceeds the general limit. The test uses the gas limit of the transaction, so a swap sent with a 30,000,000 limit is admitted only while no general gas has been used in that block. The fee document gives a floor of 600 million and a cap of 12 billion attodollars per gas and a general limit of 30M gas per block. The cost figures follow: 30,000,000 gas is 0.018 USD at the floor and 0.36 USD at the cap, and 540,000 gas is 0.0003 USD at the floor. I listed the 167 Initialize logs of the PoolManager and read slot0, both fee growth globals and liquidity of every pool with extsload. 70 of the 147 pools without a hook have both globals nonzero, so the precondition holds on live pools. I did not repeat the harness simulation that plants positions and swaps. The per crossing figure rests on the slot probe above and on the source.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.updateTick writes the two fee growth outside values only when the tick is at or below the current tick (src/libraries/Pool.sol:533-538), so a tick first used above the price keeps both at zero. Pool.crossTick writes global minus outside to both slots with no condition (src/libraries/Pool.sol:606-609), and the swap loop calls it for every initialized tick it reaches (src/libraries/Pool.sol:413-428). For a price raising swap the first argument is the stored feeGrowthGlobal0X128 and the second is the running value for currency1 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:416-418), so both writes create a slot when both globals are nonzero. modifyLiquidity has no owner or allowlist check and takes msg.sender as position owner (src/PoolManager.sol:145-168). A range above the price owes currency0 only (src/libraries/Pool.sol:209-217). The swap loop has no bound on the number of crossings other than the price limit and the amount (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344), and a revert from lack of gas undoes the whole swap. Liquidity removal has no loop over ticks. It updates two tick slots, at most two bitmap words, the position slots and the pool liquidity (src/libraries/Pool.sol:159-203, src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102), so it stays far below the cap. take and mint add one TIP-20 transfer or one claim balance write each (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 322-329). I found no guard that the finding missed. The actor is right: the planter needs no role and the victims use a pool without a hook and with ordinary tokens. No funds move to the planter and no withdrawal is blocked, which fits low.
verification.corrections: The pathUSD and USDC.e pool with fee 375 and spacing 4 (id 0x2fafb8d5...297d) is initialized and empty on chain: liquidity, feeGrowthGlobal0X128 and feeGrowthGlobal1X128 all read zero. The measured figures therefore describe a state that the harness built by override, and the finding should say so. The count of 58 crossings ignores the 63/64 rule. The swap runs at least two call frames below the transaction, so the count is a little lower. The statement that price lowering swaps are not affected is too wide. A tick at or below the price that was initialized while a global was zero starts with an empty slot, and a downward crossing writes zero when the global equals the stored value, after which the next upward crossing creates the slot again. The cost figures are upper bounds. The PoolManager account holds 13 storage credits (balanceOf on 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000), removals that clear tick or position slots mint more, and settle_storage_credit_refunds returns 245,000 gas per credit at the end of a transaction that created slots in PoolManager storage. The refund lowers the fee and leaves the needed gas limit unchanged. Because the builder admits by gas limit, any earlier transaction of the general lane with a higher tip defers a swap that carries a 30,000,000 limit in that block. This strengthens the degrade effect for large swaps and does not touch withdrawals, whose gas limits are small.

findings.title: Interest bearing receipt tokens and time indexed tokens grow in the PoolManager on thirteen networks and the growth can be neither claimed nor captured
findings.difference: F-037 recorded four Aave aTokens on Arbitrum One. The sweep finds the same class on eleven more networks and in more protocols: Aave v2 and v3, Spark, Radiant, Seamless, Moola, Neverland, Horizon, DeltaPrime, ExtraFi, Compound III and Wildcat. It also finds tokens with a pure time index: 666, EXPT and EXPT2 on Robinhood Chain and two test tokens on Arbitrum One.
findings.mechanism: balanceOf of these tokens is a stored amount times an index that is computed from block.timestamp at read time. Inside one transaction the timestamp is constant, so a sync and a settle in the same transaction see the same index and no caller is credited (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289, 349-365). The growth between transactions stays in the PoolManager balance and belongs to no pool. 666 at 0x73eb4a9db8d8c7539ba5701cf1cdd3452038970b has DAILY_GROWTH 1.33e18, MAX_DAYS 200 and a start time 4.3 days before the read, and the PoolManager balance rose from 1,936,719 to 2,595,372 in 93,084 seconds while one Transfer of 34,778 went out. Two side observations. First, when someone supplies to Aave v3 on behalf of the PoolManager, the aToken logs a Transfer for the supplied amount plus the interest accrued since the PoolManager's last index update, so the logs overstate what arrived; this explains the negative differences on aEthDAI, aEthUSDT, aAvaUSDT, aAstarASTR and aBnbUSDT. Second, Compound III lets anyone call CometRewards.claim for a third party; simulated for the PoolManager on Ethereum, Arbitrum One and Optimism it moved no reward token, with 0.000016 COMP owed on Ethereum and nothing on the other two.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers in these pools forgo the interest or the index growth for as long as the tokens stay pooled. Largest balances: 3,410.66 aEthUSDC, 2,268.28 aEthUSDT and 4,565.90 USPD on Ethereum, 60,244 rzRDNT and 1,504.67 aArbUSDT on Arbitrum One, 24,696 nWMON on Monad, 2,786.51 aBasUSDC on Base, 2,501.34 aASTR on Soneium, 548.71 aBnbUSDT on BNB Smart Chain, 845.05 aOptUSDC on Optimism. 666: the PoolManager holds 2,595,372 tokens, 37.9 percent of the supply, and its balance grows by about a third per day. Principal is not affected and no ordinary account can collect the surplus.
findings.preconditions: A pool in such a token. Nobody has to act. I did not test whether a flash loan premium or another call can move an Aave style index inside one transaction on these networks; F-037 checked that for Arbitrum One only. A caller who paid such a premium would be credited only the PoolManager's share of it, which is below 1 percent of supply for every receipt token found except rzRDNT at 3.8 percent.
findings.mitigations: Pool the wrapped form with a fixed balance, for example the static or wrapped aToken, or accept that the yield is lost. Interfaces should mark these currencies.
