verification.factCheck: I sampled the class on five networks. Two Multicall3 reads 24 to 27 seconds apart, each stamped with the block timestamp, show balanceOf(PoolManager) growing with no transaction of mine in between: aEthUSDC 3,410.687144 to 3,410.687210, aEthUSDT by 51 base units and aDAI by 83,765,025,440 base units on Ethereum; aArbUSDT by 28 base units and rzRDNT by 19,962,354,109,229 base units on Arbitrum One; nWMON by 851,920,932,989,994 base units on Monad; aOptUSDC by 2 base units and exOptOP by 459,244,053,601 base units on Optimism. These balances follow the block timestamp at read time. On Robinhood Chain 666 grew by 54 tokens in 6 seconds, and index(), DAILY_GROWTH(), MAX_DAYS(), startTime() and totalSupply() return 3.53e18, 1.33e18, 200, 1795033136 and 7,017,240. EXPT and EXPT2 did not move in those 6 seconds. Their balance rose in steps over the last 800,000 blocks, their bytecode holds EPOCH(), currentEpoch(), rebaseIndex() and startTime() as views, and the only state changing functions are transfer, transferFrom and approve, so the step comes from the timestamp and no caller can trigger it. The PoolManager holds the whole EXPT supply of 713,731,483.6. The researcher's classification of the 177 lending rows is by symbol pattern (classify.py, the LEND expression), so only the tokens I sampled and those the researcher read one by one are confirmed as time indexed. One exception to the statement that nothing moves inside a transaction: the Aave v2 pool on Ethereum returns FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TOTAL 9 and is not paused, and in Aave v2 the flash loan premium is added to the supplier index. I did not read the Aave v2 pool source in this session; the on-chain setting is the evidence. I did not rerun the CometRewards simulation.
verification.codeCheck: sync records the balance at the time of the call and _settle credits the balance now minus that record (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). Both run in one transaction with one timestamp, so growth that depends only on the timestamp is inside the record and produces no credit. The growth between transactions belongs to no delta, and take, burn and collectProtocolFees pay accounted amounts only (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 332-336, src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). Where a caller can raise the index inside a transaction by paying a premium, the credit is the premium times the PoolManager's share of the token supply, which is 50.49 of 8,146,003 aDAI and 60,244 of 1,568,330 rzRDNT, so the caller pays more than the credit. A supply on behalf of the PoolManager is a payment by the caller and settle credits the real rise, whatever the Transfer log says.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is acceptable only in the sense that no privilege is needed. No account acts and no account gains, nothing leaves the PoolManager and nothing is frozen, so this is lost yield for providers who pool a rebasing receipt token and it lies outside the goal of the review. The title says the growth can be neither claimed nor captured. That holds for growth that comes from time. For Aave v2 and its forks a flash loan premium moves the index inside a transaction and a bracket would capture the PoolManager's share of it at a net loss to the caller; the finding says this in its preconditions and the title should be read with that limit. The 177 rows were classed by symbol, and a token with a stored index that a public call updates would belong to the class of finding 0. I found none in my sample.

findings.title: A sync left earlier in a shared transaction makes a later native payment revert for routers that settle value without their own sync
findings.difference: Ethereum has the same code path. The networks differ in how often one transaction carries the operations of several users. Among the most recent transactions that hold a PoolManager Swap event, 342 of 463 on World Chain, 300 of 600 on Soneium and 62 of 600 on Base were ERC-4337 handleOps calls, and bundles with two or three user operations occur on all three. On Ethereum the count was 7 of 600. EntryPoint v0.6 to v0.9, Multicall3 and the public Simple7702Account hold code on all 21 networks, and senders with an EIP-7702 delegation were among the sampled swap senders on 13 of them. Tempo is left out of the chain list because no transaction there can carry native value (cleared in an earlier cycle), so the path has no target.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync has no lock check and no caller check. For a token it stores the currency and balanceOf(PoolManager) in two transient slots and returns (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). Nothing clears the currency slot when the call ends. Only a later sync or a later ERC-20 settle changes it (src/PoolManager.sol:283, 286, 361). 2. unlock returns with the lock flag false and reverts unless every delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The synced currency and its reserves are therefore the only PoolManager values that one party can leave for the next party inside one transaction. 3. _settle reads the synced currency first. When it is nonzero and msg.value is above zero the call reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:349-356). The comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 tells integrators to call sync before a native settle. 4. The attacker needs one call, sync(X) for any token X, that runs before the victim's operation in the same transaction. Carriers: an earlier user operation in a handleOps bundle, the validation step of any operation in the bundle (all four EntryPoint versions run every validation before the first execution), a pre hook of a CoW order, a call in a relayer or delegated account batch. 5. Test, read only. For recent swaps the original call was replayed at its parent block by eth_call. The sender address received the code of the public Simple7702Account by state override and ran executeBatch of [original call] as control and of [PoolManager.sync(token), original call] as test. Of the replays whose control succeeded, 209 native value replays and 193 token input replays gave the same result, and 9 and 7 reverted in the test only. The revert data was ExecuteError(1, NonzeroNativeValue) in 15 of the 16 cases and a router specific error 0x81ceff30 in one (Elysium, cause not decoded). 6. Contracts that reverted: Ethereum 0x3e8282bd1bfabd23249701e978e9db3df3d7073a (unverified, 187,745 transactions). Soneium LiFiDiamond 0x864b314d4c5a0399368609581d3e8933a63b9232 on routes through EisenDiamond 0x7e36665858d17fd1cbfd4fd464d2a3da49aa3b9d, whose facet 0x0b20601669dbce7e14210e24ca2b748cfb6dfc08 is unverified; EisenDiamond was the swap sender in 18.1 percent of 4,082 recent Soneium Swap events. Avalanche AvaxHookRouterV2 0xc8b2b67a1e286f74648a705617d54a0415fc651a (verified source line 103 calls settle with value and no sync), SwapHelper 0xde9d7290959b6060860b983b32f2d65b2701ebc2 and 0xfe807eb087439ec6e59ed5f93fad011223cb50f9. Arc 0x944fe8becf9a02a3e9378b4cadde1b14ef8d2ed9. BNB Smart Chain 0xdc0e98fd40ccd1c1d7084de9f254d7853846cc6e and 0x95337791024b5f0480b353fbafd2882b4d8e99c8. Monad 0x7db99f225af7a1a21b7b6468ed28f4bc60fbe937. Robinhood Chain 0x29d8d0a5c38716ebb4ae1786a46cf0ab74d480db, the sender of 11.0 percent of 5,624 recent Swap events. Zora 0xdb2e211c43ee4ac4665c44e8ae6723adfd62a07f. Elysium 0xa834e70303322d86e5dae95ee47e9c6a073d9812. 7. By source reading only, without a replay: the verified NodeRouter implementation 0x893f30424f8e6064b1d7284e5415be8413901c0d on World Chain (4.3 percent of sampled swaps there) calls settle with value and no sync at line 1127, as do the verified Bot 0xe41698520e4817b55c1841859a36847d50f0c82f (line 1014) and Router 0xeff6cb8b614999d130e537751ee99724d01aa167 (line 836) on Ethereum. 8. Inside a real bundle: three Base handleOps transactions replayed through eth_simulateV1 with a sync placed before handleOps kept UserOperationEvent.success true and lost their PoolManager swaps (5 to 4, 1 to 0 and 2 to 0 Swap events). The account behind them, with swap sender 0x5c40d83c6361aef9604c3d9a20d8452d496035eb, catches the failed leg and ends without trading. 9. No wrong credit follows from the leftover state. A payer that calls sync itself replaces both slots (src/PoolManager.sol:286). A payer that sends value without sync reverts at line 356. A zero value settle against the leftover credits its own caller with the balance rise since the stale sync, which is the attacker's own donation, or reverts on the checked subtraction at line 360 when the balance fell.
findings.impact: No funds move to the attacker and none are locked. The victim's native input swap reverts and the victim pays the gas of the failed operation. In an ERC-4337 bundle that fee still goes to the bundler. Accounts that catch the failure end the operation without the trade. The attacker can repeat this in every transaction it shares with the victim. Users of the canonical Universal Router, the PositionManager and the 0x Settler are unaffected. The largest exposed public paths found are LI.FI routes through Eisen on Soneium, where half of the sampled swap transactions travel in bundles, the NodeRouter on World Chain, where three quarters do, and launchpad routers on Avalanche.
findings.preconditions: The victim's call and the attacker's sync run in one transaction with no sync and no ERC-20 settle by anyone in between. The victim pays native value through a contract that does not call sync before settle. The attacker holds no role. It needs a place ahead of the victim in the same transaction: its own operation in the same bundle, or a bundle that it submits itself, since handleOps accepts any caller. A sync costs 27,891 to 35,717 gas as a standalone transaction on seven networks by eth_estimateGas, and less inside a bundle, plus the overhead of one user operation. Not confirmed: how often an outsider's operation lands directly ahead of a given victim in the bundles of World Chain, Soneium and Base, and whether the listed unverified contracts are open to the public or are single operator bots.
findings.mitigations: Router authors: call sync(address(0)) immediately before every settle that carries value, as the canonical routers and the 0x Settler do. Smart account users: place a sync(address(0)) call first in the same batch when a route pays native value through another router. Deployer: the state cannot be removed without a code change. A change that clears the synced currency when unlock begins would remove it and would break callers that sync before unlock. Publishing the rule at src/PoolManager.sol:348 for integrators on bundle heavy networks costs nothing.

verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier and no caller check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). For a token it writes the currency and balanceOf(PoolManager) to two transient slots (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). For address(0) it writes zero to the currency slot only (src/PoolManager.sol:283, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-25). The currency slot is written at three places in src/: the two branches of sync and the reset in the token branch of _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:361). unlock does not touch it at entry or exit (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so a value set by one party stays for the next party in the same transaction. _settle reads the slot first (line 350). When it is nonzero and msg.value is above zero it reverts with NonzeroNativeValue at line 356, before any accounting. settle and settleFor are the only payable entry points and both end there (lines 300-307). The comment at line 348 asks integrators to sync before a native settle. Guards I looked for that could change the result: none clears the slot for the victim. The subtraction at line 360 is checked, so a balance below the stale reserves reverts and cannot credit. The credited currency (line 364) and the measured balance (line 359) come from the same slot, so a stale sync cannot turn a payment in one currency into a credit in another. The int128 cast at line 364 and the delta count check at line 112 work as usual. The only other reader of the slot is collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), which reverts for the stale currency and concerns the fee controller alone. A caller that runs sync itself overwrites both slots (line 286) or zeroes the currency (line 283), which is why the canonical routers pass. A liquidity removal produces credits that leave through take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and never calls settle with value, so this path cannot block a withdrawal. The code path is as the finding states: a repeatable revert for payers of native value that skip sync, and no movement of funds. Actor check: sync is open to any account, so unprivileged is right. The victims are users of third party routers that skip the sync asked for at line 348; users of the canonical routers are outside it. Severity check: no loss path and no blocked withdrawal, which is the low level of the scale.
verification.corrections: The mechanism and the actor stand. Six points need adjusting. 1. Ref: F-014 already records that a stale sync makes a later native settle revert at src/PoolManager.sol:356. This entry extends F-014 with carriers and exposed routers and should carry that id. 2. Soneium: the revert data is ExecuteError(1, 0x9eea691b(bytes)) with 0xb0ec849e inside the inner payload, where the finding quotes ExecuteError(1, 0xb0ec849e). 3. Carriers: the statement that handleOps accepts any caller holds for EntryPoint v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8. The verified v0.9 source requires tx.origin == msg.sender and a caller without code (lines 68 to 75), so on v0.9 a sync cannot be placed in front of handleOps inside one transaction, and the carrier must be an operation inside the bundle. 4. Carriers: a sync made in the validation step works only in a bundle that the attacker submits itself. ERC-7562 treats TSTORE like SSTORE (OP-070) and limits validation to the account's own or associated storage, so a bundler that follows it rejects such an operation. A sync in the execution step of an earlier operation is under no such rule. 5. Preconditions: top level value is not needed. The Monad and Robinhood Chain transactions carry zero value at the top level and still end in NonzeroNativeValue, so routers that pay native value from their own balance are exposed too. 6. Reach: an exposed router or account was shown on 11 of the 20 listed networks (Ethereum, Base, Zora, World Chain by source only, Soneium, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, Arc). On the other nine the path exists in the code and no exposed integration was shown. Also: every replay ran against the PoolManagers deployed today, which are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. For this build the finding rests on the source lines, which I read. The position of the attacker ahead of the victim inside a third party bundle remains unconfirmed, as the finding says. The finding is outside the review's stated goal: it takes no funds held by the PoolManager and blocks no withdrawal.

findings.title: Source disagrees with two interface comments and two test conditions, and none of the four changes who can move funds
findings.difference: None. These are differences inside the repository, between src and its own comments and tests.
findings.mechanism: First, src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says collectProtocolFees reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code checks only the caller and whether the currency is the synced ERC-20 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). _isUnlocked is declared at ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 and nothing calls it. The tests agree with the code: they expect ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced in both lock states (test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039). Second, src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 says only initialize and updateDynamicLPFee can be called without unlocking. sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279) and test/Sync.t.sol:36-41 calls it while locked. Third, test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut when amountSpecified >= 0 at a 100 percent fee, while src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316 reverts only for amountSpecified > 0 and line 320 returns a zero delta for amountSpecified == 0. Fourth, Pool.t.sol:143 treats a zeroForOne price limit below MIN_SQRT_PRICE as out of bounds, while Pool.sol:328 also rejects a limit equal to MIN_SQRT_PRICE. I traced each one for a fund effect. Fee collection inside an unlock changes protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount and touches no delta. A sync outside an unlock only sets two transient slots that the next sync overwrites. The zero amount swap changes no state. The stricter limit keeps slot0.tick from reaching MIN_TICK - 1.
findings.impact: No loss or freeze found. A reader who trusts the two interface comments gets the wrong picture of when sync and fee collection can run. The fuzz test at Pool.t.sol:129 would fail on an input with amountSpecified equal to zero and a 100 percent fee if the fuzzer produces one.
findings.preconditions: None for the mismatch itself. I could not run forge in this environment, so I do not know whether the current fuzz seed reaches the failing input.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can correct the two comments, decide whether collectProtocolFees should use _isUnlocked or drop it, and align the two test conditions with the source.

With the stored fee controller as sender and the manager locked it returned an amount on the eight networks that have a nonzero controller. These calls show that the deployed contracts accept sync while locked, which is what the code does and what the comment at src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 denies. They do not show what collectProtocolFees does while unlocked, since a read only call cannot open an unlock with the controller as caller. That part rests on the source and the tests. Inside the repository the four mismatches are as the finding states, with the one correction below.
verification.codeCheck: src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says collectProtocolFees reverts if the contract is unlocked. src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 checks only the caller and the synced ERC-20. _isUnlocked is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60, implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 and in two test contracts, and nothing calls it. test/PoolManager.t.sol:1010-1039 attempts collection inside an unlock and expects ProtocolFeeCurrencySynced, so the tests agree with the code. src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 names initialize and updateDynamicLPFee as the only functions callable without unlocking, while sync has no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279) and test/Sync.t.sol:36-41 calls it directly. test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut for amountSpecified >= 0, while src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316 reverts only for a positive amount and line 320 returns a zero delta. test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:143 compares with < MIN_SQRT_PRICE and src/libraries/Pool.sol:328 with <=. I traced each for a fund effect. Collection lowers protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), touches no delta and cannot run between sync and settle of the same ERC-20 in either lock state. Fees accrued by a swap that is not yet paid can be collected inside the same unlock, and the unlock reverts as a whole unless the swapper settles (src/PoolManager.sol:112). PoolManager.swap rejects a zero amount (src/PoolManager.sol:193), so Pool.swap sees zero only when a beforeSwap hook delta cancels the amount (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:273-279), and then it changes no state. The stricter price limit stops a swap from ending at MIN_SQRT_PRICE and blocks no withdrawal.
verification.corrections: The fourth item cannot make the test fail. When the limit equals MIN_SQRT_PRICE the test takes neither branch and makes no swap call (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:135-146), and test/utils/Deployers.sol:43 defines MIN_PRICE_LIMIT as MIN_SQRT_PRICE + 1, which matches the source. The third item is a failing input for the fuzz test whenever the fuzzer picks an LP fee of 1,000,000 together with amountSpecified 0. The setter setIsUnlocked in src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol:27-29 is also unused by any test, which is a further sign that a lock check on fee collection was planned or removed. ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 words the guard as unlocked and synced. The code applies it whenever the ERC-20 is synced, in both lock states.

findings.title: sync runs while the manager is locked and fee collection ignores the lock, and the mainnet fee controller lets anyone trigger collection
findings.difference: On mainnet the protocol fee controller is a V4FeeAdapter contract whose collect and triggerFeeUpdate functions have no access check. Any account can therefore make the PoolManager execute collectProtocolFees and setProtocolFee at a moment it chooses, including inside its own unlock callback. Mainnet also lets several users' operations share one transaction through ERC-4337 bundles and EIP-7702 batches.
findings.mechanism: sync has no onlyWhenUnlocked modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), so anyone can set the synced currency and reserves at any point of a transaction, and the value stays until a settle or another sync in that transaction. collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts only if the currency is an ERC-20 equal to the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). It never calls _isUnlocked, which is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394 with no caller. ASSUMPTIONS.md A12 describes the guard as depending on the unlocked state; the code does not. I walked the fund-moving paths for a gain and found none. Collection of the synced ERC-20 is blocked regardless of lock state, so the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this path. Native settlement uses msg.value and no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). Collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued with checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55) and the adapter fixes the recipient. A sync left behind by an earlier operation in a bundle is overwritten by the next sync and cleared by the next ERC-20 settle (src/PoolManager.sol:361). What remains is that a stale sync makes a later native settle with value revert with NonzeroNativeValue if its caller did not sync first (src/PoolManager.sol:356), and makes collection of that currency revert for the rest of the transaction.
findings.impact: No loss or lasting freeze found. Within one transaction, a party that runs earlier can make a later native settle or a fee collection revert.
findings.preconditions: For the revert cases the two parties must share a transaction, for example an ERC-4337 bundle, and the later party must settle native currency without calling sync first. This is my own reading of the code and has not been checked by a second reviewer.
findings.mitigations: Integrators should call sync immediately before every settle, including native, as the comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 says. The deployer can decide whether sync should require the unlocked state and whether collectProtocolFees should check it, and can correct the A12 text either way.

In src/feeAdapters/V4FeeAdapter.sol, triggerFeeUpdate at lines 72 to 74 and collect at lines 87 to 94 have no access modifier. collect calls POOL_MANAGER.collectProtocolFees(TOKEN_JAR, p.currency, p.amount), and the fee value passed to setProtocolFee comes from the pool override or the policy at lines 61 to 67 and 133 to 143. The TokenJar source has an empty receive function and a release function limited to the releaser, which is 0x0d5cd355e2abeb8fb1552f56c965b867346d6721 on chain. ERC-4337 says transient storage persists across UserOperations in one bundle and must be cleaned up manually when it guards access. I read only the adapter and jar files in the Sourcify bundles.
verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), and the repository's tests call it while locked (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41, test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1023). collectProtocolFees checks the caller and then reverts when the currency is an ERC-20 equal to the synced currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). It does not read the lock. _isUnlocked is declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 and implemented at src/PoolManager.sol:391-394, and a search of src finds no caller. The comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 says the call reverts if the contract is unlocked. The code and the tests at test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1038 behave otherwise. I traced the fund paths myself. The synced check does not depend on the lock, so collection of a synced ERC-20 always reverts and the balance cannot fall between a sync and its settle through this call. Collection of another currency during an unlock lowers the balance by at most protocolFeesAccrued (checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55) and changes no delta. Fees accrue in _swap before the swapper pays (src/PoolManager.sol:238), and the swapper's negative delta must be cleared before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112) or the whole transaction reverts, collection included. Native settlement credits msg.value only (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). A collection with the PoolManager as recipient leaves an ERC-20 balance unchanged and reverts for native currency, because src has no receive or fallback function. A sync left by an earlier caller gives a later settler credit only for a real balance increase since that sync, and a native payment then reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356), which test/PoolManager.t.sol:987-988 covers. I found no path that raises a settle credit or pays out more than accrued fees. This agrees with the researcher and answers the researcher's first lead from a second reading.
verification.corrections: The code facts hold on every network. Only the permissionless controller is specific to mainnet. The repository's own tests expect the present behaviour, so the disagreement is between the code and two texts: the comment at src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40 and assumption A12. The synced check as written rejects collection in more situations than a check tied to the lock would, so the difference removes no protection.

findings.title: Four interface comments and two test helper remarks disagree with the source, and none of them changes who can move funds
findings.difference: None. These are differences between the source text and the repository's own comments, tests and test doubles. They are the same on every network.
findings.mechanism: This unit compared every NatSpec sentence in src/interfaces with the function it describes and read every helper in src/test and test/utils. Six statements do not match the source, in addition to the four recorded in F-006. First, src/interfaces/IHooks.sol:102 says the fee returned by beforeSwap is used only if it is at most 1,000,000. The source reverts with LPFeeTooLarge when the override flag is set and the fee is above the maximum (src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:75-78). The test agrees with the source and expects the revert (test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:151-162), although its own comment says the large fee is not used. Second, IHooks.sol:50 and IHooks.sol:81 describe the delta handed to afterAddLiquidity and afterRemoveLiquidity as the sum of principal, fees and hook delta. The source passes principal plus fees, and subtracts the hook delta only after the hook returns (src/PoolManager.sol:171-178, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:219-243). The test doubles rely on the source behaviour (src/test/FeeTakingHook.sol:54-91, test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:270-322). Third, src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:85-86 calls the Swap event amounts the deltas of the pool's balances. The emitted values are the swapper's deltas, negative for the amount paid in (src/PoolManager.sol:241-250), and the tests expect -100 and 98 for an exact input of 100 (test/PoolManager.t.sol:500-503). Fourth, IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts if the requested amount is not available. That holds for native currency and for tokens with code, and test/PoolManager.t.sol:917-922 states it for an empty manager. For a currency address without code the transfer call succeeds with empty return data and nothing moves (src/types/Currency.sol:60-74), which earlier cycles recorded under assumption A4. Fifth, test/utils/CurrencySettler.sol:20-25 settles native currency without a prior sync and says a sync is not required, while the comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 tells integrators to call sync before a native settle. A native settle that follows a token sync by other code in the same transaction reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:353-356, test/PoolManager.t.sol:976-989). Sixth, src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol:27-33 offers setIsUnlocked and an _isUnlocked override, no test calls setIsUnlocked, and collectProtocolFees never reads the lock (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). This is the test double side of the first item of F-006. I traced each item for a fund effect. A hook that returns an oversized fee can only stop swaps in its own pool. The delta seen by a liquidity hook is the amount the hook can charge against, and the caller delta plus the hook delta still equals the pool delta in every replayed case. The event wording affects readers of logs only. The native settle revert needs code that runs earlier in the same transaction, and it returns the caller's value with the revert.
findings.impact: No loss or freeze found. A hook author who trusts IHooks.sol:102 may ship a hook that makes swaps in its own pool revert when it computes a fee above 100 percent. An integrator that copies the native branch of the test helper without sync(address(0)) can have a native settle reverted by a token sync left earlier in the same transaction.
findings.preconditions: None for the comments. The native settle revert needs a call to sync with a token address earlier in the same transaction, for example from a hook of a pool the caller used or from a contract that bundles several actions.
findings.mitigations: Correct the six texts. Hook authors should cap the fee before setting the override flag. Integrators should call sync(address(0)) before every native settle, as the comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 says.

verification.factCheck: The finding states no chain fact. Its field difference says that the six items are the same on every network, so the fact check is whether the deployed contracts behave as the source reading says. I ran read-only calls on all 21 RPC endpoints of state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 (Ethereum block 26,474,254, Celo 83,493,046, Polygon 97,792,226, Arc 32,649,308, the others at latest). From an unrelated address, sync(address(0)) returned success on all 21, sync of an address without code (0x00000000000000000000000000000000dead0001) reverted with empty data on all 21, settle() and take reverted with ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d) on all 21, and a call with empty calldata reverted on all 21. That matches the source: sync has no lock check, balanceOf on an address without code fails in the return decoding, and the contract has no receive or fallback function. For the fifth item I tested the guard on the deployed code. A caller placed by state override opened unlock, called sync(X) and then settle with 1 wei. Every path of that caller ends in a revert, so nothing is credited. With X set to the identity precompile 0x04, which answers balanceOf with its 36 input bytes, all 21 deployed PoolManagers returned NonzeroNativeValue (0xb0ec849e). The same caller with value 0 after sync(X), and with 1 wei after sync(address(0)), got past settle on all 21. With X set to the native face on Celo (0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438), Polygon (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010) and Arc (0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000), and to USDC on Ethereum, the result was the same. The four interface comments and the two helper remarks are facts of this repository and I read each cited line. Not confirmed: forge is not installed, so I did not run the tests, and I did not exercise take with a currency without code inside an unlock on chain.
verification.codeCheck: All six items hold as stated. One. src/interfaces/IHooks.sol:102 says the returned fee is used only if it is at most 1,000,000. src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305 calls removeOverrideFlagAndValidate when the override flag is set, and src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:75-78 with 43-45 reverts with LPFeeTooLarge above the maximum. test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:151-162 expects that revert, and its comment at line 158 says the large fee is not used. The comment at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:261-262 agrees with the source. Two. IHooks.sol:50 and 81 describe the delta passed to the hook as including the hook delta. src/libraries/Hooks.sol:219-243 encodes the delta it received, which src/PoolManager.sol:171 builds as principal plus fees, and subtracts the hook delta only at lines 230 and 242. src/test/FeeTakingHook.sol:53-91 computes its fee from that value. Three. src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:85-86 calls the event amounts the deltas of the pool balance. src/PoolManager.sol:241-250 emits the delta that src/libraries/Pool.sol:451-462 builds, which is negative for the amount paid in, and test/PoolManager.t.sol:500-503 expects -100 and 98. Four. IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts if the amount is not available. src/types/Currency.sol:60-74 accepts a call that does not revert and returns no data, with no code size check, so take of a currency without code debits the caller and moves nothing. Five. test/utils/CurrencySettler.sol:20-25 settles native currency without sync and says sync is not required. The comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 asks for sync first. Lines 353-356 revert with NonzeroNativeValue when a token is synced and value is sent, and test/PoolManager.t.sol:976-989 covers it. Six. src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol:27-33 has setIsUnlocked and an _isUnlocked override. A search of test/ and src/ finds no call to either, and src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 never reads the lock. I traced each item for a path to funds and looked for missed guards. An oversized override fee reverts the swap before any state change in Pool.swap, so it can only stop swaps in the pool of that hook. The delta shown to a liquidity hook does not change the sum: Hooks.sol:230 and 242 subtract the hook delta from the caller delta, and PoolManager.sol:181-183 books both, so caller delta plus hook delta equals principal plus fees. The subtraction goes through the int128 casts of src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46. The event wording touches no accounting. A take of a currency without code leaves the caller with a negative delta in that id (PoolManager.sol:294). sync of the same address reverts, mint adds to the debt (line 326), clear accepts only a positive delta (lines 311-314), and a pool can return that currency only after someone paid it in, so the unlock ends in CurrencyNotSettled (line 112). The native settle revert returns the value to the caller. Fee collection is limited to the controller (ProtocolFees.sol:48) and to protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction (line 55).

findings.title: Two more places where the repository's tests and test doubles disagree with the library source, and neither changes who can move funds
findings.difference: None. The disagreements are between files of this repository and hold on every network.
findings.mechanism: This extends F-006 with what a replay of test/libraries, test/Tick.t.sol, test/types and the test doubles in src/test found. First, test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:73-83 expects SafeCastOverflow from Pool.modifyLiquidity only when a token amount is above 2^128 - 1. The variable is named maxInt128InTypeU256 and holds Constants.MAX_UINT128. The source casts both amounts to int128: Pool.sol:212-235 takes the signed results of SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288 and SafeCast.toInt128 (SafeCast.sol:40-43) reverts once the amount of an add is above 2^127. For amounts from 2^127 + 1 to 2^128 - 1 the source reverts and the test expects success. One case from the replay: spacing 32767, price 735853766953812733719635225319847024411115828962 (tick 873548), range -131068 to 98301, liquidity 2300850342447660200206975412810193765, which is below the per tick cap 6076470837873901133274546561281575204. The amount of currency1 is 313585663563401618519606321096647269736 and the source reverts with SafeCastOverflow. Out of 400,000 random parameter sets 346 fell in this window. Every other outcome, including the order of the eight revert conditions at Pool.t.sol:51-70, matched the source. Second, src/test/SqrtPriceMathEchidnaTest.sol:144-197 asserts that the signed helpers return a positive amount for positive liquidity and a non-positive amount for negative liquidity. The source returns minus the rounded up amount for positive liquidity and the rounded down amount for negative liquidity (SqrtPriceMath.sol:266-270 and 283-287). On 200,000 random inputs the assertion for positive liquidity fails 135,655 times and the one for negative liquidity 48,354 times as written, and every other invariant of that file holds. The forge tests use the sign of the source: a negative delta is owed by the caller (PoolManager.sol:183 and 368-378), and test/libraries/StateLibrary.t.sol:300-301 negates the delta of an add to get the amount paid. The echidna harness is not part of forge test, so nothing in the repository runs it. Third, a correction to the fourth item of F-006: test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:135-158 calls swap for a nonzero amount only when it expects a revert. It makes no call for a valid limit and no call when a zeroForOne limit equals MIN_SQRT_PRICE, so that file says nothing about the boundary that Pool.sol:328-330 rejects and contains no successful nonzero swap. The third item of F-006 was replayed: 8,795 of 120,000 random cases had a zero amount with a 100 percent swap fee, where Pool.t.sol:129-131 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut and Pool.sol:311-320 returns a zero delta without touching state.
findings.impact: None on funds. In the first case the source refuses an add that the test would let through, so it is stricter than the test. A removal whose amount is 2^127 or more reverts at the same cast and has to be split, which an earlier cleared item on the int128 casts already covers. In the second case the source sign is the one the accounting in PoolManager needs: with the sign of the echidna file an add would credit the caller.
findings.preconditions: None. No account gains anything from these disagreements.
findings.mitigations: Change the bound at test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:73 to the int128 maximum and bring the sign assertions in src/test/SqrtPriceMathEchidnaTest.sol in line with SqrtPriceMath, so that the tests and the harness can serve as a reference for the source.

verification.factCheck: The finding claims no chain fact. Its claims concern files of this repository. I checked each one against the text and with a Python transcription of the libraries that I wrote myself with EVM word semantics. Case one reproduces exactly. With spacing 32767 the per tick cap is 6076470837873901133274546561281575204. The price 735853766953812733719635225319847024411115828962 lies in tick 873548. The ticks -131068 and 98301 are multiples of 32767. getAmount1Delta rounded up for liquidity 2300850342447660200206975412810193765 gives 313585663563401618519606321096647269736, which is above 2^127 and below 2^128, and the source path reverts with SafeCastOverflow. The reference that the test uses (test/utils/LiquidityAmounts.sol:99-107, rounded down) stays below Constants.MAX_UINT128 (test/utils/Constants.sol:21), so the test sets no expectRevert and that input would fail. Case two reproduces in direction. On 100,000 random inputs the assertion for positive liquidity failed 49,865 times for each of the two signed helpers, and the assertion for negative liquidity failed 46,525 and 48,375 times. No file under test/ imports SqrtPriceMathEchidnaTest. Case three matches the text of test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129-170. The cast in modifyLiquidity cannot be reached by a plain eth_call because the function needs an unlock callback from a contract, so I did not test it on chain. The on-chain queries I ran for this unit are listed under the spot checks.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.modifyLiquidity passes the signed results of SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta through SafeCast.toInt128 in all three branches (src/libraries/Pool.sol:209-236). The signed helpers return minus the rounded up amount for a liquidity delta of zero or more and the rounded down amount for a negative delta (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288). toInt128(int256) reverts when the value does not fit (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). An add therefore reverts when its rounded up amount is 2^127 + 1 or more, and a removal reverts when its rounded down amount is 2^127 or more. test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:73-83 compares the amounts with Constants.MAX_UINT128, so the source is the stricter side for amounts from 2^127 + 1 to 2^128 - 1. The eight earlier branches at Pool.t.sol:51-70 follow the order in which the source reaches them: checkTicks (Pool.sol:94-98), the underflow in LiquidityMath.addDelta for a negative delta on an empty tick (Pool.sol:529, src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19), the empty position check (src/libraries/Position.sol:84-87), the cap on the lower tick before the upper tick (Pool.sol:165-173), and flipTick for the lower tick before the upper tick (Pool.sol:175-180). The sign in the source is the one the accounting needs. A negative delta is added to the caller's slot (src/PoolManager.sol:183 and 368-384), settle adds what was paid (PoolManager.sol:364) and unlock reverts while any slot is nonzero (PoolManager.sol:112). src/test/SqrtPriceMathEchidnaTest.sol:144-197 asserts the opposite sign. Pool.swap reverts at a 100 percent fee only for a positive amount and returns a zero delta for a zero amount before any state is written (Pool.sol:311-320), while Pool.t.sol:129 expects a revert for zero. Pool.t.sol:135-158 calls swap for a nonzero amount only inside the branches that expect a revert. I looked for a guard or a path that would turn one of these disagreements into a fund effect and found none. A removal that hits the cast can be split, because both amounts scale with the liquidity delta. PoolManager.swap rejects a zero amount (PoolManager.sol:193), so Pool.swap sees zero only when a beforeSwap hook cancels the amount in its own pool (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:273-279), and then nothing is written.
verification.corrections: No party gains or loses through these disagreements, so the actor value carries no weight here; unprivileged is the value the existing F-006 entry already has. The counts 346 of 400,000, 135,655 and 48,354 could not be reproduced because the finding does not state its sampling distribution; the direction of each result reproduces. The third part repeats a correction that the cycle 1 verification of F-006 already recorded. The statement that nothing in the repository runs the echidna harness needs one addition: .github/workflows/mythx.yml:60 lists SqrtPriceMathEchidnaTest under contracts/test/, a directory that does not exist in this repository, and echidna.config.yml is present. No forge test runs the harness. On the limit for an add: an amount of exactly 2^127 passes, because the amount is negated before the cast and -2^127 fits int128. A removal passes up to 2^127 - 1.

findings.title: Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
findings.difference: Ethereum has no party that can make a chosen transaction fail. Robinhood Chain runs the ArbOS 61 compliance filtering feature. Its sequencer drops transactions that involve an address on a restricted list, and an operator account can write any transaction hash into the ArbFilteredTransactionsManager precompile at 0x74. The state transition then skips that transaction, raises the sender's nonce and consumes its gas, even when the transaction was force-included from Ethereum. On chain, filtering has been enabled since 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC and one externally owned account, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7 with nonce 6,237, is the registered filterer.
findings.mechanism: Every way to move funds out of the PoolManager is a call made inside unlock: modifyLiquidity with a negative delta, burn of ERC-6909 claims, and take. The contract has no exit that works without a successful child chain transaction. Step 1: the sequencer simulates each transaction and rejects it when it breaks a configured rule. The documented rule types cover a restricted sender or recipient, CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 or SELFDESTRUCT against a restricted address, and token transfers from or to one. Step 2: a user who then sends the transaction through the delayed inbox on Ethereum gets it included after the delay, but the filterer registers its hash first and RevertedTxHook skips the EVM call. The client code checks only whether the hash is in the list, so the list is whatever the filterer writes. Step 3: the user's liquidity and claims stay in the PoolManager with no other route out. The same rules mean that a take to a restricted recipient, or a hook or token that calls a restricted address on every operation, makes the transaction unacceptable to the sequencer. If the PoolManager, the PositionManager, or a widely used token or hook were put on the list, every transaction that calls it would be rejected. I could not confirm which rule set Robinhood has configured or whether any core contract is exempt, because the list is held off chain as salted hashes.
findings.impact: Funds are frozen for the affected sender or contract and cannot be taken by the filterer through this path. At the time of the query the PoolManager on this chain held 21,321 ETH, 16.98M USDG, 1,321 WETH and 3,134 ANT stock tokens. A listing of one LP freezes that LP's positions. A listing of a shared contract freezes every position that depends on it.
findings.preconditions: The filterer account, the compliance list provider or the chain owner must act. No unprivileged party can add a hash or an address. A third party can cause rejection of someone else's transaction only if that transaction already executes code or transfers chosen by the third party, for example a hook that pays out to addresses the third party controls.
findings.mitigations: Nothing in core can restore a forced exit. The deployer can ask the operator for a written commitment that the PoolManager and periphery addresses are never listed and can monitor FilteredTransactionAdded events on 0x74. Pool creators on this chain should avoid hooks that call or pay addresses supplied by third parties. LPs should treat force inclusion as unavailable when sizing positions.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the Robinhood Chain page on differences from Ethereum. It says that sequencer-level screening excludes any transaction associated with a sanctioned address. I fetched the Arbitrum compliance filtering page. It describes sequencer simulation against a restricted address list, rule examples for the origin, for CALL, CREATE, CREATE2 and SELFDESTRUCT targets and for token transfers, and a precompile where an authorised account registers the hash of a delayed inbox transaction so that the state transition fails it on inclusion and consumes its gas. I read arbos/tx_processor.go at Nitro v3.11.3. RevertedTxHook reads FilteredTransactions().IsFilteredFree(txHash), raises the sender nonce, sets the remaining gas to zero and returns an error. The caller in core/state_transition.go of the Offchain Labs go-ethereum fork (master branch) skips evm.Call when that error is set. StartTxHook sends a filtered deposit to the filtered funds recipient. I read precompiles/ArbFilteredTransactionsManager.go at v3.11.3. AddFilteredTransaction checks only that the caller is in the filterer set. On chain at Robinhood Chain block 120,625,526 on 2026-11-22: getAllTransactionFilterers() returns one address, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7, which has no code and nonce 6,237. getTransactionFilteringFrom() returns 1782295200, which is 2026-06-24 10:00 UTC. getFilteredFundsRecipient() returns 0xbbbd433db8700d8927faaaaf482e007e293ed568. A scan of all logs of address 0x74 from block 0 to the head returns 6,234 FilteredTransactionAdded events, the first on 2026-06-30 and the last on 2026-11-20, and no FilteredTransactionDeleted event. The filter is in regular use. The PoolManager held 21,372 ETH, 16.84M USDG, 1,314 WETH and 3,134 ANT. The ethbeat page says that users can be censored when the operator registers their transaction hash in the precompile, even when the transaction is force-included through the delayed inbox. Not confirmed: which rules Robinhood configured at its sequencer, and that the running client v3.13.0-rc.9 carries the same hook code as the v3.11.3 tag I read. The on-chain events are consistent with the tagged code.
verification.codeCheck: take is the only user path that transfers a currency out of the PoolManager, and it requires an open unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/PoolManager.sol:96-99). The only other transfer is collectProtocolFees, which accepts the fee controller alone (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). Liquidity removal and claim burning only create a positive delta for msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336), and unlock reverts unless every delta is cleared (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Positions are stored under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161) and a burn of claims needs the holder, an operator or an allowance (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). A holder therefore needs at least one successful transaction of its own before any other account can exit for it. The code has no exit that works without a successful child chain transaction. No guard in src/ can help, because a filtered transaction never reaches the EVM call. Hook calls forward all gas and revert the action when the call fails (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-137). This matters only for the sequencer rule on CALL targets. No test in test/ models a chain that fails a transaction before execution.
verification.corrections: The severity stays high because the freeze needs the filterer account, the list provider or the chain owner. The profile quotes a dashboard figure of about 1,351 filtered hashes. The chain shows 6,234 add events from the one filterer account. The claims about a take to a restricted recipient and about hooks or tokens that touch a restricted address depend on the configured rule set, which is still unknown. The finding cites the precompile source at the v3.11.0 tag. I read that file at v3.11.3. A filtered deposit or retryable is redirected to 0xbbbd433db8700d8927faaaaf482e007e293ed568. That redirect moves bridged funds of the filtered sender and does not touch PoolManager balances.

findings.title: Robinhood Stock Tokens and USDG let the issuer block, pause, burn or upgrade the tokens held by the PoolManager
findings.difference: The assets this chain is built for are issuer-controlled in a more concentrated way than a typical Ethereum token. All Robinhood Stock Tokens are beacon proxies behind one contract, 0xe10b6f6b275de231345c20d14ab812db62151b00, which is both the upgrade beacon and the access registry with isBlocked, blockAccounts, pause and upgradeTo. The shared logic contract has adminBurn(address,uint256) and pause. USDG is an upgradeable Paxos token with isFrozen and decreaseSupplyFromAddress. The PoolManager already holds both.
findings.mechanism: Step 1, block or pause: if the registry blocks the PoolManager address or a token is paused, the token's transfer call fails. Currency.transfer treats a failed call as an error and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed, so every take and every collectProtocolFees in that token reverts. Settling needs a transfer into the PoolManager, which a pause or a block on the recipient would stop as well. One registry entry covers every stock token at once, and A6 applies because one address holds all pools. An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair and call mint to hold the frozen side as an ERC-6909 claim, because mint moves no tokens. The claim cannot be turned into tokens until the block is lifted. Step 2, burn: adminBurn against the PoolManager lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no matching delta. Pool reserves, claims and accrued fees then exceed the balance. Takes keep succeeding until the balance runs out, and the last LPs and claim holders bear the shortfall. Step 3, upgrade: upgradeTo on the beacon changes the code of every stock token in one transaction, which removes the A4 expectation that token code is fixed. I read function selectors and view results from chain. I did not read verified source, so the exact transfer check against the registry and the role holders are unconfirmed. Stock token splits and dividends do not create a balance change, because they move uiMultiplier and leave balanceOf fixed.
findings.impact: At the time of the query the PoolManager held 3,134.87 ANT stock tokens and 16,984,261 USDG. A block or pause freezes the stock token side of every pool that uses the affected tokens. A burn creates a loss equal to the burned amount, carried by whoever withdraws last. The other currency in each pair stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer (Robinhood Assets (Jersey) Limited for stock tokens, Paxos for USDG) or a holder of the relevant role must act. isBlocked(PoolManager) and isFrozen(PoolManager) are false today and both tokens are unpaused. No unprivileged party can trigger any of these functions.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can ask both issuers to confirm in writing how the PoolManager address is treated and can monitor the registry and beacon for block, pause and upgrade events. Pool creators and LPs should size stock token and USDG positions with a freeze and a shortfall in mind. A later cycle should read the verified source of the logic and registry contracts.

With the PoolManager blocked or the token paused, msg.sender of that call is the PoolManager and Stock.transfer reverts, so both functions revert for the token. A payment into the PoolManager is a token transfer with the PoolManager as recipient, which the same checks stop. sync still works because balanceOf has no check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). mint moves no tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), so an LP can remove liquidity and hold the blocked side as a claim. A later burn of the claim still needs take to reach the tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). A burn by the issuer lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no delta. The only place the code compares balances is the checked subtraction in _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), which would revert one settle if the burn fell between sync and settle of the same transaction. At any other time nothing reconciles the balance with pool accounting, and takes succeed until the balance runs out. I found no guard the finding missed. test/types/Currency.t.sol and test/PoolManager.t.sol:947 cover a token whose transfer reverts. No test covers a token that lowers the PoolManager balance on its own.

The seizure path for a frozen address is wipeFrozenAddress in the facet, whose source I did not read. USDG is a claimable rewards token. findings.title: One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
findings.difference: This is a property of assets on mainnet, and mainnet protocol rules are the reference. USDC, USDT and PYUSD each let one issuer role block a single address. USDC blocks transfers from and to a blacklisted address. USDT blocks transfers sent by a blacklisted address and lets the owner call destroyBlackFunds, which sets that address's balance to zero. PYUSD blocks transfers from and to a frozen address and lets the asset protection role call wipeFrozenAddress, which sets the balance to zero.
findings.mechanism: All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all accrued protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. take calls currency.transfer and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86), so once the address is blocked nobody can withdraw that token from any pool. collectProtocolFees fails the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). For USDC and PYUSD a transfer into the PoolManager also fails, so settle can no longer be funded in that token (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). For USDT the blocked address can still receive, so users can keep paying USDT in while nothing can leave. If the issuer then zeroes the balance, the pools keep their accounting but the tokens behind it are gone, which is the undercollateralised state described in A2. LPs can still remove liquidity, take the other currency of the pair, and convert the blocked currency's delta into ERC-6909 claims with mint, which does no token transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claims stay unredeemable while the block lasts.
findings.impact: At block 26470360 the existing PoolManager holds 79,953,224 USDT, 63,053,277 PYUSD and 30,404,253 USDC. One blocklist transaction per token freezes that token for every LP, every claim holder and the protocol fee balance at once. A wipe by Tether or Paxos turns the freeze into a loss of the full balance. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The issuer role must act: the USDC blacklister (0x0a06be16275b95a7d2567fbdae118b36c7da78f9), the USDT owner (0xc6cde7c39eb2f0f0095f41570af89efc2c1ea828) or a PYUSD ASSET_PROTECTION_ROLE holder. The PoolManager is not blocked on any of the three today. I found no way for an unprivileged party to cause the block directly. I did not research what legal or policy triggers each issuer applies to contract addresses.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove this from a singleton. Interfaces and LPs can treat issuer-controlled tokens as carrying whole-protocol exposure instead of per-pool exposure. Monitoring isBlacklisted, isBlackListed and isFrozen for the PoolManager address gives early warning. Routers can fall back to ERC-6909 claims for settlement when token transfers to the PoolManager fail.

findings.title: Role holders on GHO, syrupUSDC, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD can pause, burn, move or replace balances that the Monad PoolManager holds
findings.difference: Five further tokens with issuer controls sit at the single PoolManager address on Monad, next to the dollar tokens that F-015 already lists. The PoolManager holds 2,729,903 GHO, 1,645,837 mUSD, 1,561,546 syrupUSDC, 299,944 apxUSD and 269,214 shMON.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager records what each pool is owed and trusts balanceOf to stay equal to the sum. GHO, apxUSD, shMON and mUSD are proxies, so the party that controls the proxy can replace the token logic. The apxUSD and mUSD implementations contain pause, and a paused token makes every take of that currency revert at src/types/Currency.sol:73-86, which stops removals and swaps in every pool that uses it. The syrupUSDC and apxUSD code contains burn(address,uint256), and the mUSD implementation contains forceTransfer(address,address,uint256) and freeze. If the role holder applies one of them to the PoolManager address, the balance falls while the pool accounting stays unchanged, and the last liquidity providers to withdraw cannot be paid. This reading rests on the selectors found in the deployed bytecode. Which accounts hold the roles, and whether burn(address,uint256) needs an allowance, was not confirmed.
findings.impact: All pools on Monad that use the affected token. The amounts at the time of the query are listed above: about 6.2 million units of dollar tokens and 269,214 shMON.
findings.preconditions: The issuer or the holder of the relevant role acts against the PoolManager address or pauses or upgrades the token. An ordinary account cannot trigger it.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers can weigh the issuer controls of each token before they supply it. The deployer cannot remove the dependency, because one address holds the balances of every pool.

verification.codeCheck: A token payout is one call to transfer, and take reverts when that call reverts or returns anything other than nothing or a 32 byte true (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86, src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A token payment is measured as balanceOf(PoolManager) minus the synced value (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), so a token that blocks transfers to the PoolManager also blocks payments. The PoolManager stores no reserve per currency. Pool state is liquidity, price and fee growth (src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91), and claims are ERC-6909 balances (src/ERC6909.sol:15-19). A burn or forced transfer of the PoolManager balance therefore changes no accounting, and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last, because their take reverts in the token for lack of balance. One guard reduces the pause case. modifyLiquidity and swap only write deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:145-227), and mint and burn close deltas through ERC-6909 claims without any call to the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). During a pause or a freeze of the PoolManager address a provider can still remove liquidity into claims and a swapper can still trade from and into claims. The token itself cannot enter or leave the PoolManager until the issuer lifts the measure.
verification.corrections: The mechanism says a paused token stops removals and swaps in every pool that uses it. The code stops take and settle for that currency. Removals and swaps that are closed with mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims continue (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), so the effect of a pause is that the token cannot be paid out or paid in. The balances at block 124498672 are 2,640,693 GHO, 1,650,963 mUSD, 1,561,546 syrupUSDC, 299,944 apxUSD and 268,856 shMON. shMON has a proxy admin at 0x00b16590295092f12f4cec655296b6129c49489c in addition to the owner named in the finding. The actor value issuer is correct. No step is open to an ordinary account.

findings.title: USDC and USDT0 issuers can block the PoolManager address, which stops every pool in that currency, and USDT0's owner can burn the blocked balance
findings.difference: Ethereum has the same class of issuer control for USDC, so this is a property of the assets pools hold on HyperEVM and is listed for completeness of the per network picture. On HyperEVM the two main stablecoins are native Circle USDC at 0xb88339CB7199b77E23DB6E890353E22632Ba630f and USDT0 at 0xB8CE59FC3717ada4C02eaDF9682A9e934F625ebb. USDC has a blacklister role (0x33aa4e959132e49552cb754fb6585bdcdf874beb) and a pauser, and a blacklisted address can neither send nor receive. USDT0 has an owner (0xb64a89ad247a2d691a728bb6822a85eedd7fc541) that maintains a blocklist and can call destroyBlockedFunds on a blocked address. Both tokens sit behind upgradeable proxies. USDC is also the asset HyperCore treats specially under AQAv2, which raises the share of pool liquidity likely to sit in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, all ERC-6909 claims and all protocol fees in one currency share one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. Every payout runs take, which calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as sender and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. If the USDC blacklister lists the PoolManager, or the USDC pauser pauses the token, every USDC transfer from or to the PoolManager reverts. take of USDC fails for all pools and inbound payment fails too, so the balance check in settle never sees new funds (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). 4. If the USDT0 owner blocks the PoolManager, transfers out revert while transfers in still succeed, so users can pay in and nobody can take out. The owner can then call destroyBlockedFunds and burn the whole PoolManager balance. Pool state still says the tokens are owed, and every later take of USDT0 fails for lack of balance. 5. modifyLiquidity and swap only move deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184 and 187-227). An LP can still remove liquidity, take the other currency and call mint to hold the blocked currency as an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The claim is redeemable only if the block is lifted.
findings.impact: All USDC or all USDT0 held by the PoolManager across every pool, plus claims and protocol fees in that currency. A block freezes them. destroyBlockedFunds on USDT0 removes them for good. The other currency of each affected pool stays withdrawable.
findings.preconditions: The token issuer acts against the PoolManager address: Circle's blacklister or pauser for USDC, the USDT0 owner for USDT0, or the proxy admin of either token through an upgrade. No unprivileged party can trigger this. On-chain reads at block 51,941,800 show isBlacklisted(PoolManager) false, paused() false and isBlocked(PoolManager) false.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot remove the control. LPs can limit exposure by choosing pool pairs with that risk in mind. Front ends can watch for Blacklisted and BlockPlaced events that name the PoolManager and tell LPs to exit the other side of each pool with take and to hold the blocked side with mint. Integrators should not treat ERC-6909 claims in these currencies as equal to the token while a block is in force.

findings.title: Celo governance can move native CELO out of the PoolManager through the CELO token proxy and the transfer precompile
findings.difference: On Ethereum no contract can debit ETH from another account. On Celo a precompile at 0xfd transfers native CELO from any address named in its input to any other address. The precompile accepts calls only from the CELO token address 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438. That address is an upgradeable proxy owned by the Celo Governance contract.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager keeps native CELO as its own account balance. Pools that use currency address(0) and pools that use the CELO token address both draw on that balance (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96, and the on-chain balances are equal). The precompile reads the debited account from its first argument and checks only the caller. The current token implementation passes msg.sender or an allowance checked from address. A new implementation installed through _setImplementation could pass the PoolManager address as from and any recipient as to. The PoolManager has no code that runs on such a debit and no way to veto it. After the debit, take for either CELO currency pays out until the balance is exhausted (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the last LPs to withdraw bear the loss. A new implementation that makes transfer revert would freeze every pool that uses the CELO token address, because take calls transfer on it (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). Pools that use address(0) would still pay out by value transfer in that case. Governance returns stage durations of 1 day, 7 days and 3 days, which this review reads as approval, referendum and execution, so a standard proposal is public for days before it can execute. The hotfix path needs the approver multisig and the Security Council and has a 1 day execution window with no referendum.
findings.impact: All native CELO in the PoolManager, 6,167.7 CELO at the time of the query, across both currency faces. Every CELO holder on the chain carries the same exposure. Other tokens in the PoolManager are not reachable by this path.
findings.preconditions: A Celo governance proposal or a hotfix approved by the approver multisig and the Security Council must replace the CELO token implementation. No unprivileged path was found: an eth_call to the precompile from an address other than the token fails, and _setImplementation reverts for a sender other than Governance.
findings.mitigations: Watch the value of _getImplementation() on the CELO token proxy and the Governance contract for queued proposals and hotfixes that target 0x471E...a438. The referendum stage gives LPs days to withdraw before a standard proposal executes. A hotfix gives no such window. LPs who want protection from a token contract that reverts can use pools with currency address(0), which pay out without calling the token.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the celo-kona precompile source. The transfer precompile sits at 0xff minus 2, which is 0xfd. It halts unless the caller equals the chain's CELO token address, then reads from, to and value from a 96 byte input and calls the internal transfer between those two accounts. Nothing ties from to the account that called the token. The former op-geth client does the same in celo_contracts.go: IsCallerCeloToken, then a transfer between the decoded from and to. The Celo token duality page says the precompile changes balances in the state database and can only be called by the CELO token. On chain at Celo block 83,451,124: _getOwner() on 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 returns 0xD533Ca259b330c7A88f74E000a3FaEa2d63B7972, and the registry at 0x000000000000000000000000000000000000ce10 returns that address for Governance and the token address for GoldToken and CeloToken. _getImplementation() returns 0xFeA1B35f1D5f2A58532a70e7A32e6F2D3Bc4F7B1 and getVersionNumber() returns 1, 2, 0, 0. eth_getBalance of the PoolManager and CELO.balanceOf(PoolManager) both return 6166941836241617055206 wei. An eth_call of _setImplementation from Governance returns and the same call from 0xA1 reverts with 'sender was not owner'. An eth_call to 0xfd with input (PoolManager, 0xA1, 1) succeeds when the caller is the token address and fails with a precompile error when the caller is 0x01. The GoldToken source on the monorepo master branch passes msg.sender in transfer and an allowance checked from in transferFrom. That source reports version 1.3.0.0 and the deployed implementation reports 1.2.0.0, so I could not match the deployed code line by line. Governance.stageDurations() returns 86,400, 604,800 and 259,200 seconds. Proposals.sol on master declares the struct fields in the order approval, referendum, execution, which settles the reading the researcher left open. hotfixExecutionTimeWindow() returns 86,400. In Governance.sol approveHotfix accepts the approver or the Security Council, prepareHotfix requires both approvals, and executeHotfix requires both and an unexpired time limit. No referendum is involved. approver() is a contract whose required() returns 3 and whose getOwners() returns 14 addresses. securityCouncil() is 0x51a3a77bAF58FEf0309452ceacB09221E556F223, which has no code on Celo and equals the Ethereum Safe 0x4092A77bAF58fef0309452cEaCb09221e556E112 plus the alias offset. That Safe has threshold 2 and two owners, each a Safe with threshold 6 and 8 owners.
verification.codeCheck: balanceOfSelf returns address(this).balance for address(0) and token.balanceOf(address(this)) for any other currency (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). On Celo both expressions read the same number, so pools on address(0) and pools on the CELO token share one balance. take debits the caller's delta and then calls transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The native branch is a call with value that reverts with NativeTransferFailed when it fails (src/types/Currency.sol:45-53), so after an outside debit takes succeed until the balance runs out and later ones revert. The token branch calls transfer(address,uint256) on the currency and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed on failure (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), so an implementation whose transfer reverts blocks every take of the token currency. sync on the token calls balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). I looked for a guard and found none. The contract has no receive or fallback function and the only payable functions are settle and settleFor (src/PoolManager.sol:300 and 305). Nothing in src/ compares the balance with pool accounting outside the sync and settle pair. The delta count check at the end of unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112) covers one transaction and cannot see a debit made by another contract. I also looked for an unprivileged route to the same debit. The PoolManager calls only transfer and balanceOf on a currency, so it never grants a token allowance and transferFrom cannot debit it. The token address cannot be used as a hook: its low 14 bits are 0x2438, which sets the before swap returns delta flag without the before swap flag, and isValidHookAddress rejects that (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:111). test/Sync.t.sol:255-276 covers a settle with value while a NativeERC20 is synced. No test models a third party debit of the manager's native balance or a change of token implementation.
verification.corrections: 1. The impact is wider than stated for pools that list the CELO token as a currency. A replaced implementation could report a larger balanceOf between sync and settle. _settle credits the difference to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), and the caller can swap that credit for the paired currency in every pool that lists the CELO token and take it out. The statement that other tokens are not reachable holds for the precompile debit alone. Pools on address(0) are exposed to the precompile debit alone. 2. The hotfix path needs 3 of 14 approver signers and the Security Council. The Security Council address is the alias of the Ethereum Safe that also owns Celo's ProxyAdmin on both layers, so one signer set sits in the predeploy upgrade path and in the CELO token hotfix path. 3. If transfer reverts, an LP in a CELO token pool can still turn a positive delta into ERC-6909 claims with mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which makes no token call. The claim stays inside the PoolManager, so this is bookkeeping and gives no exit. 4. The balance was 6,166.94 CELO at my read against 6,167.7 in the finding. 5. Severity stays high because the actor is chain governance. The exposure today is small and is shared by every CELO holder.
