findings.title: B20 precompile tokens on Base give the issuer seize, pause and policy control over the PoolManager balance, and their rules change at hard forks
findings.difference: Since the Beryl upgrade on 25 June 2026, Base has a native token standard called B20. Anyone can create a token through a factory precompile at 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000, and all B20 tokens share logic that runs natively in the node. Each token has role gated mint, burn and seizeWithMemo, a pause switch per feature, and policy slots that are checked on every transfer against the sender, the receiver and msg.sender. The policies are allowlists or blocklists stored in a shared Policy Registry precompile, and one policy can back many tokens and be administered by a third party. Base changes the shared logic at hard forks: Cobalt added seize, and Denim on 5 November 2026 started to enforce the executor policy on plain transfer calls. Ethereum has no enshrined token logic of this kind.
findings.mechanism: 1. A pool is created with a B20 token as one currency. Users pay in with sync, a token transfer and settle, which credits balanceOf(PoolManager) minus the synced reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). 2. Every payout calls transfer on the token with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). For a B20 token that call passes through the TRANSFER pause check, then TRANSFER_EXECUTOR_POLICY on msg.sender, TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY on from, and TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY on to. msg.sender and from are both the PoolManager. 3. If the token admin pauses TRANSFER, binds a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager, or the admin of a referenced policy removes the PoolManager from an allowlist or adds it to a blocklist, the transfer reverts and take reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. Every pool, every ERC-6909 claim and the protocol fee balance in that currency are stuck together because they share one holder address. collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer path (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 4. If the issuer has configured SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY so that the PoolManager is not exempt, an account with SEIZE_ROLE can call seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, amount, memo). The seize skips allowances and the three transfer policies. The PoolManager balance falls without any delta being recorded, so the pools hold less than their accounting says, and the last LPs and claim holders to withdraw cannot be paid. 5. A hard fork can produce the freeze in step 3 with no action by the issuer after pool creation. Before Denim a token with a restrictive executor allowlist still allowed holder initiated transfer, so the PoolManager could pay out. Since Denim the same token rejects transfer from any msg.sender that is not on the executor allowlist. 6. A seize or pause in the middle of a settlement cannot be turned into credit: a lower balance makes reservesNow minus reservesBefore underflow and revert (src/PoolManager.sol:360).
findings.impact: All liquidity, ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees held in the affected B20 token on Base. A seize is a direct loss for LPs of that token. A pause or policy change freezes the token side of every pool that uses it. The other currency of each pool is not affected. Which B20 tokens the Base PoolManager holds today, and in what amounts, could not be listed in this cycle because the public RPC rate limited log queries and the Base explorer blocked the request. The PoolManager's ETH, WETH and USDC on Base are not B20 tokens: the factory returns false for isB20(USDC).
findings.preconditions: A B20 token with market value is used in v4 pools on Base. For a freeze, the token admin, the pauser, or the admin of a policy the token references must act, or a Base hard fork must tighten enforcement for a configuration the token already has. For a seize, the issuer must hold SEIZE_ROLE and must have set SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY to a policy that does not authorise the PoolManager. With the slot unset no account is seizable. An unprivileged attacker cannot do any of this to a token issued by someone else. An attacker who issues their own B20 token gets no more than a hostile ERC-20 already gives on any chain.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators and LPs should read, for every B20 currency, the three transfer policy slots, the seize policy slots, the holders of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and PAUSE_ROLE, and the admin of each referenced policy, and should treat a non renounced admin as able to freeze or seize. Front ends and routers on Base can call isAuthorized on the Policy Registry for the PoolManager under each bound policy and warn when it is false or when the policy admin is live. LPs caught by a freeze can still remove liquidity and keep the frozen side as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which does not call the token, and take the other currency. The deployer should track each Base upgrade changelog for B20 changes before activation.

sources.supports: B20 runs as precompiles in the Base node, is upgraded through hard forks, is created by anyone through the factory, and has roles, pause vectors and policies.
Policy scopes and the account each one checks: sender, receiver, msg.sender as executor, mint receiver, seize exempt and seize receiver. Policies are shared and updated by a policy admin.
seizeWithMemo moves a holder balance to a destination, skips allowances and transfer policies, and works only for holders not authorised under SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY.
Denim enforces TRANSFER_EXECUTOR_POLICY on msg.sender for transfer as well as transferFrom, a breaking change for tokens with a restrictive executor policy.
Precompile addresses of the factory, the Policy Registry and the Activation Registry, and the role and policy identifiers.
Activation dates of Beryl, Cobalt and Denim on Base mainnet.

On chain check: eth_getCode at the factory returns empty code while eth_call isB20(PoolManager) and isB20(USDC) return false and getB20Address returns an address starting 0xb2. policyExists(2) returns true. balanceOf and transfer on an uninitialised 0xb2 address revert.

verification.factCheck: All six Base docs pages were fetched and say what the finding reports. The upgrades page lists Beryl on 25 June 2026, Cobalt on 30 September 2026 and Denim on 5 November 2026 for Base Mainnet. The introduction states that B20 runs as precompiles in the node, that Base upgrades the logic through hard forks, that every token is created through the factory, and that TRANSFER, MINT, BURN and SEIZE can be paused separately. The policies page gives the scope table: sender policy on from, receiver policy on to, executor policy on msg.sender, and a policy admin who can change membership for every token that references the policy. The Cobalt note confirms that seizeWithMemo skips allowances and the three transfer policies and that an unset SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY makes no account seizable. The Denim note confirms that the executor policy now runs on transfer and calls the change breaking for tokens with a restrictive executor policy. On chain at Base block 60,794,561 on 22 November 2026: eth_getCode at the factory is empty, isB20(PoolManager) and isB20(USDC) return false, policyExists(2) returns true, and balanceOf and transfer on the uninitialised address 0xb200000000000000000001000000000000000001 revert. I also closed the gap the finding left open about exposure. The explorer lists recent transfers between the PoolManager and two B20 tokens. OUSD (name OpenUSD, 0xB2000000000000000000002fEb517dFeC7415344, isB20 true, code 0xef, 6 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 5,341,029 of a total supply of 93,186,135. Its TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY is policy 122, whose admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246 has no code. The other five scopes are unset, pausedFeatures is empty, and the PoolManager is authorised under policy 122 today. AMDC (name Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., 0xB2000000000000000000000d8Ce462E99ee7A47B, 8 decimals): balanceOf(PoolManager) is 34.38. Policy 5 (admin 0xec0f05c174e54fbf0fe16ad930a8afebce612812) is bound to the sender, receiver, executor and mint receiver scopes, and SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY is policy 129 (admin 0x38467be00970af18076fd08f6b4cf38ba91572b1). The PoolManager is authorised under both today, so it can transfer and is seize exempt. Not confirmed: who holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE, SEIZE_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE on either token, because the public endpoints refused archive log queries. The list of B20 tokens at the PoolManager is a sample of the 50 latest transfers and is incomplete.
verification.codeCheck: sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) for the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). _settle credits balanceOf minus the stored reserves with checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), so a balance that fell between sync and settle reverts and gives no credit. take records the negative delta and then calls transfer with the PoolManager as msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). A reverting token call ends in a revert that wraps ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). No storage in src/ tracks reserves per currency: every payout depends on the live token balance, so a seize or burn of the PoolManager balance is not detected and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last. mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims do not call the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), and modifyLiquidity does not call it either (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), so the claim based exit in the mitigations works at the core level. The balanceOf call decodes return data, and the transfer call is a raw call with no code size check, so a token whose code is the single byte 0xef works with this code. The live OUSD balance supports that. Tests cover a transfer that fails (test/PoolManager.t.sol:924-957) and a balance that only grows between sync and settle (test/Sync.t.sol:82-253). No test in test/ models a token that pauses, blocks the PoolManager, or lowers its balance from outside.
verification.corrections: 1. The finding misses a second loss path. burnBlocked(from, amount) has existed since Beryl and is still callable. It destroys the balance of a holder that is not authorised under TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY, and it needs BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE and an unpaused BURN feature. It does not read SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY. The statement that no balance can be removed while the seize slot is unset is therefore too strong: an issuer who blocks the PoolManager under the sender policy and holds BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE can burn its balance. OUSD has a sender policy bound, so this path applies to it if that role is granted. 2. The exposure is no longer hypothetical. The PoolManager holds about 5.34 million OUSD, and one account without code administers the policy that decides whether the PoolManager may send it. 3. take reverts with WrappedError that carries ERC20TransferFailed as context. 4. The claim based exit needs a caller whose unlock callback can call mint. Whether the deployed position manager offers that is outside this repository and was not checked. 5. The fork driven freeze in step 5 is a documented behaviour change. Neither of the two tokens found at the PoolManager has an executor allowlist that excludes it, so no instance of that freeze was observed. 6. PAUSE_ROLE, not the admin role, is what pauses TRANSFER. The admin can grant it.

findings.title: Blacklist and freeze roles on the pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them, because one address holds all balances
findings.difference: The issuer model matches USDC on Ethereum, but the role holders are set per chain and several of the largest PoolManager balances in this unit are tokens that Ethereum pools do not hold in this form. On Soneium the bridged USDC.e returns one address, 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59, for owner, pauser and blacklister. On Ink and Unichain USD₮0 exposes isBlocked. On Ink USDG and on Soneium USDSC expose isFrozen. Circle USDC on OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain, World Chain and Ink each has its own blacklister and pauser address.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a currency sit in one token balance at the PoolManager address. 2. FiatToken transfer carries the modifiers whenNotPaused, notBlacklisted(msg.sender) and notBlacklisted(to). When the PoolManager pays out, it is msg.sender (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86, called from src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 3. If the blacklister lists the PoolManager address, or the pauser pauses the token, every take of that currency reverts with ERC20TransferFailed. sync still works because balanceOf is a view call. 4. The freeze covers every pool on the chain that uses the token, regardless of which pool or user caused the listing. 5. The freeze functions on USD₮0, USDG and USDSC were confirmed to exist by eth_call. Their effect on transfers and any balance destroying function were not read from source in this cycle.
findings.impact: At read time the PoolManager held about 12.25 million USDC on Base, 978,360 USDC and 180,746 USD₮0 on Unichain, 1.52 million USD₮0, 767,333 USDG and 676,274 USDC on Ink, 1.90 million USDSC and 517,001 USDC.e on Soneium, 323,556 USDC on OP Mainnet and 66,644 USDC on World Chain. A listing of the PoolManager freezes the whole balance of that token for all LPs, claim holders and the protocol. isBlacklisted, isBlocked or isFrozen returned false for the PoolManager on every token checked.
findings.preconditions: The token's blacklister, freezer or pauser acts against the PoolManager address or pauses the token. This is a privileged issuer action. An unprivileged attacker cannot trigger it directly. A realistic trigger is a compliance response to tainted funds that were routed through a pool.
findings.mitigations: LPs can exit the non frozen currency normally and hold the frozen currency as ERC-6909 claims through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) until the listing is lifted. Integrators should monitor the blacklist and pause state of each large pooled token for the PoolManager address on each chain. For Soneium USDC.e, the deployer should identify who controls 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59 before treating it like Circle issued USDC.

verification.factCheck: The Circle source was fetched: FiatTokenV1.transfer carries whenNotPaused, notBlacklisted(msg.sender) and notBlacklisted(to) (lines 287-293), and transferFrom also checks from. I repeated the on-chain reads on 22 November 2026. Soneium USDC.e returns 0x8be79275fcfd08a931087ecf70ba8a99aee3ac59 for owner, pauser and blacklister. Blacklister addresses on OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain, World Chain and Ink match the finding. isBlacklisted, isBlocked and isFrozen return false for the PoolManager on every token, and paused is false where the call exists. Balances at the PoolManager: 12.57 million USDC on Base, 980,196 USDC and 180,760 USD₮0 on Unichain, 1.53 million USD₮0, 779,410 USDG and 767,378 USDC on Ink, 1.90 million USDSC and 516,436 USDC.e on Soneium, 335,159 USDC on OP Mainnet and 66,519 USDC on World Chain. These are within normal drift of the figures in the finding. One link is weaker than stated: the Base USDC and Soneium USDC.e proxies report version 2 and point to a 23,464 byte implementation, and I read only the V1 source. The implementation bytecode contains the blacklist(address) selector, so the list exists there. I did not read that the later version keeps the same three modifiers on transfer. For USDG the isFrozen call answers, but I did not find the freeze selectors in the implementation behind the EIP-1967 slot, so where that logic lives was not established.
verification.codeCheck: Every payout of an ERC-20 currency is a transfer call made by the PoolManager (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), reached from take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). There is one holder address for all pools, claims and fees, so a listing of that address or a token pause makes each of these calls revert. sync only reads balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:285), which the Circle source does not gate. A listed PoolManager also cannot receive, because transfer checks the recipient, so a settle that follows a token transfer fails as well. mint and burn of ERC-6909 claims do not touch the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), so positions can still be closed into claims and swaps can still be settled in claims. No guard in src/ was missed. test/ has no case for a paused or blacklisting token.
verification.corrections: 1. The effect is understated for USD₮0. The USD₮0 implementations on Unichain (0xaf37e8b6c9ed7f6318979f56fc287d76c30847ff) and Ink (0x06d886ff518b5e642e7e6aad3ce797b7dabd8e9a) contain the selectors of addToBlockedList(address) and destroyBlockedFunds(address). A blocked PoolManager could therefore lose its whole USD₮0 balance, about 1.53 million on Ink and 180,760 on Unichain, which is a loss for LPs and claim holders. I matched selectors in bytecode and did not read the source or the access control. USDSC on Soneium has freeze and unfreeze and none of the wipe selectors I tried. 2. The difference from Ethereum is thin. The Ethereum PoolManager is exposed to the same issuer roles. What is specific to this unit is the set of role holders and balances, and the single account behind all three roles of Soneium USDC.e. 3. The claim based exit depends on the contract that owns the position being able to call mint in its unlock callback. That was not checked. 4. Severity stays high: the actor is a token issuer and the frozen amount is the full balance of the token across all pools.

findings.title: TIP-20 issuer roles can burn, freeze or pause the PoolManager balance of a Tempo stablecoin
findings.difference: On Tempo every stablecoin is a TIP-20 precompile with issuer roles built into the protocol. burnAt(from, amount), live on mainnet since T12 on 13 October 2026, lets a BURN_AT_ROLE holder burn any balance with no transfer policy check, unless the holder is on a protected list. burnBlocked lets a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder burn the balance of an address that fails the sender policy. The protected list is FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve, ReceivePolicyGuard, the token's own address and Zone Portal addresses. The PoolManager is not on it. pause stops every transfer of the token. The admin of a TIP-403 policy can block an address for every token bound to that policy, and pathUSD and OUSD are both bound to policy 2, a blacklist administered by 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. Ethereum has no protocol-level burn of another account's ERC-20 balance. Each token there has whatever controls its own contract code contains.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees for a token sit in one TIP-20 balance at the PoolManager address. 2. A BURN_AT_ROLE holder calls burnAt(PoolManager, x). The TIP-20 precompile debits the PoolManager and reduces total supply. No PoolManager function runs. 3. The PoolManager tracks no per-currency reserve in storage. sync reads balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and take pays out with transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75), so the claims recorded in pool state and ERC-6909 balances now exceed the tokens held. Withdrawals succeed until the balance runs out, then transfer reverts with InsufficientBalance and the remaining LPs and claim holders cannot exit. 4. The freeze variant: the policy admin adds the PoolManager to blacklist policy 2, or a PAUSE_ROLE holder pauses the token. Every take and every inbound payment for that token then reverts with PolicyForbids or ContractPaused, and settle cannot complete because the payment transfer fails. Once the PoolManager fails the sender policy, a BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE holder can also burn its balance. 5. If a burn lands between sync and settle inside one transaction, the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 reverts that transaction and nothing else changes.
findings.impact: At block 50,261,382 the PoolManager held about 406,197 OUSD and 19,727 pathUSD. A burn destroys part of the shared balance and the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws last, across every pool that uses the token. A blacklist entry or a pause freezes the full balance of that token, and policy 2 covers pathUSD and OUSD at once.
findings.preconditions: A holder of BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE or PAUSE_ROLE on the token, the token admin, or the admin of the TIP-403 policy must act. An unprivileged attacker has these roles only on tokens they created through the TIP-20 factory, which harms only pools that chose to hold that token. I could not list the current holders of BURN_AT_ROLE and BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE on OUSD and pathUSD, because the public RPC limits log queries to 100,000 blocks. I confirmed that both role constants exist on both tokens, that both tokens use policy 2, and that the PoolManager is authorized under policy 2 today.
findings.mitigations: LPs should treat every TIP-20 as an asset its issuer can burn or freeze at the PoolManager address, and check role holders and the policy admin before providing liquidity. The deployer can ask Tempo to add the PoolManager to the protected address list for burnAt and burnBlocked, and can ask issuers to confirm in writing that the PoolManager will not be blacklisted. Interfaces can warn when a pool token has a BURN_AT_ROLE holder.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the TIP-20 specification, the T12 upgrade page, the TIP-403 specification and the upgrade schedule. They say what the finding says. burnAt(from, amount) requires BURN_AT_ROLE and an unpaused token, ignores transfer policy authorization, debits from and reduces total supply. burnBlocked requires the source to fail the sender policy. Both reject FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve, ReceivePolicyGuard, the token's own address and Zone Portal addresses with ProtectedAddress. T12 went live on mainnet on 13 October 2026. I read the client source on the main branch. burn_at calls check_not_paused, check_role, check_burn_address and then moves the balance to the zero address. The PROTECTED list holds only the four system addresses, and check_burn_address adds the token itself and the Zone Portal prefix. The PoolManager address matches none of them. On chain between blocks 50,274,136 and 50,275,429: pathUSD (0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000000) and OUSD (0x20c0000000000000000000006a37da5c996874be) both return transferPolicyId 2. policyData(2) returns type 1 and admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. isAuthorized(2, PoolManager) returns true. balanceOf(PoolManager) was 403,954.29 OUSD and 19,644.52 pathUSD. I then ran three read-only simulations with eth_simulateV1 against live state. In the first, 0x79c6631fa15cda38777fb9dd7a6348baee794a4e grants itself BURN_AT_ROLE and calls burnAt(PoolManager, 1). Both calls succeed on OUSD and on pathUSD, and balanceOf(PoolManager) falls by one unit. In the second, the same account grants itself PAUSE_ROLE and calls pause, after which transfer from the PoolManager reverts with ContractPaused on both tokens. In the third, 0x251d2711...5246 calls modifyPolicyBlacklist(2, PoolManager, true), after which isAuthorized(2, PoolManager) returns false, transfers from the PoolManager revert with PolicyForbids on both tokens, and a transfer to the PoolManager reverts with PolicyForbids. No transaction was sent.
verification.codeCheck: sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) in transient storage and nothing in persistent storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). take debits the caller's delta and calls transfer with no comparison against any recorded reserve (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A failed token call reverts the take with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). No function in src/ observes a balance that fell outside take or collectProtocolFees, so a burn leaves pool state and ERC-6909 balances above the tokens held and the last withdrawers meet InsufficientBalance. After a blacklist entry or a pause, take reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, a payer cannot move tokens to the PoolManager so _settle credits zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and collectProtocolFees reverts at src/ProtocolFees.sol:56. A burn between sync and settle in one transaction makes the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert. I found no guard the finding missed. The tests do not cover this case. A search of test/ and src/test/ finds no token mock with an issuer burn, a blacklist or a pause.
verification.corrections: The finding could not list role holders. I read every RoleMembershipUpdated log on both tokens from block 0 to block 50,274,300 in 100,000 block windows. There are 16 events, and none grants BURN_AT_ROLE, BURN_BLOCKED_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE or UNPAUSE_ROLE. hasRole returns false for those roles on every account that appears in the logs. So nobody holds a burn or pause role on OUSD today. pathUSD had one admin set at genesis without an event, so I cannot exclude a genesis holder there. The roles are one transaction away. 0x79c6631f...4a4e holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on both tokens, getRoleAdmin returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE for all of them, and the simulation shows it can grant itself a role and use it. That account and the policy 2 admin both carry 23 bytes of code, the EIP-7702 designator 0xef0100 followed by 0x000000fb7702036ff9f76044a501ac1aa74cbab16b. They are signer-controlled accounts and I did not find out how many signers control them. Step 4 says every pool operation stops. The transfers stop. Swaps and liquidity changes that settle with ERC-6909 mint and burn (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) still run, so holders can trade a frozen token for another token inside the PoolManager while other reserves last. The severity stays high under the scale: a token issuer or policy admin must act, and the whole balance of the token is in reach.

findings.title: A pause of the USDC token on Arc stops the ERC-20 face and leaves native transfers open over the same PoolManager balance
findings.difference: The pause flag of USDC on Arc lives in the token contract and guards transfer, transferFrom, mint, burn and the signature-based entry points with whenNotPaused. Native value transfers are checked by the EVM against the blocklist only. On Ethereum a paused USDC has no second way to move.
findings.mechanism: 1. The pauser (0x51fa31e029abf0ce307bca9ee6bf48aed6345212) calls pause on the USDC proxy. 2. take of currency 0x3600 calls transfer and reverts with 'Pausable: paused' (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86), and no payer can move ERC-20 USDC to the PoolManager, so settle for 0x3600 credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). collectProtocolFees for 0x3600 reverts as well (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. take of address(0) still pays with a value call (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52) and settle with msg.value still works (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). 4. Claims and pool balances are recorded per currency id, so holders of 0x3600 claims cannot leave while holders of address(0) claims on the same balance can. A pool that pairs the two faces becomes the only exit for 0x3600 holders, at whatever price that pool reaches.
findings.impact: Every pool and claim denominated in 0x3600 is frozen for the length of the pause. At block 32,584,426 the PoolManager held 2,445,327.82 USDC in total for both faces. I did not split that figure between the two ids. Native-denominated pools keep working.
findings.preconditions: The USDC pauser, a Circle role, must pause the token. An ordinary account cannot reach this path. The asymmetry was reproduced with eth_call and a state override of the paused bit and no transaction was sent.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers who want an exit during a token pause can hold USDC positions under address(0). Interfaces should state which face a pool uses.

verification.factCheck: In the verified source of NativeFiatTokenV2_2 the Pausable contract declares pauser and then paused, so both share storage slot 1, and whenNotPaused guards transfer, transferFrom, mint, burn and the four authorization functions of the native token contract (lines 3086, 3109, 3188, 3230, 3321, 3354, 3388, 3426) as well as approve, permit and the allowance functions. _balanceOf carries no pause check. On Arc, slot 1 of 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 holds the pauser 0x51fa31e029abf0ce307bca9ee6bf48aed6345212, pauser() returns the same address and paused() returns false. I repeated the test with an eth_call state override that sets the byte above the pauser address in slot 1: paused() then returns true, USDC.transfer of 1 unit from the PoolManager reverts with 'Pausable: paused', USDC.transfer of 1 unit to the PoolManager from the PositionManager address reverts with the same message, a native send of 10^12 wei from the PoolManager succeeds, and balanceOf(PoolManager) still answers. The files evm.rs, handler.rs and opcode.rs of arc-node main contain no reference to a pause flag. Value-bearing frames are checked against the blocklist only. I did not rerun the fee adapter calls.

An ERC-20 credit needs the token balance of the PoolManager to rise after sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), which a paused token prevents for ordinary transfers. collectProtocolFees pays through the same transfer routine (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). findings.title: Issuer block lists on USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC cover the single PoolManager address on Arbitrum One
findings.difference: This is the same issuer power that exists on Ethereum, and cycle 1 did not record it for Arbitrum One. Native USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC on Arbitrum One each have a role that can block an address, and USDT0 has an owner function that destroys the balance of a blocked address. The PoolManager holds every pool's balance of each token at one address.
findings.mechanism: Step 1: the role holder lists the PoolManager address. Step 2: the token's transfer then fails when the PoolManager is the sender. Currency.transfer reverts on a failed call, so every take and every protocol fee collection in that token reverts. Where the token also rejects a listed recipient, a settle cannot be funded either. I did not test which of the four tokens check the recipient. Step 3: liquidity providers can still remove liquidity and keep the blocked side as ERC-6909 claims through mint, which moves no tokens, but the claims cannot be turned into tokens while the block stands. Step 4, USDT0 only: the owner calls destroyBlockedFunds for the PoolManager, which lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) with no matching delta. Pool reserves, claims and accrued fees then exceed the balance and the last withdrawers bear the shortfall.
findings.impact: All pools and claims in the listed token. At the time of the queries the PoolManager held 8.99M USDC, 0.98M USDT0, 28,236 PYUSD and 14.8 cbBTC.
findings.preconditions: The blacklister of USDC (0xac5b4946a8c29eafb42e1742b3ab82e6d5771329), the owner of USDT0 (0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8), the PYUSD role holder or the cbBTC blacklister must act. All four tokens report the PoolManager as not blocked today. An arbitrary caller is rejected by each of these functions.
findings.mitigations: None in the PoolManager. Liquidity providers can watch the block list views for the PoolManager address. A blocked side can be held as claims until the block is lifted.

findings.title: X Layer voids blacklisted L1 deposits at the execution layer, so forced inclusion is no guaranteed exit from the PoolManager
findings.difference: On Ethereum nobody can stop a valid transaction from executing once it is in a block. On a standard OP Stack chain a deposit sent through the OptimismPortal on Ethereum must be executed on L2 as written, which gives users an exit that the sequencer cannot refuse. The X Layer execution client adds a consensus rule: before it runs a user deposit it asks the TxBlacklist contract at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 whether the deposit's source hash is listed, and a listed deposit is recorded as a failed deposit without running its call. The contract is an upgradeable proxy. Its owner and the owner of its proxy admin are one account without code, 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every pool's funds leave the PoolManager through take inside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-297), and a liquidity position belongs to the msg.sender that created it (src/PoolManager.sol:159-167). An exit is therefore a transaction that must execute on X Layer from the position owner's address. 2. Cycle 1 recorded that the X Layer block builder can leave out sequencer submitted transactions through a risk control filter, and that an L1 deposit remained as the exit. 3. In the client source at tag xlayer/v0.1.7, OpEvm::transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit before it executes a transaction. For a deposit that is not a system transaction and does not come from the L1 attributes depositor, it makes an uncommitted system call isBlacklisted(sourceHash) from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe to the address that the source fixes for chain id 196. 4. When the call returns true, the client builds the result through the handler's failed deposit path: every change of the transaction is reverted, the sender nonce is bumped, the mint is kept and the call to the target is never made. The deposit is included in the block and has no effect. 5. A source hash is known from the moment the deposit event is emitted on Ethereum. User deposits are executed in the first L2 block of the epoch whose origin is that Ethereum block, and the sequencer builds this block after the Ethereum block exists and may lag behind it inside the sequencing window. The party that controls the blacklist therefore has time to list the hash before the deposit is executed. 6. On chain, addToBlacklist(bytes32) reverts for an arbitrary sender, for the owner and for the PoolManager. The implementation has an operators(address) mapping and the setOperator(address,bool) selector, so the owner appoints the accounts that can list hashes. The same owner can replace the implementation through the proxy admin. 7. A liquidity provider whose ordinary transactions are filtered by the builder and whose deposits are listed has no remaining way to call the PoolManager. The code in src/ has no path that works without transaction execution.
findings.impact: Funds of any chosen liquidity provider, swapper or claim holder on X Layer can be held in the PoolManager for as long as the operator keeps filtering and listing. This covers 307.9 OKB and 5,889,016 USDT0 at the time of the query. Nothing is taken: the code has no time dependence, so the funds are intact when the block is lifted. The rule is part of the state transition that every X Layer node applies. The release notes say the same Rust stack is used for proof generation, so a proof would be expected to accept a voided deposit as correct. I did not read the proof program to confirm this.
findings.preconditions: The holder of 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, or an operator that this account appoints, must list each deposit's source hash before the deposit is executed, and the sequencer must also keep the same user's ordinary transactions out of blocks. An ordinary account cannot list a hash. Whether any hash has been listed could not be read, because the public endpoint limits log queries to 100 blocks. The tag xlayer/v0.1.7 is the op-node release that operators had to run by 10 November 2026. The exact submodule commit that the mainnet sequencer runs was not confirmed, and the blacklist file is also present at tag xlayer/v0.1.6.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat X Layer positions as dependent on one operator account and should not rely on L1 forced inclusion as an exit. The deployer can ask OKX to publish the conditions under which deposits are listed and to move ownership of the blacklist and its proxy admin to a multisignature account with a delay. Integrators can monitor the blacklist contract for operator changes and new entries.

sources.supports: The mainnet blacklist address is fixed to 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 for chain id 196. isBlacklisted(sourceHash) is called with transact_system_call from SYSTEM_ADDRESS. Only user deposits are eligible: system transactions and the L1 attributes depositor are excluded.

transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit before executing. On a hit it passes an invalid transaction error with the text 'deposit blacklisted' to the handler's catch_error and returns that result with the finalized state.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the three client files at tag xlayer/v0.1.7 of okx/optimism. xlayer_blacklist_contract.rs maps chain id 196 to 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727, calls isBlacklisted(sourceHash) through transact_system_call from the EIP-4788 system address, treats a revert or a malformed answer as false, and exempts system deposits and the L1 attributes depositor. The function returns early for anything that is not a user deposit, and on a hit it passes an InvalidTransaction error with the text 'deposit blacklisted' to OpHandler::catch_error and returns the finalized state. In op-revm handler.rs, catch_error for a deposit reverts to the first journal checkpoint, bumps the caller nonce, adds the mint and commits. The same two files are present with the same mainnet address at the okx/optimism ref xlayer-dep/a492b62bbecbdcf3be90719e042c9abca47c8cc6 and on main. The release page for xlayer/v0.1.6 lists 'feat(rcs): intercept blacklisted L1 deposits before execution (51ce81a)' and says that release was for testnet only. The release pages for xlayer/v0.1.7 and xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 say operators must run both by November 10, 2026, and neither page names the blacklist. Cargo.toml of xlayer-reth at tag v0.0.7.3 takes alloy-op-evm and op-revm from the path deps/optimism/rust, and .gitmodules points that path at okx/optimism. On chain at X Layer block 76,601,162 on 2026-11-22: the endpoint reports reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with the suffix xlayer/v0.0.7. The blacklist address holds 1,059 bytes of code, its EIP-1967 implementation slot holds 0xe44bfef30cfd8ecbfb917d78fa2ac215b3397f8e (3,516 bytes) and its admin slot holds 0x57ffb399eb2d8fb1831001ba893483bc13bd8c2f. owner() on the proxy and on the admin both return 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, which has no code and account nonce 2,098. pendingOwner() is zero. The implementation bytecode contains the selectors of isBlacklisted(bytes32), blacklisted(bytes32), addToBlacklist(bytes32), removeFromBlacklist(bytes32), batchAddToBlacklist(bytes32[]), batchRemoveFromBlacklist(bytes32[]), operators(address) and setOperator(address,bool). addToBlacklist reverts with 0x7c214f04, the selector of NotOperator(), for an arbitrary sender and for the owner. setOperator(address,bool) succeeds in simulation from the owner and reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount for another sender. isBlacklisted returns false for a test hash when called from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe. eth_getLogs for the contract over the last 100 blocks returned nothing. The OP Stack derivation specification says user deposits are placed in the first L2 block of an epoch, before sequenced transactions, and that an L2 block may keep an L1 origin whose timestamp is up to max_sequencer_drift older than its own. A hash therefore has to be listed in an L2 block that precedes the block of the deposit, and the sequencer chooses when it advances to the L1 origin that holds the deposit. One link is backed by release documents and not by direct observation: I could not read the submodule pointer of xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3, and I found no deposit that was voided on mainnet.

A liquidity position is stored under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so only that account can reduce it. ERC-6909 claims are burned from an account by that account, by its operator or by a spender with allowance (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and each of these still needs a transaction on X Layer. collectProtocolFees pays out accrued protocol fees only and needs the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). No function in src/ depends on block time or lets a third party withdraw for an owner without the owner's earlier approval. A user whose transactions are never executed therefore cannot move funds out. I found no guard in src/ that the finding missed, and none could exist, because the hazard sits below the contract.

An account that already holds an ERC-6909 operator approval, an allowance or a PositionManager approval from the owner can act for the owner from a different sender, and the operator would have to filter or list that transaction as well. findings.title: The GoodDollar owner has blocked the PoolManager address on Celo, so 550 million G$ held for pools cannot leave
findings.difference: G$ on Celo is a Superfluid Super Token with an owner controlled list of accounts that can neither send nor receive it, and with an owner function that burns from any account. After the Superfluid incident of September 2026 the owner put the Uniswap v4 PoolManager on that list and has not removed it. Ethereum's PoolManager holds no token in this state.
findings.mechanism: 1. On 11 September 2026 at 13:48:08 UTC (Celo block 77,233,730, transaction 0x22cd34a5f179dfa342fd3659d029e4d40469ca8fa02abd032145f162b0b8dd4d, sent by 0x6823a04a6fd4148167567d5ef6dcca1f34db0494 to the contract 0xa2521e8f5a990903fdd8afa6570c52526e7e0d5e) the token emitted BlockedUpdated with value true for eleven addresses, one of which is the PoolManager 0x288dc841A52FCA2707c6947B3A777c5E56cd87BC. setBlocked is restricted to the owner role. isBlocked(PoolManager) returned true at block 83,475,285 on 22 November 2026. 2. Every ERC-20, ERC-677 and ERC-777 movement of G$ runs _processFees, which reverts with SUPER_GOODDOLLAR_BLOCKED (0xe7d0c09e) when the sender or the recipient is blocked. An eth_call of transfer from the PoolManager reverts with that selector for amounts 1 and 0. A transfer of 1 unit from the owner account to the PoolManager reverts the same way, and the same transfer to another address returns true. 3. take debits the caller and then calls transfer on the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A failed transfer makes take revert (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). Every take of G$ therefore reverts, including a take of zero. The PoolManager's 550,022,104.456 G$ stay where they are. 4. A position owner who removes liquidity from a G$ pool receives a positive G$ delta. The owner can take the other currency. For the G$ side the remaining choices are mint, which turns the delta into an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), and clear, which gives it up (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319). A swap that buys G$ ends the same way. 5. A payment of G$ into the PoolManager by transfer reverts as well, so a seller needs a G$ claim to burn (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). The token source says a blocked account can still be credited through Superfluid agreements. Such a credit would raise balanceOf(PoolManager), and sync followed by settle would credit it to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). I did not simulate that path. 6. The owner can also call adminBurn(account, amount), which skips allowance, hooks, pause and the block list. A burn of the PoolManager's balance would leave pool liquidity and G$ claims without tokens behind them. Superfluid's report says 544 million G$ was burned elsewhere during the recovery.
findings.impact: 550,022,104 G$, which is 13.7 percent of the G$ supply and about 60,000 USD at the price Blockscout shows (0.00010924 USD). GoodDollar names one position holder with two wallets as the depositor. Because all pools share one address, the block also covers every other G$ pool in this PoolManager, every G$ claim and any protocol fee accrued in G$. The paired currencies of those pools can still be withdrawn.
findings.preconditions: None remain. The block is in force. It ends when an account with the G$ owner role calls setBlocked with false for the PoolManager. owner() returns 0x495d133b938596c9984d462f007b676bdc57ecec. GoodDollar states it will do so once the position holder contacts Good Labs or moves the position to the Good Labs Safe.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot lift the block. Interfaces should stop routing through G$ pools on Celo and should show G$ positions as withdrawable only as claims. Liquidity providers can remove liquidity, take the paired currency and mint the G$ side as a claim. Integrations should not value G$ claims or G$ pool liquidity at the market price while the block and the admin burn function exist. New deployments should treat any token with a per address block list as able to freeze every pool of that token at once.

An eth_call of transfer(address,uint256) with from set to the PoolManager reverts with 0xe7d0c09e for amounts 1 and 0. I computed that selector myself: it is the first four bytes of keccak256 of SUPER_GOODDOLLAR_BLOCKED(). A transfer of 1 unit from the owner account 0x495d133b938596c9984d462f007b676bdc57ecec to the PoolManager reverts with the same selector, and the same transfer to an unrelated address returns true. eth_getLogs for block 77,233,730 and topic 0x148a8679 (keccak256 of BlockedUpdated(address,bool), also computed here) returns 11 logs with value true in transaction 0x22cd34a5f179dfa342fd3659d029e4d40469ca8fa02abd032145f162b0b8dd4d. One of the 11 accounts is the PoolManager. The block timestamp is 2026-09-11 13:48:08 UTC, the sender is 0x6823a04a6fd4148167567d5ef6dcca1f34db0494 and the target is 0xa2521e8f5a990903fdd8afa6570c52526e7e0d5e. The endpoint limits log queries to 5,000 blocks, so I did not scan for a later unblock event. The current value of isBlocked answers that question. The ERC-1967 slot and getCodeAddress() of the G$ proxy both hold 0xb4419A3Df33b9aa6fbE452Df8816389E599C29eF. Blockscout returns verified source for that address under the name SuperGoodDollar. I read it: isBlocked is a public mapping (line 48), setBlocked(address[],bool) and adminBurn(address,uint256) call _onlyOwner (lines 365 to 391), transfer, transferFrom, send and transferAndCall all pass through _processFees, and _processFees calls _onlyNotBlocked for the sender and for the recipient (lines 434 to 470). The comment on setBlocked says a blocked account can still be credited by agreements. The library SuperGoodDollarFlows rejects, for a blocked account, a higher CFA deposit, a higher GDA buffer, a lower GDA balance and every IDA write. The GoodDollar post of 20 October 2026 says all liquidity pools were unblocked on 28 September except the Celo Uniswap V4 pool, which holds 550M G$, and that it stays blocked until the position holder contacts Good Labs or moves the position to the Safe 0x4e31993d9F13F940828bf9eC2f643A7E55B21e8C. The Superfluid technical report of 2 October 2026 gives 2,801,252,167 unbacked G$, the 900 KB callback return data, the 30 million block gas limit, the host upgrade of 4 September and 544 million G$ burned. Blockscout shows a G$ price of 0.00011464 USD today, which values the balance at about 63,000 USD. Not confirmed: that a Superfluid agreement can still credit the blocked PoolManager in practice. I read the guard code and it lets a balance increase pass, and I did not simulate a distribution or a stream.
verification.codeCheck: take is at src/PoolManager.sol:291-297. It debits the caller at line 294 and calls currency.transfer at line 295. For an ERC-20 the call is at src/types/Currency.sol:73, and a reverting token gives success zero, so lines 82 to 85 revert through CustomRevert.bubbleUpAndRevertWith (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The whole take reverts, including the debit, for every amount including zero, because the token checks the block list before it looks at the amount. There is no other function in src/ that moves an ERC-20 out of the PoolManager except collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), which uses the same transfer. A positive G$ delta can be closed by mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which only writes an ERC-6909 balance, or by clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319), which gives the amount up. unlock reverts while any delta is open (src/PoolManager.sol:112). An inbound payment needs the token balance to rise between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), and an ERC-20 transfer to the blocked PoolManager reverts, so a seller needs a claim to burn (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336) or a credit through an agreement. I found no guard that the finding missed. The freeze follows from one address holding all pools (assumption A6) and from core having no reaction to a failing transfer.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right. The block was set by the G$ owner role, an ordinary account can neither set nor lift it, and no step lets an ordinary account take funds. The mitigation that tells liquidity providers to mint the G$ side as a claim does not hold for positions held through the PositionManager. In core the position owner is the msg.sender of modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so only the contract that opened a position can remove it. The runtime code of the Celo PositionManager 0xf7965f3981e4d5bc383bfbcb61501763e9068ca9 (23,877 bytes) contains the selectors of take, clear, settle, sync, modifyLiquidity and unlock and does not contain the selector of mint(address,uint256,uint256) (0x156e29f6) or of burn(address,uint256,uint256) (0xf5298aca). A holder of such a position who removes liquidity must close the G$ delta with take, which reverts, or with clear, which forfeits the G$. I did not establish whether the PositionManager can move the G$ delta into another position inside the same unlock. setBlocked takes an array of accounts. At today's Blockscout price the balance is worth about 63,000 USD. The statement that no later unblock event exists was not checked by a full log scan here.

findings.title: Issuers of the tokens that make up most pool value on Celo and X Layer can pause, block, burn or upgrade the PoolManager's balance
findings.difference: The pooled value on these two networks sits in issuer controlled tokens that are small or new: wBRL and wARS on Celo, and USDT0, USDG, two USDC contracts and tokenized stocks on X Layer. On Celo the PoolManager holds 83.7 percent of all wBRL and 59.0 percent of all wARS. Each of these tokens has roles that act on a single holder address.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools keep a currency in one balance at the PoolManager address, and that balance leaves only through transfer inside take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). A role that stops transfers for that one address stops every pool of the token. 2. wBRL and wARS are proxies of LatamStable. Its compliance role can switch the blocklist on and block the PoolManager, after which _update reverts for it as sender and as recipient. Its pauser role stops all transfers. Its upgrader role can replace the implementation through UUPS and with it the balance logic. The blocklist is switched off today and neither token is paused. 3. On X Layer USDT0 has addToBlockedList and destroyBlockedFunds, USDG has freeze and wipeFrozenAddress, both USDC contracts have a blacklister and a pause, and xETH has a deny list and a pause. A wipe or a destroy sets the PoolManager balance to zero while pool accounting and ERC-6909 claims still count the tokens. 4. BMNRx and ANTx report balanceOf as shares times a multiplier that a multiplier updater role sets, and a fee per period can lower the multiplier over time. A lower multiplier lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) without a take, which leaves pools with less than their accounting says (assumption A2). A higher multiplier adds tokens that no settle credits. The multiplier is 1.0 and the fee is 0 today. 5. On Celo the owner of USDm, which is Celo Governance, can name operators and burners that move or burn the balance of any account. 6. core has no function that reacts to any of these actions. Liquidity providers who exit first after a partial loss take the remaining tokens, and later exits revert when the balance runs out.
findings.impact: On Celo about 522,000 USD of wBRL and 129,000 USD of wARS at the prices Blockscout shows, plus the USDC paired with them. On X Layer about 5.97 million USDT0, 459,000 USDG and 97,700 USDC, plus the 4.67 million USDe that trade against USDT0 in the largest pool. USDe itself has no block or pause function in its code. A freeze stops withdrawals of the affected token for every pool. A wipe, burn or lower multiplier is a loss shared by all liquidity providers and claim holders of that token.
findings.preconditions: An action by a role holder of the token: compliance, pauser or upgrader for wBRL and wARS, the owner of USDT0 (0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8), the asset protection role of USDG, the blacklister or pauser of each USDC contract, the multiplier updater or owner of the stock tokens, and the owner of USDm, which is Celo Governance (0xD533Ca259b330c7A88f74E000a3FaEa2d63B7972). No such flag is set for the PoolManager on either chain at blocks 83,476,610 (Celo) and 76,608,329 (X Layer).
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should size positions in these tokens with the issuer roles in mind, and pool interfaces should show them. Monitoring should watch the PoolManager address in each token's block, freeze and pause state and the stock token multiplier. Pools in rebasing stock tokens should use the wrapped ERC-4626 versions, which keep a fixed balance. The deployer cannot remove any of these roles.

findings.title: A two signature Safe can pause ten wrapped stock tokens or list the PoolManager as sanctioned, which would stop pools that hold 7.9 million dollars on Monad
findings.difference: On Monad the second largest asset class at the PoolManager is a set of wrapped stock tokens (wSPYx, wSPCXx, wTSLAx, wQQQx, wEWYx, wSMHx, wNVDAx, wSKHYx, wMUx, wANTx). The PoolManager holds between 89.4 and 99.8 percent of the supply of each. Every transfer of these tokens checks a pause flag and a sanctions list that the issuer controls. cbBTC on Monad adds freeze, pause and burn roles. The exposure comes from the tokens that make up the pooled value on this network. The Monad client plays no part in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools of a currency share one balance at the PoolManager address, and take pays out with currency.transfer and reverts when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 2. The wrapper's transfer hook requires that isPaused is false and that neither sender nor recipient is on the sanctions list of the underlying stock token (WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol lines 178 to 193). 3. setPause can be called by the pauser, a Safe with threshold 2 of 4. The sanctions list at 0x615dd3b9445a94334c1579f68115042d77cc7c44 has addToSanctionsList and is owned by a Safe with threshold 2 of 3, which also owns the wrappers and the proxy admin and can replace the wrapper code. 4. If the pauser pauses a wrapper, or the owner lists the PoolManager address, every take of that wrapper reverts, so no liquidity removal and no swap that pays out the wrapper can settle in any pool of that token. Transfers into the PoolManager revert as well, so settle cannot be funded. 5. isPaused is false for all ten wrappers and isSanctioned(PoolManager) is false today. 6. cbBTC (40.0 coins at the PoolManager, 43 percent of supply) has freeze(address), pause() and burn(address,uint256) behind FREEZER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE and BURNER_ROLE. A freeze of the PoolManager or a pause has the same effect, and a burn would leave pool accounting above the balance. 7. A live example of this class exists at small size. Curvance has paused the market manager 0xbc4cd7bbd8d38027a88838b88ba04561fa778c35, and a transfer of cWBTC or ceBTC from the PoolManager reverts today with MarketManager__Paused(). Five pools use each of the two tokens, and the PoolManager holds about 83 dollars of each. 8. No ordinary account can trigger any of these steps. A third party cannot move the PoolManager's wrapper shares, because redeem and withdraw spend an allowance of the owner (lines 265 to 273) and delegatedTransfer needs an ECDSA signature that recovers to the owner address (lines 112 to 131).
findings.impact: A pause or a sanctions entry freezes about 7.9 million dollars of wrapped stock tokens together with the other side of those pools while it lasts, for every liquidity provider in them. A freeze or pause of cbBTC does the same for about 2.5 million dollars of cbBTC. A burn of the PoolManager's cbBTC would leave the last providers unpaid. The Curvance pause already locks about 170 dollars.
findings.preconditions: Two signers of the pauser Safe or of the owner Safe act, or the holder of a cbBTC role acts. No action by an ordinary account leads there.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat the issuer's pause and sanctions rights as a condition of these pools. The deployer can list these tokens in user documentation as issuer controlled. Core cannot route around a token that rejects transfers from the PoolManager.

verification.factCheck: The chain facts hold. I fetched WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol from the Backed repository. _beforeTokenTransfer requires isPaused to be false and asks the sanctions list of the underlying token about the sender and the recipient (lines 178 to 194). setPause accepts only the pauser (lines 142 to 146). A withdraw or redeem by another account spends the owner's allowance (lines 265 to 274), and delegatedTransfer requires that ECDSA recovery returns the owner address (lines 112 to 132). On Monad at block 124,634,156 I read eight of the ten wrappers: wSPYx 0xe7e553cd128f0011777323a0b44a7b96ea1cb540, wTSLAx 0xc3fdbe3a68ee5de461d30415a8165cf9aefe1171, wSPCXx 0x8e2eed8b8b5e13ea7bf38e50d7821d2c57309072, wQQQx 0x4c1ae29c159838fc1b224636e28e086eb69101f7, wSMHx 0x23c4bddea5e7e284fb4027c6050bc5e6f7fae23f, wSKHYx 0x6215a58ed045d71f2561aaabe54f4c885c522998, wANTx 0xabec6aeab037b77c09a2a99264f9c81a35b02649 and wMUx 0xe2047ee3bddb5c99ae428ab83df63f8730698e30. Each has implementation slot 0x76c6851ea0b2741eedcbbed240715e8817e85583, owner 0x49754062e35f7591b93cc4f9915965be89643a65, pauser 0x8768cda7a463dae1baa6b2500efb025ebd7ffc50 and isPaused false. The PoolManager holds between 89.2 percent (wANTx) and 99.8 percent (wTSLAx) of the supply of each. For wSPYx and wMUx I also read the admin slot, which is 0x312063009e74142339edc92bcff6cfcfaa958bfa, and the owner of that contract is the same Safe 0x4975. The underlying token of wSPYx (0x90a2a4c76b5d8c0bc892a69ea28aa775a8f2dd48, SP500 xStock) names sanctions list 0x615dd3b9445a94334c1579f68115042d77cc7c44. The owner of the list is the Safe 0x4975 and isSanctioned(PoolManager) is false. getThreshold and getOwners give 2 of 3 for Safe 0x4975 and 2 of 4 for Safe 0x8768, both Safe version 1.3.0. The implementation bytecode (11,606 bytes) contains 46 function selectors. They equal the 46 selectors I derived from the source file and its OpenZeppelin parents, with none missing and none extra. Simulations with eth_call: setPause(true) from an arbitrary account reverts with Only pauser and succeeds from the pauser Safe. addToSanctionsList with the PoolManager address reverts for an arbitrary account with the Ownable message and succeeds from the owner Safe. A prestate trace of the simulated setPause shows that it writes slot 0x132 of the wrapper. With that slot set by state override, transfer from the PoolManager address reverts with token transfer while paused, and a transfer to the PoolManager reverts with the same message. With the code of the sanctions list replaced by a stub that answers true, transfer from the PoolManager reverts with sender is sanctioned. Without overrides a transfer from the PoolManager address succeeds for all eight wrappers. From an arbitrary account, redeem, withdraw and transferFrom with the PoolManager as owner revert with insufficient allowance, and delegatedTransfer and permit with an arbitrary signature revert with invalid signature. GeckoTerminal prices give 5.68 million dollars for the seven wrappers I priced, and each of the seven is within one percent of the figure in the research file. I could not find the addresses of wNVDAx and wEWYx, so 1.54 million dollars of the 7.92 million total were not read again. cbBTC (0xd18b7ec58cdf4876f6afebd3ed1730e4ce10414b) is a proxy over 0xd1611e6e93ec512bfbd2b6428a26c463c1dce6f9. The PoolManager holds 39.92 of 93.26 coins, which is 42.8 percent. paused() is false and isFrozen(PoolManager) is false. The implementation bytecode contains the selectors of freeze(address), unfreeze(address), pause(), burn(address,uint256), FREEZER_ROLE(), PAUSER_ROLE() and BURNER_ROLE(). freeze, burn and pause from an arbitrary account revert with error 0xe2517d3f, which carries the caller and the missing role. cWBTC and ceBTC both name market manager 0xbc4cd7bbd8d38027a88838b88ba04561fa778c35. A transfer of half the balance from the PoolManager address reverts with 0xf47323f4 for both, and I computed that value as the selector of MarketManager__Paused(). The PoolManager holds 0.00134 units of each.
verification.codeCheck: take is open to any caller inside an unlock. It debits the caller and then calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For an ERC-20 the library calls transfer on the token and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the call fails or returns anything other than no data or a 32 byte true (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). CustomRevert.bubbleUpAndRevertWith always reverts (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The code has no custody per pool, so one balance serves every pool of a currency, and a token that rejects transfers from the PoolManager address makes every take of that currency revert. collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). settle credits only the rise of balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), so a token that rejects transfers to the PoolManager cannot be paid in. Actor check in the code: the PoolManager calls a currency address only with transfer and balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, 94), sends native value with empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48), calls unlockCallback on the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:110) and calls hook addresses with the IHooks selectors (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). None of the ten hook selectors and not unlockCallback occurs in the wrapper or cbBTC implementation bytecode. No caller can therefore make the PoolManager approve, redeem, pause or sign anything on these tokens, and the issuer rights are the only way to the freeze. One guard the finding leaves out: mint, burn and clear do not call the token (src/PoolManager.sol:310-336, src/ERC6909.sol:79-89). While a token is paused, a caller who is owed that token can still close the delta by minting ERC-6909 claims for it, and can take the other currency of the pool as usual.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right and the severity high fits the scale. The impact statement is too wide at one point. A pause or sanctions entry does not freeze the other side of those pools at the level of the PoolManager. A liquidity provider who can call the PoolManager directly can remove liquidity, take the other currency and mint ERC-6909 claims for the blocked wrapper (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), and a swap that pays out the wrapper can be closed the same way. What is frozen is the wrapper itself: no take and no settle of it works until the issuer lifts the block. Whether providers who hold positions through the deployed PositionManager can use this route depends on that contract, which is outside this repository and was not read. Two of the ten wrappers (wNVDAx and wEWYx) were not located by me, so the statement that all ten share the roles rests on eight read here and on the research file for the other two. The burn right on cbBTC was confirmed as a selector and a role check only. I did not read which accounts hold the cbBTC roles.

findings.title: A TIP-20 issuer has already frozen a pooled token on Tempo by setting the always reject transfer policy
findings.difference: A TIP-20 token carries a transfer policy id that its admin can change at any time. Policy 0 is built in and rejects every sender and recipient.
findings.mechanism: 1. GABAGOOL at 0x20c000000000000000000000030a4c7f7b8f3586 was used as a currency in two pools of the PoolManager, which still holds 600,000 base units (0.6 tokens). 2. transferPolicyId() on the token now returns 0, and isAuthorized(0, PoolManager) is false. 3. take calls transfer on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The precompile reverts with PolicyForbids and the take reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error. I simulated a take of 1 unit and of the full balance. Both revert. 4. A holder of a position in those pools can still remove liquidity, take the other currency and turn the GABAGOOL delta into an ERC-6909 claim or clear it (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329). The GABAGOOL itself cannot leave. 5. Of the 73 currencies that Tempo pools name, this is the only one where a take of the PoolManager balance fails today.
findings.impact: This instance concerns 0.6 tokens of a token with a supply of 310.6. It shows that the issuer control described in F-031 is used in practice on this network. The same single call by the policy admin of OUSD or pathUSD would stop takes of 406,692 OUSD and 19,629 pathUSD.
findings.preconditions: The admin of the token calls changeTransferPolicyId, or the admin of the policy changes its lists. No action by an ordinary account produces this state.
findings.mitigations: List the transfer policy id and its admin for each pooled TIP-20 in the deployment notes and monitor changes. Liquidity providers should treat TIP-20 tokens with an active admin as revocable.

findings.title: A Stylus program used as a hook or token stops answering calls on expiry or a Stylus version change, and activation is blocked
findings.difference: On Ethereum, code at an address keeps answering calls. On Arbitrum One a contract can be a Stylus WASM program. A call to it fails unless the program was activated at the current Stylus version and its last activation or keepalive is less than 365 days old. ArbOS 61, active since 2026-08-20, moved the Stylus version from 2 to 3. On chain, ArbWasm.activationGas() is 2^64-1, which makes activateProgram fail for everyone, so a program that has expired or needs the new version cannot be brought back by its users.
findings.mechanism: Hook path: the PoolManager calls the hook with call() and reverts the whole action when the call fails. For a hook address with the before or after remove liquidity flag, modifyLiquidity with a negative delta calls the hook, so a hook that no longer answers blocks every liquidity removal in its pools. Hooks with swap or donate flags block those actions the same way. Token path: transfer and balanceOf on a Stylus token that no longer answers revert, so take, sync and settle revert for that currency in every pool. Step 1: a pool is created with a Stylus hook or a Stylus token while the program is active. Step 2: the program reaches 365 days without a keepalive, or an ArbOS upgrade changes the Stylus version. getActiveProgram returns ProgramExpired or ProgramNeedsUpgrade and the call fails. Step 3: anyone who tries activateProgram is charged activationGas first, which exceeds any gas limit, so the call fails. Keepalive works only while the program is still active and at least 31 days old. ArbOS 61 also removed WASM multi-value support, so a program that relies on it cannot be reactivated even when activation reopens. I did not enumerate which pools on Arbitrum One use a Stylus hook or token, and I did not establish the date on which activation gas was raised, so I cannot say how many programs missed the move to version 3.
findings.impact: LP principal and fees in pools whose hook gates liquidity removal are stuck for as long as activation stays closed. For a Stylus token, every balance of that token in the PoolManager is stuck. No funds move to an attacker. Pools without Stylus hooks or tokens are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use a Stylus program as its hook or as one of its currencies. Then either nobody pays for keepalive within the 365 day window, or governance ships a Stylus version change. No attacker action is required and none can speed it up. The Arbitrum Foundation or Security Council can reopen activation.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators on Arbitrum One should prefer EVM hooks. LPs in a pool with a Stylus hook should check ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft for the hook and for each token, and anyone can pay codehashKeepalive once the program is 31 days old. A hook author can leave the remove liquidity flags unset so that removals never depend on the hook.

sources.supports: CallProgram calls getActiveProgram, which returns an error when the program version differs from the Stylus version or the program is older than ExpiryDays. ProgramKeepalive requires an active program at least KeepaliveDays old.
The ArbOS 59 upgrade step calls UpgradeToVersion(3) on the Stylus parameters.
ActivateProgram burns the configurable activation gas before activation. CodehashKeepalive does not.

Stylus contracts must be reactivated once per 365 days or after any Stylus upgrade, and otherwise become uncallable.
The proposal to reopen activation through an Arbitrum Foundation process was put on hold on 2026-11-18, and a later ArbOS proposal plans the ability to deactivate a Stylus contract.

The ArbOS 59 step calls UpgradeToVersion(3), which sets the Stylus version from 2 to 3. I read precompiles/ArbWasm.go. ActivateProgram burns the stored activation gas first. CodehashKeepalive does not. On chain at Arbitrum One block 526,514,058 on 2026-11-22: stylusVersion() is 3, expiryDays() is 365, keepaliveDays() is 31 and activationGas() is 2^64-1. A simulated activateProgram with 30,000,000 gas reverts. I tested the effect directly. ProgramActivated logs of ArbWasm around block 496,578,581, the first block at or after the ArbOS 61 activation time, show version 2 before it and version 3 after it. The program 0x2e5d89a229cbd17efb0a731d26232f88c3746aa9, activated at version 2 in block 495,363,914 and not reactivated, now fails every eth_call with the error ProgramNeedsUpgrade(2, 3). The program 0xaff2f129d2bcba4649a54fb516be0cc78288898d was reactivated at version 3 in block 496,871,745 and answers calls. The finding did not establish when activation was closed. The Security Council report gives the date: on 2026-10-02 the council called ArbOwner.setWasmActivationGas(2^64 - 1) on Arbitrum One and Nova. ArbOS 61 activated on 2026-08-20 at 17:00 UTC, so programs had 43 days to move to version 3. The pause notice, the ArbOS 61 release notes, the Stylus introduction and the forum proposal say what the finding reports. The last post of the forum thread, by the authors on 2026-11-18, says they will integrate feedback before taking the proposal further, and the first post says protocol-level activation controls and the ability to deactivate a Stylus contract are planned for a later ArbOS proposal. I also measured exposure. The PoolManager on Arbitrum One emitted 28,689 Initialize events from block 290,000,000 to block 526,516,712, with 923 distinct hook addresses and 9,417 distinct currency addresses. None of them has code that starts with the Stylus prefix 0xeff0. No pool therefore has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today. This check reads the code at the hook or token address only. It does not see an EVM contract that forwards to a Stylus program.

A call that succeeds with fewer than 32 bytes also reverts with InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). For a negative or zero liquidityDelta, beforeModifyLiquidity calls the hook when the address has the before remove liquidity flag, and afterModifyLiquidity does so for the after remove liquidity flag (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:209-245). Both run inside modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:156, src/PoolManager.sol:178). The only bypass is noSelfCall, which skips the hook when the hook itself is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:217). A program that cannot run cannot be the caller. Permissions come from the address bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:337-339) and the hook address is part of the pool identifier, so an LP cannot route around it. For a token, balanceOfSelf is a high-level call that reverts when the call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96), and transfer reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:54-87). sync, the ERC-20 branch of _settle and take all revert for that currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Claims in that currency can still be minted, burned and transferred. test/PoolManager.t.sol and test/DynamicFees.t.sol cover a hook that reverts or returns a bad response. No test covers a hook or token whose code stops answering after pool creation.
verification.corrections: The mechanism and the chain facts hold. The scope needs two changes. First, no pool on Arbitrum One has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today, so no funds are frozen through the direct path at present. Indirect use through an EVM proxy or an EVM hook that calls a Stylus program was not checked. Second, the date the finding could not establish is 2026-10-02, 43 days after the version change. The same mechanism reaches Robinhood Chain. Its ArbWasm precompile emitted 26 ProgramActivated events between 2026-07-25 and 2026-10-02, all at version 3, and activation gas there is also 2^64-1. I read the code of the 1,500 most used hook addresses, which cover 377,624 of the hooked pools, and none starts with 0xeff0. I did not read the code of the remaining hooks or of the currencies, so a contract that shares its code hash with an activated program is not excluded there. The severity stays medium because the freeze is limited to pools that depend on a Stylus program and needs either a missed keepalive or a governance upgrade.

findings.title: A pool's hook can block or reprice every liquidity removal in that pool, and core has no path that skips the hook
findings.difference: None. The code path is the same on every network. Networks where the code behind an address can change after pool creation (A7) add ways for a hook that was harmless at creation to start doing this.
findings.mechanism: modifyLiquidity calls the hook library's beforeModifyLiquidity before it touches the pool (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when address bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts the whole call when the hook reverts (Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or carries the wrong selector (Hooks.sol:152-154). A hook address with no code returns empty data, so it also reverts. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set, and when bit 0 is also set it reads a BalanceDelta from the return data, subtracts it from the caller's delta without any bound and credits it to the hook (Hooks.sol:232-243, src/PoolManager.sol:177-183). The hook call is skipped only when msg.sender is the hook itself (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). No other function removes liquidity. The swap path has the same shape: beforeSwap and afterSwap deltas move value between swapper and hook (Hooks.sol:248-315), and the hook of a dynamic fee pool can set the LP fee to 100 percent (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
findings.impact: Principal and uncollected fees of every position in the affected pool. A reverting hook freezes them. A hook with the return delta bit can take part or all of what a removal would pay out, up to what the LP's router accepts. Funds in other pools are not reachable this way, because the caller delta plus the hook delta always equals the pool delta (Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312) and each party must net to zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112).
findings.preconditions: The pool's hook address has bit 9 (0x200) or bit 8 (0x100) set, and for taking funds also bit 0. The hook code reverts, returns a bad selector, returns a hostile delta, or is replaced or removed after LPs deposit. LPs must have chosen that pool. This is how the hook design works; I list it because it is a path to a freeze or loss that the text of core does not limit.
findings.mitigations: LPs and position managers can read the low 14 bits of the hook address before depositing and treat bits 9, 8 and 0 as custody risk unless the hook code is immutable and reviewed. Routers should enforce minimum amounts on removal so a hostile return delta reverts. The deployer cannot change this without adding a removal path that skips hooks.
