Its fxChild() is 0x8397259c983751daf40400790063935a11afa28a and its l1Owner() is 0x1a9c8182c09f50c8318d769245bea52c32be35bc. Sourcify holds a match for the owner as EthereumProxy. processMessageFromRoot requires msg.sender to be fxChild and the sender argument to be l1Owner, and then performs the listed calls. FxChild.sol in the fx-portal repository requires msg.sender to be 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001001 and forwards the decoded root sender. It never reads fxRoot. Bor v2.11.0 sends each record from 0xffffFFFfFFffffffffffffffFfFFFfffFFFfFFfE to the StateReceiver through a direct EVM call (consensus/bor/statefull/processor.go, consensus/bor/contract/client.go) and reads the records from Heimdall (consensus/bor/bor.go). Polygon documentation says a record enters Heimdall state after two thirds or more of validators agree. This closes the link the finding left open. The v2.11.0 release notes confirm that Uburu replaced the StateReceiver at mainnet block 96787900 and that the public release followed a private one. That block has timestamp 2026-11-05 14:01:46 UTC and the release was published at 14:45 UTC on the same day. The fee adapter returns the proxy for owner() and feeSetter(). Accrued protocol fees were 539.8 POL and 137.8 USDC. I found a weaker precondition than the finding states. The content of a record is authenticated on Ethereum only by StateSender.registrations. FxRoot 0xfe5e5d361b2ad62c541bab87c45a0b9b018389a2 reports stateSender() 0x28e4f3a7f651294b9564800b2d01f35189a5bfbe, and registrations(FxChild) on that contract is FxRoot. StateSender.register lets the StateSender owner set the sender for any receiver. owner() of the StateSender is 0xfa7d2a996ac6350f4b56c043112da0366a59b74c, a Safe version 1.4.1 with 9 owners and threshold 5. An eth_call of register(0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222, FxChild) from that Safe succeeds. findings.title: Thirteen Wormhole guardians can act as PoolManager owner on Monad and MegaETH
findings.difference: On Ethereum the PoolManager owner is the governance timelock itself. On Monad and MegaETH the owner is a Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver contract (0xe783de89a7f0408687f051e3e6d0beb62719ebad and 0xa107580f73bd797bd8b87ff24e98346d99f93ddb). It executes any list of calls carried by a Wormhole message whose emitter is the Uniswap Wormhole Message Sender on Ethereum (0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a, owned by the timelock). Whether such a message is genuine is decided by the Wormhole core contract on each chain, which accepts a signature set from 13 of 19 guardians and is itself an upgradeable proxy governed by guardian-signed messages. The established-l1 unit reported the same path for BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche in this cycle.
findings.mechanism: 1. setProtocolFeeController is restricted to the owner (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The owner modifier comes from solmate's Owned, imported at src/ProtocolFees.sol:9. lib/solmate is empty in this checkout, so that file could not be read. 2. Thirteen guardians can sign a message that names the Ethereum sender as emitter, chain 2 as origin and the receiver on Monad (Wormhole chain 48) or MegaETH (chain 64) as destination. The receiver bytecode contains checks for emitter address, emitter chain, sequence number, a 172800 second lifetime, destination contract and destination chain. All of them are fields of the signed message. 3. The receiver then calls the PoolManager as owner and sets a controller chosen by the signers. 4. The controller sets a protocol fee of up to 1000 pips per direction on any pool (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32) and withdraws accrued fees to any address (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 5. The withdrawal is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued through a checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55, so pool reserves and claims are out of reach. 6. The Wormhole core at both addresses has a non-empty EIP-1967 implementation slot, so a guardian governance message can also replace the verification logic.
findings.impact: Protocol fees only. The controller is the zero address on both networks and protocolFeesAccrued is zero for the currencies checked, so nothing can be withdrawn today. After a takeover the signers could divert up to 0.1 percent of swap input per direction on every pool from then on. Liquidity provider principal and ERC-6909 claims are unaffected, and no operation is blocked.
findings.preconditions: Thirteen of the nineteen guardians in guardian set 7 must sign a forged message, or the guardian governance path must upgrade the core contract. An unprivileged attacker cannot do either. The honest path needs a Uniswap governance vote through the Ethereum timelock.
findings.mitigations: Treat the guardian set as part of PoolManager governance on these networks. Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated events and owner() on both PoolManagers and upgrades of the two Wormhole core proxies. A governance message through the same path can reset the controller after an incident, provided ownership was not transferred.

An eth_call of setProtocolFeeController from an arbitrary address and from the zero address reverts with UNAUTHORIZED, and from the owner address it succeeds. Both owners are immutable contracts with an empty EIP-1967 slot. NAME() returns 'Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver', messageSender() returns 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a, MESSAGE_TIME_OUT_SECONDS() returns 172800, chainId() returns 48 on Monad and 64 on MegaETH, and nextMinimumSequence() returns 0 on both. The dispatcher has eight selectors: receiveMessage(bytes) and seven getters (NAME, messageSender, MESSAGE_TIME_OUT_SECONDS, chainId, nextMinimumSequence, ETHEREUM_CHAIN_ID, which returns 2, and EXPECTED_MESSAGE_PAYLOAD_VERSION). There is no owner, admin or setter function. The bytecode holds the parseAndVerifyVM selector, the Wormhole core address for that chain, and the revert strings for emitter address, emitter chain, sequence, age, payload version, destination contract and destination chain. The Wormhole core contracts 0x194b123c5e96b9b2e49763619985790dc241cac0 (Monad) and 0xabf89de706b583424328b54dd05a8fc986750da8 (MegaETH) return chainId 48 and 64, governanceChainId 1, guardian set index 7 with 19 addresses and no expiry, and quorum(19) = 13. Both are 680 byte proxies with a non-empty implementation slot. The Wormhole address page lists both addresses for these chains, and the guardian page says every message is a 13 of 19 attestation. On Ethereum the sender's NAME() is 'Uniswap Wormhole Message Sender' and its owner() is the timelock 0x1a9c8182c09f50c8318d769245bea52c32be35bc, which is also the owner of the Ethereum PoolManager. verification.codeCheck: setProtocolFeeController is the only onlyOwner function in src/ (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32, found by searching src/ for onlyOwner). The modifier comes from solmate's Owned (src/ProtocolFees.sol:9). lib/solmate is an empty directory in this checkout, so Owned was not read. Its behaviour is backed by the on-chain calls above and by test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol:42-47, which expects UNAUTHORIZED. The controller can set a fee, and each 12 bit half must be at most 1000 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). It can withdraw up to protocolFeesAccrued, with a checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). I checked that the accrued amount cannot exceed what swappers pay. It grows only at src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70, called from src/PoolManager.sol:238 for the input currency. The amount is computed at src/libraries/Pool.sol:391-396 and taken out of the step fee. The step fee is at least amountIn times swapFee over (1e6 minus swapFee), rounded up (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-74, src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:104), or the unspent remainder (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:82). swapFee is never below the protocol fee (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). So the share is never larger than the fee collected. No owner or controller function touches pool liquidity, currency deltas or ERC-6909 balances. Liquidity provider principal and claims are out of reach, as the finding says. No test covers a cross-chain owner.
verification.corrections: 1. The 13 of 19 threshold is confirmed on chain through quorum(19) on the core contract each receiver embeds. 2. nextMinimumSequence is 0 on both receivers, so no governance message has been executed there yet and the first accepted message would name the first controller. 3. The timeout check reads the block timestamp, which is volatile data on MegaETH. This only lets a caller make its own receiveMessage call revert. 4. Low stands. Nothing has accrued and no controller exists. After a takeover the reach is a fee of at most 0.1 percent of swap input per direction on later swaps, paid by swappers. The established-l1 verdict for the same receiver design on BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche reached the same rating.

findings.title: MegaETH has one sequencer, so an exit from the PoolManager that it refuses to include depends on L1 forced inclusion with a 12 hour bound
findings.difference: Ethereum has many block proposers and no party that can keep a valid transaction out for long. MegaETH has a single sequencer that decides ordering and inclusion and sets the transaction gas cap and size limits by configuration. The only path around it is a deposit transaction through the OptimismPortal on Ethereum, which the documentation says must be included within 12 hours. The L1 contracts that define this path are upgradeable by one Safe with a threshold of 6 of 10 owners, and L2BEAT reports that upgrades have no delay and that only one whitelisted proposer can publish state roots.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every withdrawal of pool funds is a transaction that reaches unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114) and then take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) or burn. The PoolManager has no path that works without a transaction on MegaETH. 2. The sequencer can leave such a transaction out. A liquidity provider then has to send it through depositTransaction on L1. It executes with the L1 sender as msg.sender, aliased if that sender is a contract, so positions owned by an externally owned account or by a contract the user can call from that account remain reachable. 3. During the delay of up to 12 hours the sequencer can include other transactions first. It can trade against the position that is trying to leave, and it can run any hook or token call that the exit depends on. 4. Forced transactions still run under MegaEVM limits. User deposits are not exempt from the compute gas, data, KV update and state growth ceilings, and the sequencer-configured gas cap can change without a fork. Whether a forced transaction can be delayed further by the per-block state growth cap was not determined. 5. A change of the portal or of the derivation rules by the 6 of 10 Safe, or a fork that patches system contract code, could remove the forced path. That requires the chain operator to act against its users and is outside what the PoolManager code can influence.
findings.impact: Liquidity operations and swaps can be delayed by up to 12 hours for selected users or for all users. No funds move without a valid transaction, so the direct effect is a delay and adverse execution during it. At the time of the queries the MegaETH PoolManager held 2.26 ETH, 14.1 thousand USDm and 30.8 thousand MEGA. A hostile upgrade of the L1 contracts would be a wider failure of the chain and is not specific to the PoolManager.
findings.preconditions: The sequencer operator must censor or stall. For anything beyond a 12 hour delay the 6 of 10 Safe or the node software must change the forced inclusion rules. No unprivileged actor can do this. One lead remains open: the per-block state growth cap of 1,000 entries might let a paying spammer shorten blocks for everyone.
findings.mitigations: Integrators should document the L1 forced inclusion route for PositionManager calls and test it on the Sepolia deployment. Liquidity providers who hold positions through contracts should check that the contract can be driven from an L1 deposit. Monitor upgrades of the OptimismPortal proxy and changes of the SequencerRegistry roles.

Removing liquidity touches two ticks, the bitmap and one position with no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238, src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102). The confirmed effect is a delay of at most 12 hours for transactions the sequencer leaves out, with a documented route around it and no loss path. Trading against a delayed position is ordering advantage, which the review rules exclude unless it ends in loss or freeze. Comparable sequencer findings in this cycle (Soneium, X Layer) were rated low. A lasting freeze needs the 6 of 10 Safe or a fork to remove the forced path, which is a failure of the whole chain. 2. findings.title: On MegaETH a caller can make every block field and oracle read revert inside hook and token sub-calls, and one such read caps the rest of the transaction at 20 million compute gas
findings.difference: MegaETH treats block fields, the beneficiary account and Oracle storage as volatile data. Two rules follow that Ethereum does not have. First, any contract can call disableVolatileDataAccess() on the MegaAccessControl system contract at 0x6342000000000000000000000000000000000004. From then on every volatile read in that frame and in all frames below it reverts with VolatileDataAccessDisabled, uses no gas, and cannot be switched back on by a descendant. Second, when a volatile read does succeed, the whole transaction, including parent frames, may spend only 20,000,000 more compute gas, and the cap survives a revert of the frame that read.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager source uses no block field (a search of src/ outside src/test found none), so its own code never triggers either rule. 2. A swapper's contract calls disableVolatileDataAccess() and then unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The PoolManager, the hook it calls at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155 and every contract the hook or a token calls are descendants of that frame. 3. A hook that executes TIMESTAMP or NUMBER in its own frame reverts, the call at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134 fails and the PoolManager reverts at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137. The swapper only stops its own transaction. 4. A hook that wraps the read in an external call and tolerates failure behaves differently. Examples are a price feed read with a staleness check, a read of the MegaETH Oracle or high-precision timestamp contract, or a call into a rate limiter, each inside try/catch with a default branch. The swapper can now force the default branch at will and at no gas cost. If that branch skips a circuit breaker, applies a base fee where a surge fee was due, or accepts a stale price, the swapper trades against liquidity providers on terms the hook was written to prevent. The same applies to tokens that catch failures of time-based accrual inside transfer. 5. Under the second rule a hook or token that reads a block field early leaves the PoolManager 20,000,000 compute gas for the rest of the transaction. The swap loop at src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437 does a cold bitmap read per word and a tick update per initialized tick, so a single swap behind such a hook can cross several hundred initialized ticks before the budget ends. That figure is an estimate from Ethereum compute gas costs and was not measured. The swap can stop at a price limit (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344) and continue in another transaction, and liquidity removal touches two ticks (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238), so no funds are stuck.
findings.impact: Funds of liquidity providers in pools whose hook, or whose token, has a failure-tolerant path around a volatile read. No such hook was identified in this cycle, so no loss path is confirmed. Hookless pools and hooks that read block fields directly are unaffected apart from the 20,000,000 compute gas bound on work after the read.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use a hook or token that catches a failed sub-call which reads a block field, the beneficiary or Oracle storage, and the fallback branch must be more favourable to the caller. Any account can then trigger it. The compute gas bound needs no precondition beyond a volatile read in the transaction.
findings.mitigations: Hook authors on MegaETH should call isVolatileDataAccessDisabled() on MegaAccessControl at entry and revert when it returns true, or should never continue after a failed read. Reviews of hooks ported from other chains should list every try/catch and unchecked low-level call. Routers should set price limits so that large swaps behind time-reading hooks finish inside the detention budget.

verification.factCheck: The MegaAccessControl specification says disableVolatileDataAccess disables volatile data access for the caller's call frame and all descendant frames, that a blocked access reverts at once with VolatileDataAccessDisabled, that the blocked opcode consumes no gas, that a descendant calling enableVolatileDataAccess gets DisabledByParent, and that the restriction ends when the frame that set it returns. Volatile data covers NUMBER, TIMESTAMP, COINBASE, DIFFICULTY or PREVRANDAO, GASLIMIT, BASEFEE, BLOCKHASH, BLOBBASEFEE, BLOBHASH, access to the beneficiary account and SLOAD on the Oracle contract. The gas detention specification gives a relative cap of 20,000,000 compute gas after block environment, beneficiary or oracle access, says detention is transaction-scoped and applies to parent and sibling frames, and says it stays in effect when the reading frame reverts. The overview page gives 0x6342000000000000000000000000000000000004 as the MegaAccessControl address, added in Rex4. On chain the address holds 397 bytes whose keccak256 is 0x96d0f3ba6b474e9684a97e4388ec8dbb7929818b51e6b4f19f885ccbdf642f9b, the code hash the specification gives for version 1.0.0. isVolatileDataAccessDisabled() returns false in a plain call. The latest block's miner is 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000011, so that address is the beneficiary. Not confirmed: the behaviour was not exercised on chain beyond the code hash and the getter, and the client source was not read. No deployed hook with a failure-tolerant path around a volatile read was looked for.
verification.codeCheck: A search of src/ outside src/test finds no block field, blockhash or tx.origin, so the PoolManager's own frames never perform a volatile read. The beneficiary can only be touched when a caller names it as the recipient of a native take (src/types/Currency.sol:48), which is the caller's choice. Hooks are called with all remaining gas and zero value (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). A failed call reverts the whole action (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137), and so does a short or mismatched answer (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). A hook that reads a block field in its own frame under a disabled caller therefore fails the caller's transaction and changes nothing. The PoolManager has no try around hook or token calls, so the only place a blocked read can be swallowed is inside a hook or token that catches its own sub-call. That part of the finding is a statement about third-party code and is sound as a mechanism. The swap loop runs until the amount is used or the price limit is reached (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437). A swap that stops at the limit can continue in a later transaction, and liquidity removal has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238). The 20,000,000 compute gas bound after a volatile read therefore limits swap size per transaction and does not trap funds. No test covers either rule.
verification.corrections: 1. Forcing the catch branch of a try around a sub-call is possible on any chain by starving the call of gas. MegaETH adds a way that costs nothing and always works, since the blocked frame returns all its gas. The finding should say this so the difference is not overstated. 2. The estimate of several hundred tick crossings inside 20,000,000 compute gas was not measured by the finding or by me. 3. A plain account cannot call disableVolatileDataAccess before unlock by itself. The caller has to be a contract or an account with delegated code. 4. Low stands. No loss path is shown, and the hazard sits in hooks and tokens outside this repository.

findings.title: The owner on HyperEVM is a Wormhole message receiver, so a guardian quorum can exercise the owner role
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner acts through the governance timelock directly. On HyperEVM the owner is the contract 0x2d09d0c2f82c59b19b3c65a48ce2c550bf0921f9, which names itself Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver. It executes a list of target calls taken from a Wormhole message whose emitter is 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a on Wormhole chain 2. The message is valid when 13 of the 19 Wormhole guardians have signed it, and anyone can submit it. The protocol fee controller is currently the zero address.
findings.mechanism: 1. setProtocolFeeController is restricted to the owner (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 2. The controller can set a protocol fee on any pool up to 1000 pips in each direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32) and can withdraw accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 3. The withdrawal is capped by protocolFeesAccrued through a checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55), and that counter grows only by the protocol share of swap fees (src/PoolManager.sol:238, src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-398). 4. A party that can produce a valid Wormhole message from the expected emitter, or 13 colluding or compromised guardians, can make the receiver call setProtocolFeeController with an address of its choice, then set the maximum fee on every pool and collect it. 5. The receiver runs arbitrary target calls, so the same party can also make the owner address call other contracts, including CoreWriter. Owned.sol is not present in this checkout, so the ownership transfer function could not be read. The deployed bytecode contains the transferOwnership(address) selector.
findings.impact: Up to 0.1 percent of swap input in each direction on every pool is diverted from LPs and swappers for as long as the hostile controller stays in place. LP principal, ERC-6909 claims and reserves are out of reach of the owner and the controller in the code read.
findings.preconditions: A quorum of 13 of 19 Wormhole guardians signs a forged message, or the Ethereum side sender or Uniswap governance is compromised. The Wormhole core contract on HyperEVM at 0x7c0fafc4384551f063e05aee704ab943b8b53ab3 reports guardian set index 7 with 19 guardians.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can note the bridge dependency in deployment documentation and monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated events on HyperEVM. LPs can watch slot0 protocol fee values of their pools. The loss is bounded by the fee cap in the code.

verification.factCheck: owner() on the PoolManager returns 0x2d09d0c2f82c59b19b3c65a48ce2c550bf0921f9 and protocolFeeController() returns zero at block 51,949,175. The owner has 7,310 bytes of code and NAME() returns Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver. Its getters return message sender 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a, sender chain 2 and own Wormhole chain id 47, and selector 0xe9fa3162 returns 172,800. Its bytecode embeds 0x7c0fafc4384551f063e05aee704ab943b8b53ab3 and the strings Invalid Emitter Address, Message no longer valid and Sub-call failed. That core contract returns chainId 47, evmChainId 999, guardian set index 7 and a set of 19 addresses with expiration 0. The Wormhole docs state that every VAA is a 13 of 19 multisignature and that a VAA has no destination and can be delivered by anyone. On Ethereum the sender contract at 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a has 5,060 bytes of code, the name Uniswap Wormhole Message Sender and owner 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC, the governance timelock. Simulated calls to setProtocolFeeController and transferOwnership on the HyperEVM PoolManager revert with UNAUTHORIZED from a random address and succeed from the owner address.
verification.codeCheck: setProtocolFeeController is owner only (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The controller sets a fee that isValidProtocolFee limits to 1000 pips per direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32) and withdraws through collectProtocolFees, where a checked subtraction caps the amount at protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55). That counter is written only by _updateProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70), called from _swap (src/PoolManager.sol:238) with the amount computed in Pool.swap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-398). The amount per step is at most the step fee, because the swap fee is at least the protocol fee (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46) and the step fee is computed from the swap fee (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-74, 82 and 104). The owner and the controller therefore reach protocol fees and nothing else. Owned.sol was read at the commit pinned for lib/solmate (4b47a19038b798b4a33d9749d25e570443520647). It gives the owner transferOwnership and the onlyOwner modifier and no other power. collectProtocolFees has no lock check. It reverts only when the currency is the synced one (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), which the tests at test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1038 cover.
verification.corrections: The finding says the ownership transfer function could not be read. The pinned solmate file shows that the owner can also hand ownership to any address, so a forged message can make the takeover permanent until governance notices, though the reach stays limited to protocol fees. The effect is a diversion of fees and matches what other units label siphon. The protocol fee is charged on top of the LP fee, so swappers pay most of it and LPs lose the small part of their fee that applies to the protocol share. Severity low is kept, in line with the scale for a privileged actor whose reach is capped at 0.1 percent per direction.

findings.title: X Layer block builder can exclude PoolManager transactions through a rule driven risk control filter, which leaves L1 deposits as the exit
findings.difference: Ethereum has no protocol component that screens transactions by content. The X Layer execution client contains a risk control filter in the block builder. It evaluates every pool transaction after simulation against rules supplied by an external service, using the transaction's logs, call frames and native transfers. A second component drops transactions that emit bridge events for a configured token.
findings.mechanism: 1. All funds of all pools sit at one address and leave only through take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), which runs inside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). An exit is a transaction that the sequencer must include. 2. A rule that matches PoolManager events, calls into the PoolManager or transfers of a pooled token gives a deny verdict. The builder then marks the transaction invalid and removes it from the pool, so it is never included. An audit verdict holds the transaction until the external service approves it. 3. New in this cycle, read on the main branch: the builder also denies a transaction when its capture exceeds an observation limit (10,000 native transfers, 10,000 event bindings or 10,000 call frame observations), when the observed frame stack is unbalanced, and when no rule snapshot was pinned for the block although screening is enabled. With the filter enabled, every pool transaction screened in a block without a pinned rule snapshot is denied and removed from the pool. 4. Deposits are outside the filter. The builder source states that a deposit is consensus mandated and that the rule result for it is reported and never acted on. A user can call the same contracts through OptimismPortal.depositTransaction on Ethereum from the same EOA. Contract accounts arrive with an aliased sender, so a position held by an L2 contract needs an EOA that the contract accepts as caller. Finding F-046 records a separate rule that can void a deposit whose source hash is on the deposit blacklist. 5. FilterConfig::default() sets enabled to false, the filter needs a service URL to start, and the setting is read once at node start. The crate header names a requirement 'OKONE Mainnet RSC'. Whether the mainnet sequencer starts with the filter enabled cannot be read from chain. The public endpoint reports the build reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with xlayer/v0.0.7 and refuses rpc_modules, and I found no operator statement about the mainnet setting.
findings.impact: While a matching rule is active, liquidity providers and swappers cannot move funds through sequencer submitted transactions in the affected pools, or in all pools if the rule targets the PoolManager address. No funds are lost. Exit through an L1 deposit costs Ethereum gas and depends on the sequencer following derivation.
findings.preconditions: The sequencer operator must run with the filter enabled and the risk control service must deliver a rule that matches PoolManager activity, or leave a block without a pinned rule snapshot. Whether the mainnet sequencer has the filter or the bridge interceptor enabled, and which rules are loaded, is still unconfirmed after this cycle. The filter entered the code in release v0.0.7, and operators had to upgrade to v0.0.7.3 by 10 November 2026.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers who hold positions through contracts should keep an EOA controlled path so that an L1 deposit can reach the position. Integrators can prepare the L1 deposit route to the PositionManager in advance. The deployer can ask OKX to state whether the filter runs on mainnet and which contracts and tokens its rules may match.

findings.title: Soneium restricts listed contracts at its own RPC and sequencer, which leaves L1 forced inclusion as the exit for pools that touch a listed token or hook
findings.difference: Soneium has a published policy of restricting contracts it lists for intellectual property reasons and applied it to token contracts in January 2025. Soneium describes the restriction as acting on its public RPCs after a grace period of about 12 hours. Press coverage describes it as sequencer level and reports that users got around it with L1 forced inclusion. Ethereum has no operator who can apply such a list.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every v4 pool on Soneium lives in the single PoolManager at 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32. A restriction on a pooled token, on a hook, or on the router that users rely on stops normal submission of the transactions that call take or modifyLiquidity for the affected pools. 2. Core has no time based logic and no operator hooks, so nothing inside the PoolManager fails. The funds stay accounted and withdrawable. 3. An LP or swapper can still send the same call as a deposit through the Soneium OptimismPortal on Ethereum. The deposit must be processed within the sequencing window of 12 hours. Removing liquidity touches two ticks (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and fits easily in a deposit. 4. If the PoolManager address itself were listed, every pool on the chain would depend on the L1 path.
findings.impact: Delayed exits and stale prices for LPs in affected pools for as long as the listing lasts, with L1 gas cost for each forced transaction. No loss path inside core was found. The Soneium PoolManager held about 1.90 million USDSC, 517,001 USDC.e and 58 ETH at read time.
findings.preconditions: Soneium lists a contract that a pool depends on. The affected user must be able to send an L1 deposit, either from an EOA that owns the position or from any EOA that can relay a signed call to the user's L2 smart account.
findings.mitigations: Front ends on Soneium should document the OptimismPortal deposit path for removing liquidity. LPs should check the Soneium suspicious token list before entering a pool. Position managers should keep a call path that an L1 deposit can reach without an L2 relayer.

sources.supports: Soneium's statement that listed contracts are restricted at the RPC level, that a grace period of about 12 hours applies, and that the blacklist does not prevent access to the chain through other means.
Report that a token was blocked by the Soneium sequencer in January 2025 and that users bypassed the block with forced inclusion through OptimismPortal.
Users can always bypass the sequencer by sending L2 transactions to OptimismPortal on L1, processed within the sequencer window, 12 hours by default.

verification.factCheck: The Soneium post was fetched. It says the affected tokens were restricted at the RPC level, that the blacklisting applies to specific smart contracts on Soneium's public RPCs and does not prevent users from accessing the chain through other means, and that a grace period of around 12 hours applies before a contract moves from the suspicious list to the blacklist. The Blockworks article of 15 January 2025 was read through a fetch service because a direct request returned 403. It reports that the AIBO token was blocked by the sequencer and that users used forced inclusion through OptimismPortal. The OP docs state that users can always bypass the sequencer through OptimismPortal and that such transactions are processed within the sequencer window, 12 hours by default. The superchain registry file for Soneium gives seq_window_size = 3600 L1 blocks, which is 12 hours, and governed_by_optimism = true. Whether the block acted in the sequencer or only at the public RPC is not settled by a primary source: Soneium says RPC, the press says sequencer.
verification.codeCheck: modifyLiquidity, take and the pool library contain no operator switch and no time or block dependence (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184 and 291-297, src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238). A search of src/ outside src/test finds no read of block fields or tx.origin. Removing liquidity updates two ticks, the bitmap and one position, with no loop, so it fits in a deposit. Nothing in core distinguishes a deposit from a sequenced transaction, since the only caller identity used is msg.sender. A restriction outside the EVM therefore delays exits and cannot change balances. I found no loss path that the finding missed.
verification.corrections: 1. The evidence for sequencer level blocking is secondary. The primary source describes RPC level blocking only. If the block is at the RPC, any other RPC or a self run node is enough and the L1 deposit is not needed. 2. A position owned by an L2 contract account cannot be driven from the same address on L1, because a contract sender is aliased. The finding's precondition already covers this with the relay option. 3. The PoolManager balances quoted are USDSC and USDC.e figures that I confirmed in finding 1. The 58 ETH figure was not re-read. Severity stays low: an operational hazard with no loss path.

findings.title: PoolManager ownership on Tempo and Arc is exercised through Wormhole guardian signatures
findings.difference: On both chains owner() is a contract that names itself Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver. It executes calls carried in Wormhole messages from sender 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a on Wormhole chain 2. A Wormhole message is valid when 13 of 19 guardians sign it. Who can act as owner therefore depends on the guardian set and on the Wormhole core contract deployed on each chain (0xbebdb6c8ddc678ffa9f8748f85c815c556dd8ac6 on Tempo, 0xc8ad24fc6063c41cb5c12a8e3851aafc3b3cf027 on Arc), in addition to Uniswap governance on Ethereum.
findings.mechanism: 1. A guardian quorum signs a forged payload, or a flaw in the receiver or in the chain's Wormhole core contract makes the receiver accept a message. 2. The receiver, as owner, calls setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 3. The new controller sets the protocol fee on any pool up to 1000 pips per direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32) and withdraws accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). 4. In the code I read the owner and the controller have no other power. They cannot take pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees and up to 0.1 percent of future swap input per direction. On Arc the accrued amounts at block 32,554,675 were about 43.39 USDC for address(0), 67.88 USDC for 0x3600 and 3.29 EURC. On Tempo the controller is the zero address today, so nothing is collectable until the owner sets one.
findings.preconditions: 13 of 19 Wormhole guardian signatures over a payload the receiver accepts, or a flaw in the receiver or core contract. I identified the receiver from its NAME() getter, its revert strings and its immutables, and did not read its source. lib/solmate is an empty directory in this checkout, so I could not read the Owned base contract that defines onlyOwner and ownership transfer.
findings.mitigations: The deployer should record the receiver, the Wormhole core address and the guardian set index for each chain in the deployment notes and re-check them when the guardian set rotates. Loss is bounded by the protocol fee cap in the code, so no change to the PoolManager is needed.

findings.title: Elysium USDC is a bridge representation whose backing on HyperEVM sits at one address that the issuer can block
findings.difference: On Ethereum the PoolManager holds USDC issued by Circle directly. On Elysium the token called USDC is a standard gateway representation minted by the Arbitrum token bridge. Its backing is HyperEVM USDC held by one gateway contract on HyperEVM, and HyperEVM USDC has a blacklister role. The Elysium token itself has no block list.
findings.mechanism: Step 1: the PoolManager on Elysium holds about 174,155 USDC at 0xb47c4C8F73F009CC0C0d3f92B388d13E293F0B65. The token reports the HyperEVM token 0xb88339CB7199b77E23DB6E890353E22632Ba630f as its parent and the ERC-20 gateway as its minter. Step 2: all 4.03M Elysium USDC are backed by 4.26M HyperEVM USDC held by the gateway 0xd97B30dE0bA0C2eAeE942afce77530e06c5F122c. Step 3: if the blacklister of HyperEVM USDC lists that gateway, every withdrawal from Elysium fails when the gateway tries to pay out, and deposits fail when it tries to pull tokens in. Step 4: on Elysium nothing reverts. sync, settle and take keep working for the representation because its transfer and balanceOf are unaffected, so pools keep quoting a token that can no longer be redeemed. Holders sell it into the pools and liquidity providers end up holding it. The PoolManager code treats the representation as any other ERC-20 and has no way to notice the change.
findings.impact: All pools on Elysium that use USDC, and ERC-6909 claims in it. The PoolManager balance was about 174,155 USDC. Liquidity providers on the other side of USDC pairs lose the assets that are sold to them for the impaired token. No funds are moved out of the PoolManager by this path.
findings.preconditions: The blacklister of HyperEVM USDC, 0x33aa4e959132e49552cb754fb6585bdcdf874beb, must list the gateway. isBlacklisted(gateway) is false today. No unprivileged party can cause it. The same structure applies to every token bridged through the standard gateway whose parent chain contract has a block list.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat Elysium USDC as bridge exposure to one HyperEVM address and watch isBlacklisted for the gateway. Interfaces can label the token as a bridged representation. Nothing in the PoolManager can be configured against it.

findings.title: Avalanche C-Chain folds two storage slot indexes into one, which lets a hook author hide a write path that Ethereum does not have
findings.difference: On the Avalanche C-Chain the node clears the lowest bit of the first byte of every storage slot index before SLOAD and SSTORE touch the account trie. Slot S and slot S with bit 248 flipped are therefore one slot. The set bit is reserved for balances of imported X-Chain assets. Ethereum, Polygon and BNB Smart Chain treat the two indexes as different slots.
findings.mechanism: 1. The rule is in the client: partitionStateKeysHook.TransformStateKey clears bit 0 of byte 0, and libevm applies it in GetState, GetCommittedState and SetState. Transient storage is not rewritten. 2. The live PoolManager shows it. eth_getStorageAt for slot 0x01 followed by 31 zero bytes returns the owner address stored in slot 0, and extsload(bytes32) for that index returns the same word (src/Extsload.sol:10-15). 3. The PoolManager itself is not harmed. Its fixed slots are 0 to 6 (owner, protocolFeesAccrued, protocolFeeController, isOperator, balanceOf, allowance, _pools; src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:11), all with a zero first byte. Every other slot is a keccak256 output or a keccak256 output plus an offset below 7 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:66-73, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:324-326). Two such slots collide only if two hashes agree in 255 bits, which costs about 2^127 hash evaluations to find even for a party that controls both inputs. Raw writes in src use slots derived this way (src/libraries/Pool.sol:544-557, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:73), and extsload only reads. 4. A hook or token is different, because its author picks constants. A contract can keep a guarded value, for example an admin or a fee recipient, at a hand-picked slot C and expose an innocent looking setter that writes slot C with bit 248 flipped. On Ethereum, and in any audit or fork test that runs standard EVM rules, the two slots are unrelated. On the C-Chain the setter overwrites the guarded value. 5. The PoolManager calls hooks with all gas and accepts their deltas (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155), so a hook that gains control this way can do whatever its privileged path allows with the liquidity of its own pools.
findings.impact: No funds of pools without a hook are reachable. Liquidity in pools whose hook or token was reviewed on Ethereum semantics can be exposed to a storage alias that exists only on Avalanche. The size of the loss is whatever the aliased slot controls in that hook.
findings.preconditions: The attacker must be the author of a hook or token that victims choose to use, and must place two constants that differ only in bit 248. No such contract was searched for on chain in this cycle. Honest contracts that use EIP-1967 or ERC-7201 slots are affected only if two of their constants differ in exactly that bit, which was not checked for deployed periphery.
findings.mitigations: Reviewers of hooks and tokens for Avalanche should compare every constant storage slot after clearing bit 248 and should run fork tests against a C-Chain node. Interfaces can warn when a hook uses assembly sstore with constant slots. Core needs no change.

verification.factCheck: I fetched vms/saevm/cchain/libevm/extstate/statedb.go at avalanchego tag v1.15.3. Lines 45 to 56 define partitionStateKeysHook.TransformStateKey, which returns storageKey(key), and storageKey clears bit 0 of byte 0 (key[0] &^= 0x01). Lines 58 to 62 set the same bit for asset balances. I fetched core/state/statedb.go at libevm commit d398bc4dbe41. GetState, GetCommittedState and SetState call transformStateKey at lines 349, 359 and 422. SetTransientState and GetTransientState at lines 478 to 503 pass the slot index to the transient map unchanged, and opTload and opTstore in core/vm/eips.go lines 197 to 214 call them with the raw stack value. The go.mod of avalanchego v1.15.3 pins libevm v1.13.15-0.20261028200218-d398bc4dbe41, so the commit read is the one the tag builds against. On chain at Avalanche block 101090309 the endpoint reports avalanchego/1.15.3. eth_getStorageAt on the PoolManager returns the owner 0x47eb0cf11a1626462da3c830bcde64c3f582b5a6 for slot 0 and for slot 0x01 followed by 31 zero bytes. Slots 0x02 and 0x80 followed by 31 zero bytes return zero. An eth_call of extsload(bytes32) with slot 0x0100...00 returns the owner, so the rewrite applies to SLOAD inside the EVM and is more than an RPC detail. exttload(bytes32) for the same index returns zero. On Polygon and BNB Smart Chain the same getStorageAt and extsload reads return zero for slot 0x0100...00 while slot 0 holds the owner. I found no primary source that contradicts the claim. Not confirmed: no deployed hook or token with a slot pair that differs only in bit 248 was looked for, as the finding itself says.
verification.codeCheck: The fixed slots are as the finding lists them. owner is slot 0 (lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol:17), protocolFeesAccrued and protocolFeeController are slots 1 and 2 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:21, src/ProtocolFees.sol:24), the three ERC-6909 mappings are slots 3 to 5 (src/ERC6909.sol:15-19) and _pools is slot 6 (src/PoolManager.sol:93, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:11). The on-chain reads agree: slot 2 holds the fee controller on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain. I searched src outside src/test for sstore and sload. The only raw writes are src/libraries/Pool.sol:547-556, which writes info.slot of a mapping entry, and src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:67-73, which writes a keccak256 output. Every other write goes through Solidity mappings rooted at slots 1 to 6 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91, src/libraries/Position.sol:34-41, src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:324-326). Struct offsets are at most 6 for Pool.State and 2 for TickInfo and Position.State. extsload only reads (src/Extsload.sol:10-63). Two slots of the PoolManager can therefore alias only if two keccak256 outputs agree in all bits except bit 248, or if an output equals 0x01 followed by 31 bytes that encode 0 to 6. I found no path where a caller supplies a slot index that is written without hashing. The lock, the synced currency and reserves, the delta count and the deltas live in transient storage (src/libraries/Lock.sol:8-26, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:11-37, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-33, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), which the node does not rewrite. The part about hooks holds as written. callHook forwards all gas to the hook address (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-135) and hook deltas are booked at src/PoolManager.sol:181 and src/PoolManager.sol:224. Core never reads hook storage, so a slot alias inside a hook is the hook author's own construction and reaches only the pools that use that hook.
verification.corrections: The actor pool-creator and the severity low are right. Three details. First, the mitigation that asks for fork tests against a C-Chain node is incomplete. A local EVM that loads state over RPC and executes SLOAD and SSTORE itself follows standard rules and would treat the two indexes as two slots. Only execution on an avalanchego node shows the alias. This is my reasoning from the source read and I did not run such a test. Second, the alias adds no power that a hook author lacks. A hook author can already write any privileged path into the hook. The alias only lets that path pass a review done on Ethereum rules. Third, eth_getStorageAt applies the same rewrite, so off-chain tools that read a hook's slot with bit 248 set see the value of the cleared index and cannot tell the two apart from the outside.

findings.title: The MRB hard fork raised the price of seven precompiles by 5 to 40 times, which can push a hook past the 3,000,000 gas fast block
findings.difference: From block 50,988,232 HyperEVM charges 5 times Ethereum's price for ECRECOVER, 10 times for MODEXP, BN254 add, multiply and pairing and BLAKE2F, and 40 times for the KZG point evaluation. Measured on 2026-11-22: ECRECOVER 15,000 gas, BN254 add 1,500, multiply 60,000, pairing with empty input 450,000. The archive client release that carries the change was published on 10 November 2026 and asked operators to upgrade before 11 November 0:00 UTC. The official HyperEVM docs page still describes Cancun without any note on precompile prices.
findings.mechanism: Core calls no precompile: the only raw calls in src are the native payout, the ERC-20 transfer and the hook call (src/types/Currency.sol:48 and 73, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). Pools without hooks are not affected. A hook is called with all remaining gas and a failed hook call reverts the pool action (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). A hook that checks a signature or a proof now pays the multiplied price. By the multiplier a pairing check with four pairs costs 1,810,000 gas, where Ethereum charges 181,000, and each BN254 multiplication costs 60,000. Fast blocks hold 3,000,000 gas. If the hook's check runs in beforeRemoveLiquidity or afterRemoveLiquidity and no longer fits, modifyLiquidity reverts in fast blocks (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184) and the LP has to switch the sending account to big blocks through a HyperCore action before it can exit. A second repricing could put the cost above the 30,000,000 gas of a big block, and then the position could not be removed.
findings.impact: LPs of pools whose hook uses a repriced precompile in the removal path. I found no such hook on HyperEVM. No pool without a hook is affected.
findings.preconditions: A hook that calls ECRECOVER, MODEXP, a BN254 precompile, BLAKE2F or the KZG precompile on liquidity removal, and a gas need above the block limit after the repricing. The repricing itself is decided by the validators through a node release.
findings.mitigations: Hook authors should keep signature and proof checks out of the remove liquidity callbacks. LPs in hook pools should know the evmUserModify action that directs their transactions to big blocks. Integrators should follow the node release notes, since this change did not appear in the HyperEVM docs.

findings.title: A delegated session credential with a TIP-20 spending limit on Tempo can move the account's ERC-6909 claims and pool positions without limit
findings.difference: Tempo accounts can authorise additional signers in the AccountKeychain precompile, with an expiry, optional call scopes and a spending limit per TIP-20 token. A transaction signed by such a signer runs with the account as msg.sender. The limit is enforced inside the TIP-20 precompile and only when the address that moves or approves tokens is tx.origin. Tempo's documentation states that assets other than TIP-20 tokens do not count and that a signer without scopes can call any contract. Ethereum has no protocol-level delegated signer.
findings.mechanism: 1. A user holds ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager, or liquidity positions through a periphery contract, and authorises a session signer for an application or agent with a limit such as 100 OUSD per day and no call scopes. 2. The holder of that signer sends a transaction as the user that calls transfer(receiver, id, amount) or setOperator(operator, true) on the PoolManager (src/ERC6909.sol:25-33 and 58-64). The PoolManager sees the user as msg.sender. No TIP-20 leaves the user's account, so AccountKeychain.authorize_transfer is never reached for the user. 3. The receiver or operator opens an unlock, burns the claims (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22) and takes the tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The TIP-20 transfer has the PoolManager as from address, and authorize_transfer returns early because that address is not tx.origin. 4. The spending limit is never charged for any of these steps.
findings.impact: All ERC-6909 claims of that user in the PoolManager, and positions the user holds through contracts the signer may call, can be moved by a signer whose TIP-20 limit suggested a small bound. On 22 November 2026 the PoolManager held about 426,000 USD of TIP-20 tokens for all users together. Other users are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The victim must have authorised a session signer without call scopes, or with scopes that include the PoolManager or a position contract, and the attacker must control that signer. The actor value is the nearest category: the attacker holds no chain role and needs a credential the victim chose to grant, comparable to a hook the victim chose to use. I confirmed the rule in the precompile source and the documentation and did not send a transaction.
findings.mitigations: Users who keep claims or positions should give session signers explicit call scopes that exclude the PoolManager and position contracts. Wallets on Tempo can warn that a spending limit does not cover claims and positions.

sources.supports: authorize_transfer and authorize_approve return without a check when the account is not tx.origin or the transaction uses the root signer
a spending limit covers TIP-20 transfers, approvals, fees, precompile pulls and burnAt, and assets other than TIP-20 tokens do not count
a signer without scopes can call anything, and a call outside the scopes reverts with CallNotAllowed
execute_batch runs every call of the transaction with the account as caller and origin

verification.factCheck: account_keychain/mod.rs at commit 697ea97: authorize_transfer reads the transaction signer id from transient storage and returns Ok when it is zero (root signer), then returns Ok when the account argument differs from tx_origin, and only after both tests calls verify_and_update_spending. authorize_approve has the same two early returns. tip20/mod.rs: transfer, transferWithMemo and the allowance-free pull call check_and_update_spending_limit(from, amount), which is authorize_transfer(from, token, amount), and transferFrom consumes the allowance without that call. validate_call_scope_for_transaction returns Ok for a signer whose is_scoped flag is unset, so such a signer may call any contract. handler.rs: execute_batch runs every call of the transaction with the account as caller and as origin and checks the call scopes of the signer before execution. The documentation page on spending limits says 'Assets other than TIP-20 tokens, such as NFTs, don't count' and that a transferFrom that spends an allowance the account already granted does not count. The page on scopes says a signer without scopes can call anything and that a call outside the scopes reverts with CallNotAllowed. On 22 November 2026 the PoolManager held 404,991.600244 OUSD and 19,683.832162 pathUSD.
verification.codeCheck: ERC-6909 transfer and setOperator act on msg.sender with no further check (src/ERC6909.sol:25-33 and 58-64). burn lets an operator or an approved spender burn the owner's claim and credits the burner's delta (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and take pays that delta out with the PoolManager as the sending address of the TIP-20 transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The PoolManager is never tx.origin, so the spending limit of the victim's signer is not charged at any step. Core has no notion of the signer behind msg.sender and cannot add such a check.
verification.corrections: No actor value in the schema fits exactly. pool-creator is the nearest, because the victim must have granted the credential to the attacker, and the item is out of scope for the unprivileged goal. The 426,000 USD figure is the whole PoolManager balance and is an upper bound. I did not establish whether any account on Tempo holds ERC-6909 claims. The behaviour is documented by Tempo and is a property of its delegated credentials, which the PoolManager code cannot change. The same documentation sentence means that an allowance given to Permit2 before the credential was issued is also outside the limit.

findings.title: Arc keeps a denylist contract whose owner can keep transactions that name a listed sender or target out of the mempool
findings.difference: Besides the USDC blocklist, Arc has a Denylist system contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000004. Every node's transaction pool rejects a transaction whose sender, to address or EIP-7702 authority is flagged there. The client makes the check mandatory and derives the contract address from the chain specification. Ethereum has no protocol-defined admission list.
findings.mechanism: 1. The owner of the Denylist proxy (0x49ec36db19623e4dadc1aa821cba2d1476f8e859) flags an address. 2. If the address is a user's account, that user's transactions are no longer admitted by nodes that run the stock client, so the user cannot call unlock, burn claims or remove liquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 145-184). 3. If the address is the PoolManager, a router or the PositionManager, transactions sent directly to it are refused. A call that reaches the same contract from inside another contract is not checked, because the list is read at admission only and the execution layer has no denylist check. 4. Arc has no forced inclusion path, so a listed account depends on a validator that includes its transaction outside the public mempool.
findings.impact: A listed user loses access to funds held in the PoolManager for as long as the entry stands. A listed router or PositionManager can no longer be the target of a transaction, so its users must reach it through another contract that they deploy or approve. No funds move.
findings.preconditions: The Denylist owner must act. The denylist slots of the PoolManager, the PositionManager, both Universal Routers, Permit2 and the fee adapter were zero at block 32,584,426. I read the admission rule in the arc-node main branch and could not confirm which release mainnet validators run.
findings.mitigations: Users can hold positions directly or through contracts they control, so a listing of one shared periphery contract does not strand them. Deployers should monitor the Denylist contract for entries that touch the deployment.

A listing of the PoolManager address stops direct transactions to it and leaves calls that arrive through a router untouched. No funds move and no core guard is involved.
verification.corrections: The actor governance is right for the owner of the Denylist proxy. The severity low is consistent with the scale because the list acts on single accounts at admission, is not enforced during execution and moves no funds.

findings.title: Two pooled tokens make their transfer rules depend on the PoolManager address: ELO on Elysium needs a budget set by its hook, and v4CRCL on X Layer pays out only to permitted recipients
findings.difference: No chain rule is involved. These are token designs that exist on these two networks among the tokens the PoolManager holds. ELO at 0xe107e5d99910f544f88ef961e3ca6d88f06f29dd on Elysium stores the PoolManager address and has functions poolManagerGateEnabled, poolManagerTransferBudget, authorizePoolManagerTransfer, setPoolManagerGate, setHook and setBlockedVenue. v4CRCL at 0xd4f64a67b2c1295bd6c25b3a306b2a049e392397 on X Layer has POOL_MANAGER, PERMISSIONED_TOKEN, allowListChecker, allowedHooks, allowedWrappers, wrapToPoolManager and swappingEnabled, which is the shape of a wrapper for a permissioned token.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(X, to, amount) debits the caller and makes the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-75). 2. ELO: a transfer of zero from the PoolManager succeeds. A transfer of 1 base unit or of 10^18 reverts with UnauthorizedPoolManagerTransfer(bool,uint256,uint256). authorizePoolManagerTransfer succeeds when called from the address returned by hook() and reverts for any other caller, including the PoolManager. Both budgets read zero outside a transaction and the bytecode contains TLOAD and TSTORE, so the budget appears to live in transient storage. ELO can therefore leave the PoolManager only in a transaction in which its hook has authorized the amount. A pool that names ELO with another hook or with no hook can receive ELO and can never pay it out, and an ERC-6909 claim on ELO can be burned for a take only when the hook takes part (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). The owner of ELO can switch the gate and replace the hook. 3. v4CRCL: every transfer from the PoolManager to the four recipients I tried reverts with TRANSFER_FAILED, for a zero amount as well, and transfers by other senders revert with a custom error. Payouts depend on a permission list kept outside core. 4. In both cases the failed transfer makes take revert with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86), and the same holds for collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). I found no way for an ordinary account to use these rules against another currency: the checks act on the token's own balance, a zero amount poke changes nothing, and each take is debited in full.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 60,839 ELO on Elysium (about 46,000 USD of pool reserves on the tracker) and 65.98 v4CRCL on X Layer (about 1,800 USD). Holders of these tokens through pools or claims depend on the token owner and on the hook or permission list for every payout. Other currencies and other pools are not affected.
findings.preconditions: A user must hold liquidity or claims in one of these tokens. The token owner, the hook or the permission list must refuse or stop authorizing. I could not obtain verified source for either token, so the function names come from the public signature database and the behaviour from read only calls.
findings.mitigations: Front ends can flag currencies whose transfer from the PoolManager fails in simulation for a plain recipient. Liquidity providers should treat such a token like a hook that can block removal, which the state already records for all chains.

Each take is debited in full before the call and a zero amount take books nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:294, 368-369), so the token rules give an ordinary account no credit and no payout in another currency. Neither is an ordinary account. Severity low stands: the payout dependence on the hook is the hazard the state already records for hooks, and the sums are about 46,000 USD and under 2,000 USD.

findings.title: Tokens whose balance falls with time leave the PoolManager short of what pools record: TURING on Ethereum has lost 73 percent of its pooled balance in 263 days
findings.difference: These are token designs with a balance that decays by a time formula. Nobody has to send a transaction for the balance to fall, and no Transfer log is emitted.
findings.mechanism: 1. Pool accounting records amounts and never reads balanceOf again. take pays out recorded amounts with a plain transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:40-87). 2. Thirteen tokens named TURING on Ethereum lost 0.5 percent of their PoolManager balance in the one day window with no log. For 0x11fb7c5e6fe7e42fb9e28929b673d3eee20048d4 getDecayInfo(PoolManager) returns a stored amount of 999,999,999.99 tokens, a current balance of 267,590,219.70 and 263 days of decay. The contract has checkIn(uint256,bytes), lastCheckIn and hook() among its selectors, so holders who check in keep their balance and the PoolManager cannot. 3. Once withdrawals and swaps have paid out the 267.6 million that exist, every later take of this token reverts in the transfer, and the last positions cannot be closed in that currency. 4. On Robinhood Chain three tokens named PYRE fell 5.3 to 5.6 percent in the window and SMK2 fell 0.39 percent. On Arbitrum One DDL fell 3.7 percent. All without logs.
findings.impact: Each TURING token has a supply of 1,000,000,000 and the PoolManager holds about 26.8 percent of it after decay, 5.3 percent for two of them. The stored amount for the token I read equals almost the whole supply, so the liquidity is the deployer's own. The other balances are small: 9.34 PYRE, 2.12 SMK2, 3.34 DDL. I found no third party funds at risk today. The pattern matters for any future pool in a token with demurrage.
findings.preconditions: A pool in a token whose balance decays. No attacker is needed. The TURING source is not verified; I read selectors from bytecode and state through its getters. I did not read the pool positions, so the split between the deployer and others is inferred from the stored amount.
findings.mitigations: Do not pool tokens with a decaying balance unless the token exempts the PoolManager address. Interfaces can detect them with the reconcile script.

findings.title: The X Layer PoolManager is enrolled in USDG payout group 2, so every USDG transfer runs reward share accounting for it and the rewards go to a third address
findings.difference: USDG is the Paxos reward token. Each account slot packs balance, shares, payout group id and last update time. On X Layer payoutGroupIdOf(PoolManager) returns 2. The claimer and the destination of group 2 are 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72 and the group holds 23.18 million USDG in total. On Robinhood Chain, Ink, Arbitrum One and Ethereum the same call returns 0 for the PoolManager. A cleared item of cycle 3 states that enrolment needs the registrar role or the consent of the account. The PoolManager cannot give consent, so a role holder enrolled it on X Layer. I did not re-read the enrolment functions.
findings.mechanism: 1. A take or a payment of USDG on X Layer runs _updateWalletWithPayoutGroup for the PoolManager: it recomputes the shares of the PoolManager with reward preservation, writes the timestamp and applies a share delta to the totals of group 2 (ClaimableRewardsBase.sol lines 572 to 619). On the other chains the transfer takes the short path that writes two balances. 2. I traced a full round trip on X Layer. The only slot that differed afterwards was the PoolManager slot, where the timestamp field moved from 0x6b03bb26 to 0x6b03bb81 and balance, shares and group id were unchanged. Twenty five round trips in one call all succeeded and left the balance unchanged. 3. Rounding in calcShares is downward on each step, so a round trip can cost the PoolManager slot up to a few share units of one millionth of a USDG. That reduces rewards of the group destination and does not touch the balance. 4. _applyDelta saturates at zero when it subtracts and the additions are bounded by 64 bit balances, so I found no revert that a caller can cause. 5. The rewards that accrue on the USDG that pools hold are paid to the destination of group 2 by claim. balanceOf(PoolManager) does not rise, so sync and settle cannot book them (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). 6. The enrolment adds one revert path that the other chains do not have: _getMultiplierAtTime reverts with MultiplierIndexNotFound when the multiplier record of the group is empty. I did not establish whether an administrator can delete a multiplier that a live group still uses.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers of USDG pools on X Layer (385,837 USDG at the PoolManager at block 76,638,290) keep their principal. The reward on that balance accrues to 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72. Transfers cost more gas than on the other chains. A fault in the multiplier configuration of group 2 would stop every USDG take and payment at the PoolManager, which adds to the issuer powers recorded in F-057.
findings.preconditions: None for the reward routing, which is in place. The revert path needs an issuer side change of the multiplier of group 2, and that part is unconfirmed.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should know that USDG rewards on pooled balances on X Layer go to the group destination. The deployer can ask Paxos and the X Layer operator who controls group 2 and whether the PoolManager should stay enrolled.

verification.codeCheck: take and the payment before settle reach the token only through transfer and balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75, 90-96). Rewards do not raise balanceOf(PoolManager), so sync and settle have nothing to credit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360), and core has no call that could claim or register. The three registration paths in the token need the registrar role, a call of acceptRegisterRewardAddress by the account itself, or a signature checked with SignatureChecker. The PoolManager sends only transfer, balanceOf, the IHooks selectors, unlockCallback and empty calldata, and it has no isValidSignature function and no fallback, so it cannot consent. findings.title: More pooled tokens gate their own transfers on the PoolManager address: AGL on eight networks, PLAYR, MOON, INFX, A3K, LFNX, FIN and four more Securitize wrappers
findings.difference: No chain rule is involved. These tokens store the PoolManager address and allow a transfer to or from it only inside an operation of their own hook or for permitted parties. AGL (AgroLastro, 0x0000000000109de411eabc9f04906d79f06fda0e, the same address on Ethereum, OP Mainnet, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum One, Avalanche and Celo) calls its hook contract PoolAGL on every transfer that touches the PoolManager, and the hook keeps a signed quota in transient storage that only its afterSwap and its own fee collection open. PLAYR on Robinhood Chain reverts with V4NotAuthorized. MOON on Elysium reverts with selector 0x971d2ee1 and the PoolManager address for every nonzero amount. INFX on Avalanche accepts transfers into the PoolManager only up to an allowance that its tax hooks credit in the same transaction. A3K on OP Mainnet marks limited accounts, which receive only with an exception that its own contracts grant, and a transfer back to the PoolManager reverts with AccountIsLimited. LFNX on OP Mainnet and FIN on Polygon revert with the same selector on the return leg, and I did not read their source. v4MSTR, v4COIN, v4HOOD and v4VOLOROST2 on X Layer have the selector set of v4CRCL, which F-059 describes.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(X, to, amount) and a payment before settle both end in X.transfer or X.transferFrom with the PoolManager as one party (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and 349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. AGL: _update calls pool.consumirSaida(amount) when the sender is the PoolManager and pool.consumirEntrada(amount) when the recipient is. Both revert with ForaDaCota(amount, quota) unless the quota that afterSwap opened in this transaction covers the amount. From the PoolManager address a transfer of 1 AGL reverts with ForaDaCota(1e9, 0) on Ethereum, Base, Polygon and Celo, and cota() reads 0. The PoolManager holds between 99.9999 and 100 percent of the 1e21 AGL minted on each of the eight networks. 3. A take of AGL therefore works only in a transaction that also swaps in the official pool, and an ERC-6909 claim on AGL can be burned for a take only then (src/PoolManager.sol:331-336). The free round trip of this unit is not available for these tokens, because the return leg is refused. 4. The quota of AGL is one transient value for the whole transaction. It stays set when an unlock ends with claims minted in place of a take. I did not test what a later user of the same transaction meets, which belongs to the unit on shared transactions. 5. For the other tokens the failed transfer makes take revert with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86) in the same way.
findings.impact: Holders of ERC-6909 claims and any pool that names one of these tokens without the hook the token expects cannot pay the token out. For AGL the liquidity belongs to the issuer and third party liquidity is refused by the hook, so the exposed parties are claim holders and integrators. No path for an ordinary account to block other users was found.
findings.preconditions: A user holds a claim or a position in such a token outside the flow the token author intended. The token author or hook author sets the rules.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces should not offer ERC-6909 claims or hookless pools for tokens that read the PoolManager address in their transfer logic. Pool creators should simulate a transfer from the PoolManager address before pairing a token.

verification.factCheck: AGL: I fetched the verified sources of AGL and PoolAGL from Celo Blockscout. AGL._update calls pool.consumirEntrada when the recipient is the PoolManager and pool.consumirSaida when the sender is. PoolAGL keeps one signed value in transient storage, adds the negated AGL delta of each swap in afterSwap, and both consume functions revert with ForaDaCota(uint256,int256) outside that value. beforeInitialize and beforeAddLiquidity revert for every caller other than the hook itself. On the eight networks (chain ids 1, 10, 56, 137, 8453, 42161, 43114, 42220, latest blocks of 2026-11-23) eth_getCode of 0x0000000000109de411eabc9f04906d79f06fda0e has 15,125 bytes, poolManager() equals the PoolManager of networks.json, balanceOf(PoolManager) is between 99.99999999999 and 100 percent of the supply of 1e30 base units, and cota() on 0x0000000456b76bc801253ef2366664750f602840 returns 0. A transfer of 1e9 base units from the PoolManager address reverts on all eight with 0x7c467237 followed by 1e9 and 0, and a transfer of the same amount from the hook to the PoolManager reverts the same way. I computed 0x7c467237 locally from ForaDaCota(uint256,int256). PLAYR: the Sourcify record of 0x775fd5a987bf3ff5e205deabde6634ddcee3a3fc on chain id 4663 is an exact match. _enforceTradeGates reverts with V4NotAuthorized when the PoolManager is a party and a transient flag is not set. A transfer from the PoolManager address reverts with 0x19e7dcd0, which I computed as V4NotAuthorized(). INFX: the Routescan source of 0xda7ad1b3423713dc9b4275a00d59b82024b3eb0c shows that a transfer to the PoolManager must fit a transient allowance and otherwise reverts with NoHookAllowance(uint256,uint256). A transfer out of the PoolManager address returned true in my call, which agrees with the finding, since it describes a limit on transfers in. A3K: the verified IndexTokenV4 source declares error AccountIsLimited(), whose selector I computed as 0xb8b82b49, the value the finding reports for A3K, LFNX and FIN. Not reproduced: MOON on Elysium, LFNX, FIN, the four Securitize wrappers on X Layer and the on-chain behaviour of A3K and INFX on the return leg. The finding gives no address for these tokens.
verification.codeCheck: take ends in currency.transfer and a revert there reverts the take with ERC20TransferFailed (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). burn followed by take is the only way to turn an ERC-6909 claim into tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). A payment in is a token transfer by the payer before settle (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). core has no bypass for a token that refuses these transfers, and it has no code size or allow list check that would keep such a token out of a pool (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). The gates of these tokens open only inside their own hook operations in the same transaction, and their state is transient, so nothing carries over to a later transaction of another user. PoolAGL comments state the known limit that deltas netted inside one unlock and ERC-6909 claims move AGL between pools without a physical transfer, which matches mint and burn in core (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336).
verification.corrections: Actor pool-creator and severity low stand. The statement that no ordinary account can block other users holds across transactions, because every gate is transient. Inside one transaction the AGL value is shared: a buyer who ends an unlock with claims leaves a negative value, and a later sale of AGL in the same transaction then fails consumirEntrada, which requires a value that is at least the amount. The research file records this as a lead for the shared transaction unit. The entries for MOON, LFNX, FIN and the four X Layer wrappers rest on the researcher's calls alone.

findings.title: BNB Smart Chain runs a call from the system address with its stated value and moves no balance, and no ordinary sender can be that address
findings.difference: On Ethereum as the PoolManager code models it, a frame that reports CALLVALUE v exists only after v was moved from the caller to the callee. The BNB Smart Chain client treats the caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe as a system call: EVM.Call skips the balance check and skips the transfer for that caller, and still builds the callee frame with the stated value (core/vm/evm.go lines 311 to 316 and 342 to 347 on master). The same text is in go-ethereum master (lines 288 to 309), in op-geth on the optimism branch (lines 268 to 303) and in the head of the Celo fork of op-geth (lines 285 to 321). Bor, the Nitro fork of go-ethereum, libevm (Avalanche), revm and the Monad client perform the check and the transfer for every caller. A read-only probe on the 21 public endpoints showed the rule active on BNB Smart Chain only: a call from that address with value 7 and an overridden balance of 1000 left the sender at 1000 and the target at its old balance, while the target frame read CALLVALUE 7. The other 20 endpoints moved the 7 wei or rejected the transaction.
findings.mechanism: 1. settle and settleFor credit msg.value as paid when no ERC-20 is synced and read no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307 and 352-354). 2. A frame entered from the system address on BNB Smart Chain reports a value that nobody paid. If such a frame reached settleFor(recipient) while the manager is unlocked, the recipient would hold a native credit backed by nothing and could take the PoolManager's BNB (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). 3. The client itself calls with that caller in three places, the beacon root call, the parent hash call and the request queue call, each with value zero and a fixed target (core/state_processor.go lines 353 to 429). Parlia system transactions use the block's coinbase as sender (consensus/parlia/parlia.go lines 1389, 2069, 2096, 2110, 2131 and 2137), so they pay value from a real balance. 4. A signed transaction or an EIP-7702 authorization from that address needs a signature for an address with no known signing secret. 5. A system call starts a new transaction context, so the manager is locked. A probe call of settle() and settleFor(address) with value 1 from the system address returned ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d) on all 21 networks. 6. A contract that the system address calls sees the value but receives no balance, so it cannot pass the value on to the PoolManager. No step lets an ordinary account produce the frame.
findings.impact: None today. The PoolManager on BNB Smart Chain holds about 3,794 BNB plus the tokens of every pool that has BNB on one side. Those funds would be exposed only if a later client release or hard fork added a system call that carries value into contract code chosen by users, or let a public transaction type run with the system address as caller.
findings.preconditions: A consensus rule change on BNB Smart Chain (or on a network whose client carries the same rule) that makes the system address the caller of user-chosen code with nonzero value while the PoolManager is unlocked. Client developers and the validator set must act. No ordinary account can meet this.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can keep this rule on the checklist for every BNB Smart Chain hard fork, starting with Jenner on 2026-12-08, and rerun the probe from this finding after each one. A core change that removes the dependency would have sync(address(0)) record address(this).balance and have the native branch of _settle credit the smaller of msg.value and the balance rise. LPs and pool creators cannot act on this.
